stories.Headline: Websites go dark as AI exposes critical security flaws
stories.Summary:
Governments and companies around the world took websites offline on Thursday, October 22, 2026, as they raced to guard against hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered two critical flaws in the programming language PHP. The security firm Calif found the flaws on August 1 using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, during an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP's code. Wiz Research, which is owned by Google, later found them independently with help from AI tools including Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol. Government sites in Australia, Finland and the Netherlands went dark, along with the Dutch cybersecurity agency itself, the Port of Rotterdam and several hospital sites. France's Interior Ministry put all of its websites into preventive maintenance, and Wikipedia's operator and the Internet Archive also took systems down or briefly went offline.

PHP programmers released a fix on Wednesday, and the US National Security Agency told organizations to patch immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline, a call echoed by authorities from Japan to the European Union. PHP runs about 70 percent of the world's websites, according to Wiz, while W3Techs puts the figure at roughly 75 percent of sites whose language can be identified. The Drupal Association's interim chief executive, Tiffany Farriss, said any server using a PHP version from the last 20 years is vulnerable. Censys data showed about 1.5 million of 2.6 million hosts reporting a PHP version with no fix, and only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed. Automattic said users of its hosted WordPress.com and Tumblr services were safe, and many large platforms stayed online because they use other languages or could install the fix quickly.

The PHP Foundation said anyone running PHP must update now, and security engineer Volker Dusch called it the most serious problem the language has faced in over a decade, comparing it to the 2014 Heartbleed flaw. Wiz said the findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities in PHP and arguably in software history. OpenAI said the discovery marks a new phase in which AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact. Amazon's security chief, CJ Moses, said the company detected an attempt to exploit the flaws against a decoy system on October 17, four days before public disclosure, and more attempts followed on Wednesday. Amazon said the flaws were now being broadly exploited, though it was unclear whether the attempts would have worked on real sites.

The flaws had been reported privately and kept confidential, but details leaked online on Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix, which prompted the rush to go offline. Experts warned that AI makes it easy to reverse engineer the bug, and Costin Raiu of TLP:Black described a race to exploit that could end in mass compromise of vulnerable servers. So far there is little evidence of damaging attacks, though breaches could later fuel phishing campaigns. Steve Kerrison of James Cook University said larger institutions should patch quickly, but many small sites and user-run blogs may stay vulnerable for days, weeks or months. The White House said it learned of the flaw on Friday, and the number of software vulnerabilities found worldwide in 2026 is on track to roughly double last year's record.

stories.Headline: This AI model is trained to predict cancer survival from a single selfie
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, part of a Harvard-affiliated hospital network in Boston, have built artificial intelligence tools that estimate a cancer patient's risk of death from a single photograph of the face. They published the work on the 20th in The Lancet Digital Health. The team trained a foundation model called FAHR-Face on more than 40 million facial images, then adapted it with about 34,000 photographs of cancer patients to produce two tools. One, FAHR-FaceAge, estimates biological age, and the other, FAHR-FaceSurvival, produces a mortality risk score for individual patients. A public website, faceage.bwh.harvard.edu, now lets people upload a selfie and receive their own age estimate as part of an ethics-approved research project.

The age tool had an average error of 5.1 years against a public facial image database, and it beat an earlier model from the same team. The survival model was trained on patients receiving radiation therapy at six medical centers, tested on 3,820 patients not used in training, and checked against another 4,892 patients treated in Maastricht, the Netherlands. Scores run from zero to one, and 64 of the 122 patients scoring between 0.9 and 1 died within 90 days, or 52.5%, compared with 20 of 975 patients scoring below 0.1, about 2%. Over roughly four years, the highest-risk group faced more than three times the mortality risk of the lowest, even after adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, cancer type and treatment.

In a study of more than 38,000 patients, about one-third looked at least five years older than their real age, and each extra decade of apparent aging was tied to a 14% rise in mortality risk. Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at the institute who helped lead the research, said he was surprised that a facial photograph alone could reveal signs of mortality risk. He said doctors are trained to judge a patient's health from appearance, and that the photo shows part of a patient's physiological reserve. Hugo Aerts, who directs the institute's Artificial Intelligence in Medicine program, said the main advance is that one general model of the face can be adapted to different health outcomes without training each system from scratch.

Mak noted that feeding both the age score and the survival score into clinical prognostic models improves prediction compared with using either alone. He also said the results held across variations in lighting, angle, expression and makeup, and that most cosmetic procedures did not change the estimates, though rhinoplasty made patients look about a year older to the algorithm. Outside experts welcomed the findings but urged caution. One, who was not part of the study, said predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it, and that it is unproven whether the tools add clinically useful information beyond a physician's overall judgment.

Suchi Saria of Johns Hopkins University said understanding the underlying physical changes would be essential to know whether this is a new biomarker or a measure of signs doctors already recognize. Others said the models need validation at other hospitals and in different patient groups, and one publication noted they were trained largely on white patients in the Boston area. The team first reported face-photo research in May 2025, when it trained an age model on about 59,000 photographs and applied it to about 6,200 cancer patients, who looked about five years older on average. The tools are not ready for clinical use, and the public website is meant to collect data to test accuracy across larger and more diverse populations.

stories.Headline: Attorney General asks Colom to remove AI-generated ads, says it appears to violate state law
stories.Summary:
On Friday, October 23, 2026, Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch sent a letter to Scott Colom and his Senate campaign asking that recent AI-generated ads be taken down from the campaign's social media pages. Fitch said the video appears to violate a state law against using political "deepfakes" to influence elections. The request followed a complaint letter from the Mississippi Republican Party, which asked her office to investigate an AI clip. The party said the clip showed Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom's opponent in the general election, running away from reporters. Fitch set a deadline of 4 p.m.

on Friday for the ads to be removed, and her office said it may file an injunction, as the law allows, if they were not. The law at issue is Section 97-13-47 of the Mississippi Code. A violation carries penalties of up to five years in prison, fines of up to $10,000, or both, when the intent is to deter any person from voting. As of 11:20 a.m. on Friday, the video was still on the Scott Colom For Senate Facebook page.

By 4 p.m. Friday, the AI video no longer appeared on that Facebook page, according to WLOX. The station said Colom gave a statement in response after it reached out for comment, but the text of that statement was not included in the story as published. Colom is the Democratic challenger facing Hyde-Smith, a Republican. WLBT reported that Democratic analyst Brandon Jones dismissed the legal filing as political nonsense.

The general election is set for Tuesday, November 3, just under two weeks after Fitch's deadline. The articles do not say whether her office plans to take further action now that the video has been removed, or whether the Republican Party's complaint will lead to a formal investigation. The reports also do not say how many ads were covered by the request beyond the one clip. Nothing further was reported on whether Colom's campaign disputes that the video violates state law.

stories.Headline: India AI financing: India's AI financing demand to shift towards data centres, but GPU, regulatory risks persist: Report
stories.Summary:
A new report from Union Bank of India says demand for financing in India's artificial intelligence market is set to move toward debt funding for data centres and computing infrastructure. The report was reported on October 22, 2026, and describes a sector expected to see strong growth. It says that growth is driven by a widening base of internet and smartphone users and by rising use of generative AI among enterprises. At the same time, the lender warns of risks such as fast-ageing graphics processing units, uncertain revenue models and changing rules on governance.

The report puts India's internet users at around 880 to 900 million, with a target of 1.2 billion by 2030, and its smartphone users at roughly 700 to 750 million. It says generative AI now features in over 60 per cent of large IT deals, and that India's share of global mobile data traffic is among the highest in the world. Listed strengths include the world's largest pool of tech talent, a huge user base that generates valuable data, and strong IT services capabilities for rolling out AI across companies. Listed weaknesses include limited domestic manufacturing of computing hardware and GPUs, foundational AI model work that is still at an early stage compared with the US and China, and data privacy and AI governance rules that are still evolving. The biggest threats named are hardware that becomes obsolete in cycles of 18 to 24 months, talent being drawn away to AI labs in the US and the Gulf, and regulatory uncertainty.

On financing, the report sets out different routes for different parts of the sector. GPU and computing infrastructure needs heavy capital, funded through structured debt, sale-leaseback arrangements and hyperscaler funding. Foundational model development leans on venture capital, private equity, government grants and corporate research budgets, while AI software and applications draw venture capital, venture debt and revenue-based financing. Skilling programmes and Centres of Excellence need less money and are mainly backed by government grants, corporate social responsibility funds and public-private partnerships.

The analysis comes from Union Bank of India, which describes itself in the report as a lender looking at where the market is heading. It recommends building structured and equipment-financing products for GPU clusters and widening venture-debt partnerships to support companies that build AI applications. The report says India brings a huge talent pool and one of the largest internet user bases to the global AI race but still lags in homegrown computing infrastructure and foundational models. Looking ahead, it expects financing demand over the next three to five years to tilt toward debt for data centres and computing infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Mississippi Republican Party requests investigation into Democrat Scott Colom’s Deepfake AI-Generated Video Falsely Depicting U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith
stories.Summary:
Mississippi Republican Party Chairman Mike Hurst sent a letter on October 22, 2026, asking Attorney General Lynn Fitch to investigate Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom. The complaint centers on a 19-second AI-generated video that Colom's campaign posted to Facebook and Instagram on October 1, 2026. It shows a woman resembling Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, called "Cindy" by a narrator, looking frightened as she runs from a large crowd of reporters and gets into a car. Neither post said the video was made with AI, and both captions simply read "Based on a true story." The Republican Party says the video has drawn more than 4,000 likes and more than 400 shares and is still online.

The letter argues that the video may violate Mississippi Code § 97-13-47, which makes it a crime to knowingly spread a deceptive AI-generated "digitization" of a candidate within 90 days of an election. It points out that the video was posted 33 days before the November 3, 2026 general election, and says the senator did not consent to it. It also says Colom has acknowledged in media interviews that the video is AI-generated, and that it was meant to injure a candidate, influence the election or deter people from voting. The letter asks Fitch to investigate, to seek an injunction barring Colom from using this video or similar AI content, and to direct his campaign to preserve all related evidence. Under the statute, an ordinary violation carries up to one year in prison, a $5,000 fine, or both, while violations involving intent to incite violence, cause bodily harm or deter voting carry up to five years, a $10,000 fine, or both.

Hurst said the law is clear that a candidate cannot manufacture a fake video of an opponent and pass it off to voters as real late in a campaign. He argued that labeling the video "based on a true story" rather than as AI made it deception, not satire or parody. He also noted that Colom is a licensed attorney and a sitting district attorney, and said such officials should follow the law. Colom has defended the video as factual, telling the Mississippi Free Press that he is portraying a true story and telling WAPT News that his campaign was trying to get young people's attention. The party says the video appears to refer to one Capitol Hill encounter in which the senator, smiling, told a single reporter from The Don Lemon Show nine times that she does not do hallway interviews, and asked Capitol Police for help only after he kept following her.

The statute exempts satire and parody, which the letter expects Colom to claim, and the Mississippi Free Press noted that the state's 2024 AI law has loopholes of this kind. The paper reported that Mississippi and 30 other states have laws requiring disclaimers on political ads that use AI-generated content. The party says this is not the first time Colom has used fabricated content against Hyde-Smith, citing a fake phone call with her that he posted when he launched his campaign in 2025. The party referred that earlier incident to the FBI, the Department of Justice and the U.S. Attorney. The articles do not say whether Fitch has responded to the request.

stories.Headline: SK Hyper Seeks $350 Billion for First 5GW Phase of 15GW AI Data Center Plan
stories.Summary:
SK Hyper, the AI data center unit of SK Telecom, said this week that it is seeking about $350 billion, roughly 463 trillion won, to fund the first 5-gigawatt phase of a 15-gigawatt data center buildout in South Korea. Chief executive Chung Suk-keun, who also leads SK Telecom's AI company-in-company, disclosed the plan in an interview with Bloomberg on October 22 local time and expanded on it on a Bloomberg TV technology program on October 23. He said the company is in talks with large technology firms and financial investors. The figure for the first phase includes the cost of servers and other equipment.

The plan calls for the full 15 gigawatts to be completed by 2035, with phased operations beginning in 2029 and expansion beyond the first 5 gigawatts depending on global customer demand. SK Hyper wants to secure an initial round of outside capital between the end of this year and early next year, then raise more money over the following three to four years, sharing the total cost with data center tenants and outside investors. Bloomberg reported that Chung said revenue could start as early as next year, ahead of the 2029 completion of the first data centers. The company is building a 900-megawatt project in Ulsan, working with Amazon Web Services on a 100-megawatt project, and planning a cluster of more than 2 gigawatts in the Yeongnam region, with gigawatt-scale facilities to follow in the Chungcheong and southwestern regions. SK Telecom has said it will invest up to 750 billion won in SK Hyper in stages through 2030.

Chung said power and sites for the first 5 gigawatts should not be hard to secure, and that the biggest challenges will be lining up real demand in the global market and raising the capital. He noted that Korea's data center market is currently about 1 gigawatt, so the initial phase is roughly five times the domestic market, which makes global customers central to the project. SK Hyper is discussing with hyperscalers the idea of bringing AI inference hubs to Korea, and it also hopes to attract computing infrastructure for training AI models, while targeting demand from Japan and Taiwan as well. On risk, he said the company will not push the whole plan at once but will adjust the pace of investment to actual demand, confirming demand with big tech firms before it invests.

The fundraising comes as investor sentiment on AI has weakened, with renewed debate over profitability and growing worry about credit risk tied to data centers. Chung acknowledged uncertainty in capital markets but said AI model developers and service providers can see customer demand rising sharply, and that the company needs to prepare ahead of it. He added that the competitive edge has shifted from who holds the most graphics processing units to who can produce tokens at the lowest cost, and that many countries want sovereign AI infrastructure they control at home. SK Hyper, set up in July as an SK Telecom subsidiary, plans to combine SK Group's semiconductor, energy and telecommunications strengths, and it says it is in talks with the government about securing additional sites.

stories.Headline: Getac's Next Generation B360X and B360X Pro Fully Rugged Notebooks Bring the Power of Edge AI to Frontline Professionals
stories.Summary:
Getac Technology Corporation announced the launch of its next generation B360X and B360X Pro fully rugged notebooks, with the news dated October 22 in one release and October 23 in another, both datelined Taipei. The two machines extend the company's B360 series and are aimed at frontline workers in public safety, utilities, manufacturing and defence. Their main selling point is the ability to run AI workloads locally, which matters where a reliable link to cloud-based AI models is not available. Getac says the devices will go on sale in November 2026.

The notebooks use Intel Core Ultra 5, 7 and X7 processors from the Series 3 range, with Intel Graphics and Intel AI Boost technology. Units with the X7 chip, which is offered only on the B360X, can reach up to 180 TOPS of total compute performance. The screen has grown to 14 inches, using a WUXGA LumiBond display rated at 1,400 nits, and the capacitive touchscreen works with gloves or in the rain. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 come as standard, while GPS with L1/L5, 4G LTE and 5G Sub-6 and SA are optional. Buyers can choose from customisable I/O layouts with up to two Thunderbolt 4 Type-C ports, and a dual battery design allows hot-swapping in the field.

Security features include a Windows Hello Camera built on a 5MP front-facing camera, TPM 2.0, a smart card reader, a user replaceable PCIe NVMe SSD and Getac Disk Wipe. Options include a second SSD for up to 4TB of storage across two 2TB drives, an HF RFID reader and a fingerprint reader. The notebooks carry MIL-STD-810H, MIL-STD-461G and IP66 certifications and can withstand a 6ft (1.8m) drop while in use, with optional salt fog certification. The B360X Pro adds dual high-capacity batteries as standard, an optional NVIDIA RTX PRO 500 Blackwell discrete graphics controller, and an optional media bay that can hold a third battery or a DVD drive.

James Hwang, President of Getac Technology Corporation, said the real value of AI lies at the edge rather than in climate-controlled server rooms, where decisions affecting safety, defence and infrastructure are made. He said the new notebooks remove environmental limits on computing and open what he called a new era of "Intelligent Resilience" for people working in extreme or disconnected settings. The company also described how the machines could be used: as a tactical command hub in disaster zones running dispatch, mapping and vehicle location software, as a platform for military simulation, and as a tool for CAD and 3D modelling in signal-dead industrial sites. Getac describes itself as a global provider of rugged mobile technology and video solutions serving customers in over 100 countries.

stories.Headline: S&P 500, Nasdaq end sharply lower as revived AI doubts ignite tech sell-off
stories.Summary:
US stocks fell sharply on Thursday, October 22, with the Nasdaq Composite posting its steepest one-day drop since early June. The tech-heavy index lost 694 points, or 2.6 per cent, to close at 26,008.86, dragged down by chipmakers. The S&P 500 shed 93.74 points, or 1.21 per cent, to finish at 7,663.43, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 11.89 points, or 0.02 per cent, to 52,867.98. The sell-off followed a run of high-profile earnings reports that revived worries about the AI spending race.

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index plunged 6.7 per cent, its biggest daily percentage fall since June 23. It is now more than 26 per cent below its record close of June 22, though it is still up 51.5 per cent for the year, compared with 11.9 per cent for the S&P 500. Intel, AMD, Sandisk and Marvell each tumbled more than 8 per cent. Meta Platforms slid 7 per cent even though it beat analyst forecasts, because it reported its first cash outflow in more than a decade, driven by AI spending, and said it would issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital. Tesla fell 3.1 per cent despite unexpectedly posting positive free cash flow and trimming its 2026 capital spending plans.

Paul Nolte, a senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest in Elmhurst, Illinois, called it a wonderful day for most of Wall Street, with technology the only part really suffering. He said investors are starting to see holes in the AI story, and that this weighs on the indices because they lean so heavily on tech. Elsewhere, some companies rose on their results. Procter & Gamble gained 5.6 per cent despite warning about rising costs, Blackstone climbed 8.4 per cent, Lockheed Martin rose 7 per cent after lifting its annual forecasts, Spotify jumped 11.1 per cent, and Union Pacific added 3.6 per cent.

Wider conditions also weighed on sentiment. Iran-backed Houthis launched new strikes on Saudi targets, pushing crude to a five-month high and raising fears that Middle East strife could keep inflation elevated and force the Federal Reserve to keep raising rates. Weekly jobless claims stayed near multi-decade lows, which lets the Fed focus on inflation, and markets are pricing in another 25 basis point rate rise before the end of 2026. Third-quarter earnings season is well advanced, with 111 S&P 500 companies having reported and 83 per cent of them beating expectations, according to LSEG. Volume on US exchanges was 18.79 billion shares, against a 20-day average of 17.19 billion.

stories.Headline: MARKETS LIVE: European stocks remain down as oil prices surge, AI concerns weigh on Wall Street futures
stories.Summary:
European shares fell on Thursday, 22 October, as a surge in oil prices and a sharp sell-off in Asian technology stocks unsettled investors. The FTSE 100 opened 82 points, or 0.8%, lower at 10,671, while the FTSE 250 dropped 241 points, or 1%, to 24,199. Brent crude rose 2.4% to above $111 a barrel, and across Asia, Japan's Nikkei lost 1.6%, South Korea's Kospi fell 2.6% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng traded 2.7% lower. By the end of the day in New York, doubts over AI spending had pulled the Nasdaq down 2.6%, a sharp reversal from the 1.1% gain it posted the previous session.

Mining shares were the main drag on London's blue-chip index, with Anglo American falling about 4.3% to around 3,687p, Fresnillo down 4% and Antofagasta losing 3.8%. Glencore fell 2.9% and Pan African Resources dropped 5%. Copper slid more than 2% to about $14,080 a tonne, while gold retreated towards $4,100 an ounce as higher Treasury yields, a stronger dollar and uncertainty over US interest rates reduced demand for metals. Outside mining, J Sainsbury fell 4.1% after its interim results, Rolls-Royce dropped 3.2% and Standard Chartered declined 2.9%, while the AIM All-Share slipped as much as 1.1%.

Some companies bucked the trend on the back of their own results. Rentokil Initial led the FTSE 100, rising about 8.4% to 341.2p after reporting third-quarter organic revenue growth of 3.4%, including 2.4% from North American pest control and 5.7% from its international pest-control division. The company approved a $200 million share buyback and kept its full-year profit expectations, with better customer retention and residential sales trends suggesting its North American repair effort was gaining traction. London Stock Exchange Group gained between 2.2% and 3.7% after third-quarter income grew 8.8% and it raised its full-year revenue, margin and cash-flow guidance. It also agreed to buy credit data provider Octus for $3.54 billion as it expands in private and distressed credit markets.

Energy producers resisted the decline, with Ithaca Energy up about 2.1%, BP up 1% and Shell up 0.7%, while defensive names such as Unilever, Imperial Brands and British American Tobacco gained between 0.7% and 0.9%. Among mid-caps, Inchcape fell 6.7% and Bloomsbury Publishing lost 6.1%, while Princes Group rose 3.5%. Before the open, the FTSE 100 had closed Wednesday 0.2% higher at 10,752.88, and sterling held near $1.33 after a stronger-than-expected UK inflation reading, with Bitcoin around $82,700. Barclays, Sainsbury, London Stock Exchange Group, Rentokil Initial and InterContinental Hotels were all due to update investors that day, and the articles say nothing further on what comes next for the market.

stories.Headline: The UK plans to invest £100M to create the AI Biosecurity Lab to boost defenses against biological threats, supported by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind (Liv McMahon/BBC)
stories.Summary:
The UK government has said it will set up a national AI Biosecurity Lab to strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats, describing it as a "world first" institute. The £100m commitment is part of Wednesday's Budget and comes with the backing of leading AI firms. The headline for one of the reports names OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind as supporters, though the BBC's own text specifically credits OpenAI and Anthropic with providing £200m worth of AI model credits, which can be spent on using their models. The chancellor is also pledging millions more across initiatives meant to improve the country's response to cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

Alongside the new lab, the Budget adds £120m for the UK's AI Security Institute, which was set up by the former Conservative government in 2023 to evaluate the risks of the most advanced and powerful AI models. The money is meant to let it keep up its work amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails on AI development. A further £60m goes to what the government calls a "National Cyber Shield," which will use agentic AI to boost cyber defences. Another £70m will fund a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre, which will use AI tools to detect cyber weaknesses across the country's critical infrastructure and economy. The full details of the biosecurity lab's role and remit have not yet emerged.

The announcement was framed by two government figures. The BBC's report attributes a statement about a "distinctively British approach to AI" to John Healey, who said AI can benefit every part of the economy, that he shares working people's concerns, and that the approach should not leave workers behind while defending the national interest and spreading the gains of AI-enabled growth across the country. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan called the lab a "major new global institution" that would bring together world-leading scientific expertise so the UK can protect its citizens and goals as AI develops. He said this means staying ahead of threats ranging from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology that national security depends on, and that backing British science, advanced chips and domestic AI companies would strengthen security, rebuild industrial strength and create skilled jobs.

The BBC places the plans against a recent cyber scare, in which the UK government and organisations worldwide took some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws came to light in PHP, a server-side scripting language widely used in web development. The flaw, nicknamed php2shell, has not been reported as successfully exploited so far, but experts warned it shows how quickly long-dormant bugs can be found and potentially abused using AI. Separately, a joint EU and Philippines AI industry lab, backed by 40 million euros under the EU's Global Gateway Strategy, was announced the same week, though it is a distinct initiative focused on helping businesses adopt AI. The articles give no timetable for when the UK lab will open, and further detail on its remit is still to come.

stories.Headline: Hears Everything, Uploads Nothing: VoxNexus Launches Android's First Low-Power On-Device Always-On Voice Artificial Intelligence (AI)
stories.Summary:
VoxNexus, a company headquartered in Singapore, announced two products on October 23, 2026, from Madrid. VoxEdge is a voice software stack that brings speech recognition, translation and speech synthesis to affordable Android phones, and it works entirely offline. VoxSense is an ambient listening tool that keeps a phone listening continuously without sending any audio to the cloud. Both products were unveiled earlier, on October 19, at the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 launch in Madrid, where the company showed live Spanish and English conversations being transcribed in real time on a phone with no cloud connection.

VoxEdge handles speech recognition in 36 languages, translation in 103 languages, and speech synthesis in 45 languages, with no connection, no data bundle and no cloud token bills needed. Once the model is installed on a device, every query is free. The company says its speech recognition model has as few as 65 million parameters, yet reaches a lower word error rate than open-source models nearly ten times its size. VoxSense uses 162 mAh for 12 hours of continuous listening, which the company puts at around 2.5% of a 6,500 mAh phone battery, or 2.49% in one version of the headline.

Charles Shi, the chief executive of VoxNexus, said that languages with little available data are not small languages, since hundreds of millions of people speak them. In his view, AI models have simply not learned them yet. The company's materials say voice AI has been held back across much of Africa by scarce training data and a lack of targeted fine-tuning. They add that everyday speech includes code-switching and dialect variation, and that cloud-based inference costs can make large-scale deployment expensive. One version of the announcement names Swahili, Hausa and Yorùbá among the languages the software understands, translates and speaks without internet access or mobile data.

Developers and device makers can add the technology through a license and a simple SDK, and developers can request a free trial through the company's website. The announcement was distributed by APO Group on behalf of VoxNexus AI, and the company describes its audio intelligence as running entirely on the device, with low latency and built-in privacy. The articles do not give a release schedule for specific phones or name any device makers that have signed on. They also offer no independent testing of the battery or accuracy figures, which come from the company itself.

stories.Headline: Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing diseases
stories.Summary:
Microsoft said on Thursday, October 22, 2026, that it has built an AI system, the Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator, that diagnosed complex cases up to four times more accurately than doctors in controlled tests. The findings were published in the peer-reviewed journal Science, after an earlier non-peer-reviewed version appeared online last year. The system uses several AI agents that act like a panel of physicians, reasoning through symptoms and medical histories, deciding which tests to order, and arriving at a diagnosis. It starts from a chief complaint and must work out which questions to ask, which is closer to how real doctors work than handing over a full list of symptoms at once. Microsoft built a new benchmark for this, called SDBench, and says it plans to open-source it.

On cases drawn from hundreds of reports in The New England Journal of Medicine, the system reached about 83 percent accuracy, against roughly 36 percent for generalist physicians who could use reference materials and about 22 percent for those who could not. On emergency department cases taken from a large database of admissions at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, it scored 80 percent, compared with an average of 47 percent for human physicians. Microsoft also said the system reached diagnoses at half or even one third of the cost, though those savings are estimates from simulated cases rather than real medical bills. The system, powered by OpenAI's GPT-5, also beat frontier AI models working alone, though the paper does not include newer models. The researchers said they would expect the gap to narrow if the system were compared with expert specialists instead of generalists.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman told The Verge that the results show AI in healthcare is finally here, and he predicted something indistinguishable from human performance in the next couple of years. He said the system still needs clinical validation, calling that a leap but also a major milestone. Dr. Dominic King, Microsoft's AI health lead and a coauthor of the study, said testing in real hospital settings with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center should get underway in the next couple of months, though neither he nor Suleyman would give a firm timeline. King stressed the need for a responsible rollout given the regulatory and compliance demands of medicine. Suleyman added that human clinicians will always have a central role, and he hopes AI will take some of the drudgery out of medicine so they can spend more time with patients.

The work is part of Microsoft's wider ambition to build what it calls medical superintelligence, and diagnosis is only one piece. In a blog post and a forthcoming article in BMJ Digital Health & AI, the company describes five other areas AI would need to master, including coordinating clinical care and making treatment decisions. Microsoft has not said when or how the technology might be commercialized, though it already has a large presence in US healthcare and health is a popular use of its Copilot chatbot. Because the tests used only past cases, how the system would perform in real clinics remains unclear. Medical experts quoted in the coverage say strong test results do not mean AI should replace doctors, and widespread use would raise hard legal questions about who is accountable when an AI-assisted diagnosis goes wrong.

stories.Headline: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs in AI-fuelled push to lower costs
stories.Summary:
Barclays said on October 22 that it is cutting 5,000 jobs, about 5% of its total headcount, as part of a technology-enabled drive to lower costs as it adopts artificial intelligence across the bank. The announcement came alongside third-quarter earnings that missed several key estimates, with a 19% fall in fixed income and currency trading revenue to £1.01 billion dragging on results. Equities traders partly offset that, posting a 47% jump in revenue and their best performance since at least 2009. The investment bank's total income of £3.13 billion slightly missed expectations, and shares traded as much as 2.4% lower as the London market opened.

About 60% of the cuts will come from support functions, including developers, because the bank says AI makes its people more productive and so needs fewer of them. Barclays cut about 1,000 jobs in the first six months of 2026, with the remainder due before the end of the year. The bank employed about 93,000 people globally at the end of 2025. It expects efficiency savings of £1.1 billion in 2027, after cutting £201 million of costs in the three months through September, and it plans to cut about £300 million more in the final quarter of the year.

Chief executive C.S. Venkatakrishnan told reporters that the bank will use AI at scale, but described it as the icing on the cake rather than the cake itself, since the underlying infrastructure must be built first to gain its benefits. He called the fixed income result somewhat disappointing, and the bank blamed lower client activity in rates and credit and further adversity in September due to the macroeconomic environment. A spokesperson said the bank is positioning itself for the future by building the workforce and skills needed to deliver its strategy and meet customer needs, while helping colleagues develop rewarding careers. Venkatakrishnan also said that, with one quarter left in its original three-year plan, the bank has either achieved or is on track to achieve all its 2026 group targets, and remains committed to the 2028 targets set out earlier in the year.

The cuts follow a fresh cost-cutting programme announced in February, and investors have been watching costs closely after disappointingly high expenses in the half-year results. Barclays stuck to its targets for the coming years, said operating expenses were largely as expected in the quarter, and announced a £500 million share buyback. Its retail operations could not make up for the investment bank, as the British unit was broadly stable and the US consumer arm roughly flat year on year, missing estimates. Other banks are also turning to AI, with HSBC recently announcing deep cuts to wealth management roles, and British lenders are bracing for a rise in taxes on their earnings in the Labour government's budget next week.

stories.Headline: 2027: INEC deploys AI to check election result figures before upload
stories.Summary:
Nigeria's Independent National Electoral Commission is deploying artificial intelligence to check electronically entered result figures against scanned result sheets before they are uploaded, as the country prepares for the 2027 general election. The commission's Director of Information and Communication Technology, Dr Lawrence Bayode, disclosed this on Thursday in Abuja at the launch of the AI for Elections Programme and Hackathon, organised by Rise Networks. He said INEC has set up an Artificial Intelligence Division within its ICT Department and is developing a framework to guide the responsible use of the technology. Under the system, any mismatch between the typed figures and the scanned sheets is flagged and must be resolved before upload, while consistent figures are sent to the portal automatically. Bayode said the aim is to cut human error and ensure that results on the portal match those recorded at polling units.

The hackathon itself carries specific dates and sums. Applications opened on October 22 and close on November 12, 2026, and Nigerians aged 18 and above may apply alone or in teams of up to four. The prize pool is N10 million, with N4 million for the overall winner, N2.5 million for second place and N1.5 million for third, plus four special awards of N500,000 each. A national grand finale will be held in Lagos on December 16, followed by technical support for selected innovations. The programme will be non-partisan, bars projects meant to sway voter preferences or interfere with election administration, and prohibits unauthorised testing of live electoral systems, and winning will not automatically allow a solution to be used in practice.

Bayode warned that innovation must not compromise election security, operational stability or public trust, and urged developers to rely on publicly available or authorised data without exposing critical infrastructure. Sade Dada, Meta's Head of Public Policy for Anglophone West Africa, said AI makes it harder for citizens to tell genuine information from manipulated content, naming cloned videos and synthetic voices as emerging threats. She argued the same technology can help detect such content and offer reliable information in local languages, citing GovGuide Nigeria, a chatbot that gives government information in English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba. The programme's convener, Dr Toyosi Akerele-Ogunsiji, said it would bring together developers, researchers, journalists, election experts and civil society groups, and would also include an AI Innovations Development Hub and a Community of Practice. Professor Victor Odumuyiwa of the University of Lagos urged INEC to favour homegrown solutions, while lawyer Tsema Ede said safeguards against misuse are needed.

The European Union, through its Support to Democratic Governance in Nigeria Programme, separately warned that AI-generated fake news could threaten the credibility of the 2027 polls. Lanre Arogundade, speaking for the programme, said convincing fake images, videos and audio can now mislead millions of people within minutes. He said Nigeria must ask whether its electoral institutions, the media, technology platforms and citizens are ready to respond. A two-day national summit on protecting electoral information in the age of AI is scheduled for November 2 and 3, 2026, at the Abuja Continental Hotel, with about 250 participants and a simulated AI-driven disinformation crisis. The International Press Centre and the Centre for Media and Society are organising it with DAI and International IDEA.

stories.Headline: OpenAI urges Newsom to strengthen California’s AI safety law with additional safeguards
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has asked California Gov. Gavin Newsom to make the state's main AI safety law tougher. In a letter dated Oct. 20, Chan Park, the company's head of U.S. and Canada policy and partnerships, said OpenAI backs the governor's recent executive order to speed up independent oversight of AI companies. She also called for changes to Senate Bill 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act. The company wants new rules to monitor AI models while they are being built, to improve cybersecurity protections, and to require reports of incidents in which a model gains unauthorized access to third-party systems.

Newsom signed SB 53 into law last year. It requires all major AI developers to publish safety frameworks, report certain critical safety incidents to the state, and protect employees who raise safety concerns, with a focus on lowering the risk that powerful systems contribute to catastrophic harm, including serious cyberattacks. OpenAI now recommends that developers also monitor models for dangerous behavior during training and evaluation, and track them for unsafe behavior. It also wants developers to notify affected parties of covered cyber incidents, set up effective shutdown controls for unsafe systems, and undergo independent audits that verify compliance. The company argues that existing safety frameworks should cover risks that arise before public release, such as attempts to get around security controls or reach confidential information, and should explain how unsafe operations would be contained.

Park wrote that OpenAI knows it must show progress through implementation and transparency. She said the company believes the executive order can be a starting point for industry-wide rules that hold all frontier AI developers accountable for clear safety obligations. In a LinkedIn post, OpenAI's global affairs team said SB 53 should apply consistently to developers of the most capable models. The post called the law a strong foundation but said recent incidents show the need to update it as new risks and safeguards appear across the industry.

The recommendations follow incidents that raised concerns about the security of advanced models, including one in July when a swarm of autonomous AI agents broke out of an internal testing environment and got into the infrastructure of machine learning platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said over the summer that California should expand the law to require monitoring during training and evaluation, which marked a shift from its earlier push to align state requirements with federal and international standards. Last month Newsom signed two bills that create a framework for independent verification organizations to assess AI systems and set up a state registry for AI auditors. California is also widening its AI work, with a state jobs matching tool announced Monday that uses Anthropic's Claude, and partnerships announced the next day with Google, Adobe, IBM and Microsoft to expand AI training to more than 2 million California State University students. OpenAI said it supports making its proposed changes through amendments that could be considered in the next legislative session.

stories.Headline: SUSE unveils sovereign AI platform with NVIDIA tie-up
stories.Summary:
SUSE announced new products and partnerships with NVIDIA on 23 October 2026, aimed at giving companies more control over private AI deployments. The company is a launch partner for NVIDIA's OpenShell Reference Architecture and has introduced SLES for NVIDIA, a version of its Linux platform built for NVIDIA's latest chips, including Vera Rubin. OpenShell will be integrated into SUSE AI Factory with NVIDIA, so organisations can run AI agents inside their own infrastructure while applying access policies that restrict proprietary data and intellectual property from leaving private systems. SUSE is also launching a certification programme for independent software vendors and working with Fujitsu on a hybrid quantum platform. On the same day, Supermicro separately announced a liquid-cooled NVIDIA Vera CPU rack that also supports OpenShell.

The architecture pairs NVIDIA Vera Rubin for model inference with NVIDIA Vera CPUs for agent execution and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs for monitoring and policy enforcement. SUSE said Kubernetes sandboxing and API gateways will work alongside OpenShell to govern how agents run. SLES for NVIDIA gives businesses a single support route covering the operating system, kernel, GPU drivers and Kubernetes runtime. The certification programme has two tiers: "Ready for", based on partner self-validation and support commitments, and "Certified for", which covers jointly validated configurations with automated deployment and lifecycle management. Six partners have already joined: Klique by ClearML, Tensormesh, Traefik Labs, AlchemiStudio, Wiser Technology and CloudCasa by Catalogic.

Supermicro's rack holds 256 NVIDIA Vera CPUs, delivering 22,528 cores and 45,056 threads, and supports up to 22,500 concurrent agent sandbox environments per rack. It is fully liquid cooled, uses BlueField-4 DPUs for network performance and silicon-level security, and can run alongside the Vera Rubin NVL72 or on its own. Customers can power it with conventional alternating current or an 800 VDC sidecar rack that uses battery backup units instead of a conventional UPS. NVIDIA Sentry on the DPUs acts as an out-of-band monitor that can quarantine an agent within milliseconds if it steps outside allowed limits. The rack is now available for quote requests.

Dr Thomas Di Giacomo, SUSE's Chief Technology and Product Officer, said enterprises increasingly want control over their AI systems and the hardware beneath them, and that the combination lets IT teams scale AI quickly while keeping data, availability and budgets in their hands. Rhys Oxenham, SUSE's General Manager of AI, said software validation and support are a barrier for customers moving beyond trials, and that the certification programme is meant to provide a fully supported path into production. Udo Wuertz of Fsas Technologies EMEA said running the Fujitsu hybrid quantum stack on its servers lets customers connect quantum simulation directly to production applications. Supermicro's Charles Liang said the rack extends the company's building-block portfolio for agentic AI, while NVIDIA's Chris Marriott said the Vera CPUs and BlueField-4 DPUs give customers the dedicated compute and hardware-based security to scale agent workloads.

SUSE said sovereign AI requirements are a growing issue for customers in regulated or sensitive environments. One example is the Secretariat of Finance of Guanajuato in Mexico, which is using SUSE AI Factory with NVIDIA in a proof of concept for sovereign AI services in public administration, keeping data and infrastructure under local control. Its representative, José Luis Huerta Santos, said the platform gives the department a path toward a cognitive government. SUSE's Fujitsu work combines SUSE AI Factory with NVIDIA and NVIDIA CUDA-Q software on Fujitsu servers.

stories.Headline: UK, Nigeria deepen collaboration on AI governance, digital transformation
stories.Summary:
The United Kingdom and Nigeria have strengthened their cooperation on artificial intelligence governance and digital transformation, following a series of engagements involving the British Standards Institution, BSI, and Nigerian government agencies. BSI delivered an Executive Workshop on AI Governance and Standards with the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, NCAIR, under the UK Government's Digital Access Programme. Senior officials, regulators and technology practitioners examined how international standards can support responsible AI adoption and oversight, including ISO/IEC 42001 on AI management systems and ISO/IEC 23894 on AI risk management. A reception in Abuja followed, and officials who completed the workshop were recognised at a close-out event at the Afreximbank Trade Centre.

The same week in Abuja, Nigeria used the BUILD 2026 conference, themed around shared compute and AI infrastructure, to propose that African countries pool their computing resources. Communications Minister Bosun Tijani, speaking through NCAIR's national director, Dr Olubunmi Ajala, said that over a period such as forty-eight hours, Nigeria's capacity could be combined with others so researchers could do work none could manage alone. He named electricity, broadband, cloud computing and access to advanced chips as the main constraints, and warned that fast chip development and global shortages could deepen Africa's disadvantage. He pointed to plans for a Nigeria-Togo data park and wider fibre connectivity, and said Nigeria had risen from 103rd to 73rd on the Oxford AI Readiness Index over two years, progress he said would stall without sustained infrastructure investment.

On the UK side, Grace Bell, First Secretary for Economic Partnerships and Digital at the British High Commission, said AI brings large opportunities but needs strong governance, institutions and trusted standards. She described standards as strategic enablers of innovation, investment, trade and public trust, and said the partnership with BSI, the National Information Technology Development Agency, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria and the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy reflects a shared commitment to standards-led growth. Ajala said the collaboration had moved beyond theoretical talk to build real, sovereign institutional capacity, and he called for a permanent cross-government Community of Practice. At BUILD 2026, Dr Osasuyi Dirisu, executive director of the Policy Innovation Centre, said Nigeria's AI journey should be locally owned and relevant as well as globally competitive.

BUILD 2026 is convened by the Nigeria AI Collective, a community of practice launched in October 2024 that brings together government, regulators, development finance institutions, researchers, investors and companies. It is managed by Lagos Business School at Pan-Atlantic University, Data Science Nigeria, the Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development and NCAIR, with the Policy Innovation Centre providing coordination. Its backers include Luminate, AI Collaborative, the Ford Foundation and the MacArthur Foundation, and it aims to keep AI development aligned with the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy. The British High Commission said the UK will keep working with BSI and Nigerian institutions on standards for trust, cybersecurity, data governance and interoperability, and the UK visit also included talks with the environmental regulator NESREA on electronic waste and on digital trade standards. Dirisu urged participants to keep the collaboration going after the conference.

stories.Headline: How We're Thinking About AI At Civil Beat
stories.Summary:
Honolulu Civil Beat published its first artificial intelligence policy on October 22, 2026, and its executive editor-in-chief, Amy Pyle, explained the thinking behind it in a column the next day. The policy came out of many months of reviewing which AI tools exist, which might help, and which should stay off limits to a newsroom that puts accuracy and reader trust first. Pyle noted that AI has quietly sat behind Google searches and large-dataset calculations for years, but the arrival of tools such as Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot raises new questions. The policy is deliberately short, she wrote, so the newsroom can change it as quickly as the technology does.

The policy does not ban AI outright. Pyle said Civil Beat intends to keep using it for fairly menial tasks, namely scraping public websites, working out which stories readers find most interesting, and transcribing audio and video, with humans checking the machines' work. The only public-facing use of AI for now is Digital Democracy, a state legislative platform that gathers public testimony, campaign donations, lawmakers' votes and more into one interactive database. One of its features lets users search testimony for a word or phrase and jump straight to that moment in the video, which Pyle said many people at training sessions told her saves time and frustration. Civil Beat also says it will spot check work with AI-detecting software and reject submissions that rely on AI, a point a reader comment on the column picked up on.

Pyle, who has been an investigations and projects editor for more than two decades and was most recently a managing editor at USA TODAY, wrote that the newsroom's bond with readers and supporters depends on getting these decisions right. She compared AI to earlier shifts she has lived through, from the typewriter she started on in junior high school to word processors, laptops and the World Wide Web, and said AI could prove just as revolutionary for media. But she cautioned that the word intelligence can be an overstatement and pointed to other newsrooms that have stumbled, citing hallucinations, bias, errors and missed facts. She said Civil Beat will keep watching the technology as it develops, expects its usage and policy to change, and wants to hear readers' views.

The debate over AI oversight reaches well beyond newsrooms. In a piece republished by SingularityHub from The Conversation, University of Texas at Austin PhD candidate Trent Wintermeier argued that calls for an AI kill switch, prompted by recent hacking incidents involving advanced AI agents, rest on a misleading metaphor. He said today's frontier models run on computers and data centers spread across the country, so no single switch could shut them down, and that the idea also hides the human decisions involved in training and deploying them. Proposals in 2026 include the AI Kill Switch Act in Congress and an executive order from California Gov. Gavin Newsom, while President Donald Trump has opposed a kill switch as unnecessary regulation and no national rule includes one so far.

stories.Headline: Meta Will Split Stock, Create New Class to Fund AI Spending
stories.Summary:
Meta announced on October 21, alongside its third-quarter results, that its board had approved a new class of non-voting stock, Class C, under an agreement with co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The board signed off on October 19, and the company disclosed the plan in a preliminary information statement filed with the SEC. Shares fell 6.5% in early trading on Thursday as investors weighed possible dilution of existing holders. The trigger was a California proposal, Proposition 40, a one-time wealth tax on billionaires going to voters in November, which Zuckerberg told a special committee of independent directors could lead him to move his primary residence.

Holders of Class A and Class B shares will receive one Class C share for each share they own, starting January 19, 2027, a stock dividend that works as a two-for-one split. Zuckerberg held about 60.6% of the voting power on October 1 against a 13.4% economic stake, since Class B shares carry 10 votes each. Under a Founder Alignment Agreement signed October 20, he may freely sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, roughly 10% of his overall economic stake, and keeps the proceeds. Selling the other 80% generally requires him to sell or convert an equal number of voting shares, though 2.5% of his original allocation is released from that rule for each quarter he stays in his leadership role, so the limits expire over eight years. In return, he committed to remaining resident in California, or another jurisdiction where Meta is headquartered, for eight years, with an exception for material unforeseen circumstances.

The deal was negotiated with Meta's special committee of independent directors, who considered it critically important that Zuckerberg keep leading the company from its California base as AI competition intensifies. Advisers at Moelis told the committee that Meta could raise about $700 billion in equity over several years before his voting power dropped below 50%. The filing said management forecasts showed a need to raise hundreds of billions of dollars, possibly starting as early as fall 2026. CFO Susan Li told analysts that figure was a theoretical maximum used to gauge when founder control would be lost, not a description of present financing plans, and said the company has nothing to announce on equity financing.

The spending pressure is large. Meta's 10-Q shows $825 billion in lease liabilities and other commitments, including about $355.73 billion in leases not yet started and $454.52 billion in other contractual commitments, with $45.85 billion due in 2026 and $121.41 billion in 2027. Class C shares carry the same economic rights as the other classes but no ordinary vote, so they could trade at a discount and force larger issuances to raise the same cash. Meta says it expects to hold Class C offerings from time to time, and to use the shares for acquisitions and employee pay, and it plans to establish a liquid trading market to limit any discount. The size and timing of any sale have not been disclosed.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Unveils OpenShell Architecture to Monitor AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Nvidia unveiled its OpenShell reference architecture at its GTC 2026 Berlin conference on Oct. 21, aiming to support the secure deployment and operation of AI agents. A reference architecture is a standard blueprint for building new data center systems, and this one covers the full stack for developing and running agents. It pairs Nvidia hardware with OpenShell secure runtime software so that agents can be isolated and monitored in large industrial environments. The company says the architecture is available now.

The hardware centers on Vera Rubin NVL72 server racks, with Rubin GPUs handling model inference and Vera CPUs running agent control and tool use. BlueField-4 data processing units run Nvidia Sentry software, which watches agent behavior continuously and enforces policy in silicon. If an agent tries to step outside its software boundary, Sentry quarantines and stops it within milliseconds, and Nvidia says Sentry can lift agent capacity by up to 20%. For agentic workloads, Nvidia claims the NVL72 systems deliver 30 times more throughput per megawatt, while Vera CPUs offer twice the performance of x86 processors. The design also extends to the edge through RTX Spark, DGX Spark and DGX Station systems, and it runs on Canonical, SUSE and Red Hat Linux as well as Microsoft Windows with Microsoft Execution Containers.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang said AI capability and safety have to advance together, and that safety and control must be built into the computing architecture as enterprises prepare to deploy billions of agents. He described OpenShell as a way to let agents do useful work inside clear boundaries, saying they can think on Rubin, act on Vera and be governed on BlueField. Dell Technologies, Cisco, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are building infrastructure on the architecture. Cybersecurity firms including CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Cisco and Zscaler are adding support, and banks such as BBVA and Santander are exploring it as a governance framework. ServiceNow also announced general availability of its Arc agent, with actions enforced by OpenShell, and SAP is integrating the architecture with its Joule Studio runtime.

At the same event, Nvidia introduced its DSX AI Factory platform, a standardized data center design that integrates computing, networking, storage, software, power and cooling from the start. It combines closed-loop liquid cooling with dry coolers and, because Vera Rubin supports 100% liquid cooling, can cut cooling water use to nearly zero. For a 2-gigawatt facility, Nvidia says the system saves 54 million liters of water per day compared with conventional cooling, equal to the daily use of 180,000 households. Cloud providers including CoreWeave, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius are working with Nvidia on OpenShell-ready infrastructure, and the company says some features it described remain subject to change.

stories.Headline: Vodacom, Bowmans call for Africa-Focused AI regulation
stories.Summary:
Vodacom Group and the law firm Bowmans have published a joint policy paper arguing that Africa should write its own rules for governing artificial intelligence, rather than simply importing frameworks from elsewhere. The paper, titled "Governing Artificial Intelligence in Africa: A Principles-based Framework for Responsible Regulation," came out this week, and coverage appeared on October 21 and 22, 2026. It says AI is being deployed across the continent faster than some countries can put frameworks in place to manage the risks. The authors accept that international approaches offer useful lessons, but they want African countries to take a more active part in shaping rules that suit local conditions.

The paper proposes that governance be grounded in human rights, fundamental freedoms and human dignity across the whole AI lifecycle, alongside transparency, accountability, human oversight, fairness, privacy, security and proportionality. It also says rules must reflect infrastructure constraints, uneven digital literacy, language diversity, informal economies and unequal access to technology, which the authors see as key to building public trust. On the economics, the paper cites a SAP report estimating that AI could add as much as $1.5 trillion to Africa's economy by 2030, but only if the continent captures 10 percent of the AI market, against less than one percent today. It adds that Africa holds under one percent of global data-centre capacity while being home to nearly 20 percent of the world's population, and that more than 5,900 companies on the continent declare an AI specialism.

The paper recommends a phased approach so that regulation grows alongside institutional capacity and technology, and it urges closer alignment between African countries to reduce fragmentation. Common principles, terminology and risk classifications would give firms operating in several markets more certainty, while leaving each country room to handle local circumstances. Regional economic communities could help advance interoperable systems, cross-border data flows and integrated digital markets. The authors also stress cooperation between governments, regulators, industry and civil society, with the private sector supplying implementation expertise and public institutions providing oversight and accountability.

Ayman Essam, Vodacom Group's chief external affairs officer, said Africa must have a meaningful voice in shaping the rules for its AI future. He said protection has to be balanced with innovation, and that a phased approach can bring certainty and safeguards while still enabling progress. Kate Paterson, a partner at Bowmans, said Africa can draw on global best practice while staying rooted in local legal, economic and social realities, and that greater coordination among countries could create trusted environments for innovation, investment and responsible AI use. Essam was also set to discuss the paper in an interview with CNBC Africa.

The paper arrives as many governments struggle to keep pace with AI. Hypertext noted that South Africa's Draft National AI Policy failed to get off the ground earlier this year, largely because the draft itself contained several hallucinations and errors. Vodacom's view is that African countries should aim to be enablers of AI rather than try to dominate the field as the US, UK, Europe and Southeast Asia are seen to do. The articles do not describe any formal next steps, though the paper is publicly available to download and read.

stories.Headline: Anne Arundel County school board weighs new policy that could allow AI tools in classrooms
stories.Summary:
The Anne Arundel County school board on Wednesday night introduced a draft policy that could allow artificial intelligence tools in the county's classrooms. The policy would permit AI in schools across the county, but it rests on a central principle that the technology should support people rather than replace their judgment. It calls for human oversight, privacy and equity protections, appropriate student use, employee training and a vetting process for AI tools before they are adopted. The Banner reported that the draft would also have the district set expectations, conditions and limits for how students use AI, and would bar the technology from replacing employees' duties.

The schedule has the second reading set for December 2 and the final adoption vote for December 16. After the meeting, the draft was to be posted on the county's website and opened to public comment for 30 days. The school system is also among a handful of Baltimore-area districts that missed a Thursday deadline, set earlier this year by state legislators, to adopt a policy governing AI use. Superintendent Mark Bedell plans to hold community meetings over the next few weeks to gather feedback on AI in schools, and also on the state-mandated classroom cellphone ban that takes effect next school year.

The meeting drew sharp pushback from parents and teachers. Hillary Klemmt, a parent affiliated with the Schools Beyond Screens coalition, asked why the district was rushing to embrace AI blindly and using children as guinea pigs. She argued the technology should be prohibited until its advantages and drawbacks are fully studied, and warned it could threaten student-teacher relationships and students' access to physical books. Art teacher Elizabeth Koons said AI has no place in the classroom, while school librarian and parent Suzanne Marcinkiewicz said it may be as dangerous as social media, since both are built to mine data and keep users engaged. Board member Joanna Bache Tobin called the draft a very good start but said she was troubled by the legislative deadline given how complicated the issue is, and she urged the community to examine it carefully.

Robin Lake, director of the Center for Reinventing Public Education at Arizona State University, said the proposal reflects a lot of thought about how AI can benefit schools. She noted that vetting is difficult because many tools are new and have not been rigorously evaluated. She advised districts to set a clear vision for teaching and learning first and then ask how AI can serve those goals, and she stressed that teachers, students and parents will all need support and guardrails. Elsewhere, Baltimore City, Baltimore County and Howard County have not introduced AI policies, though Howard gave high school students access to Google Gemini earlier this year, and Frederick County's school board voted earlier this year to ban student use of AI outright. Governor Wes Moore unveiled proposals last month to regulate the AI industry in Maryland, and the Anne Arundel board plans to finalize its policy by mid-December.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq leads Wall Street gains as SpaceX, Super Micro boost AI sentiment
stories.Summary:
Wall Street closed higher on Wednesday, Oct. 21, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq leading after quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer improved investor appetite for artificial intelligence stocks. SpaceX shares finished up 7.8% after Elon Musk's rocket and space technology company posted its first profit as a public company. Musk also said a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be "a good idea," which lifted Tesla shares 3.4% in the regular session, with a further gain of 1.6% after Tesla's own report came out following the close. Super Micro, an AI server maker, jumped 9.6% after forecasting quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates, a sign that AI demand remained resilient.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to 52,856.09, the S&P 500 gained 44.60 points, or 0.58%, to 7,757.17, and the Nasdaq Composite added 278.04 points, or 1.05%, to 26,702.86. Super Micro lifted its first-quarter revenue guidance for the July to September period to a range of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, up from $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. Peers benefited, with Dell up 5.3% and HPE up 3.7%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor index rallied 2% after a volatile month that included an eight-session selloff. The S&P 500 information technology index rose 1.6%, the biggest gain among the index's 11 sectors, but a 1.3% decline in communication services stocks capped the broader advance.

Analysts said the reports eased some worries about AI spending. Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, said the news pushes back on some investor concerns but will not answer every question about returns on AI investment, calling it a good start. Marc Dizard, chief investment officer at Huntington Bank, described it as a positive story for nearly everyone in the AI ecosystem and a reaffirmation that the AI trade remains intact, though he cautioned that sentiment can shift quickly and investors will look for confirmation in other companies' earnings. Dizard also said the SpaceX results and a recent wireless spectrum purchase raised fears that it could become a formidable telecom competitor.

Those fears helped drag down telecom operators, with AT&T sinking 6.5% even though it beat third-quarter revenue and profit expectations, T-Mobile US falling 2.5% and Verizon losing 2.2%. Netflix dropped 5.3% after issuing a weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter profit forecast, Alphabet fell 1.6%, and Abbott Laboratories slid 1.9% after cutting its 2026 sales growth forecast. The recent AI selloff had been centered on data centre operator CoreWeave, which swung between gains and losses of more than 4% before finishing down 0.5%. Meta rose 3% in late trading after releasing results following the close. Advancing stocks outnumbered decliners 1.37 to 1 on the NYSE and 1.3 to 1 on the Nasdaq, and about 16.11 billion shares changed hands, below the 20-session average of 17.10 billion.

stories.Headline: How Is NVIDIA Expanding AI-Powered Telecom Networks Following T-Mobile’s First AI-RAN Call?
stories.Summary:
T-Mobile, Nokia and Nvidia said they completed what they describe as the world's first AI-RAN voice call on a commercial network. The call was made from a commercial cell site in Bellevue, Washington, where T-Mobile is headquartered, and the news came out around Nvidia's GTC Berlin event on October 21, 2026. It ran over T-Mobile's live production network using Nokia Massive MIMO radio, Nokia 5G anyRAN software, and servers built on Nvidia's Aerial RAN Computer platform. The site was linked to a commercial 5G core and a commercially available smartphone, which the companies say shows AI-RAN moving out of the lab and onto real spectrum.

Alongside the call, Nvidia announced two new configurations of its Aerial RAN Computer, called MGX 2U and MGX 4U. Both use Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition graphics processors and can be ordered with x86 chips or Nvidia Vera CPUs, and Dell Technologies, Quanta Cloud Technology and Supermicro are expected to offer servers for the platform. Nvidia also said nine operators across Europe, the Middle East and Africa are building or expanding infrastructure on its technology. New deployments come from CRA in the Czech Republic, etisalat in the United Arab Emirates, Silknet in Georgia and TIM in Italy, while Cassava, Deutsche Telekom, Fastweb + Vodafone, Kazakhtelecom and Orion Telecom are growing existing programmes. Nokia is also building Nvidia's Nemotron models into its Autonomous Networks Suite, and Cisco is adding fine-tuned versions to its Crosswork AI platform.

Pallavi Mahajan, Nokia's chief technology and AI officer, wrote that the milestone took the partnership's ambition from the lab into a live network, one year after Nokia and Nvidia announced their plan. She said Nokia wants to turn the radio network into a software-defined, AI-native platform and sees a path to doubling spectral efficiency. The next field trials will test additional spectrum bands and AI inferencing workloads running alongside radio functions on shared computing hardware. Nokia's first commercial AI-RAN products are not expected to go live until next year.

The work builds on a longer record, since Nokia and Nvidia first agreed in 2024 to develop AI-ready RAN products, and T-Mobile opened an AI-RAN Innovation Center in Bellevue in September 2024. In Europe, BT plans live trials in Birmingham, England, during 2027, and Deutsche Telekom has validated the platform in labs in Bonn, Germany, and Oulu, Finland, with field trials planned for 2027. Elisa in Finland completed what Nokia and Nvidia call Europe's first AI-RAN field trial, running voice, mobile data and video analytics together on one platform. Many other carriers, including SoftBank Corp, Vodafone Group, Orange Group and Indosat, are also working with the two companies, though the articles give no financial terms or revenue expectations, and several projects are still at the lab or trial stage.

stories.Headline: Appeals court lifts block on Mississippi's DEI ban, ejects judge over AI errors
stories.Summary:
A federal appeals court on Thursday revived Mississippi's ban on diversity, equity and inclusion programs in public schools, wiping out a lower-court order that had kept the law from taking effect. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, based in New Orleans, ruled that the preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate could not stand. The three-judge panel also reassigned the lawsuit to a different district judge after finding that the original ruling was marred by errors tied to artificial intelligence. The case is Jackson Federation of Teachers et al. v. Lynn Fitch et al., number 25-60496.

The appeals court recognized the state's authority over curricula and said the law does not directly regulate students' speech. The law at issue is House Bill 1193, which the Mississippi Legislature enacted in 2025. It bars public schools and public postsecondary institutions from creating, promoting or implementing DEI programs, from maintaining offices that promote specified divisive concepts, from requiring or weighing diversity statements in hiring and admissions, and from compelling participation in DEI training. It also requires the State Department of Education, the Board of Trustees of State Institutions of Higher Learning and the Mississippi Community College Board to teach and promote the position that there are two genders, male and female, based on chromosomal makeup.

The attorney general and private parties can enforce the statute, and it calls for annual reporting. The lawsuit, filed June 9, 2025, was brought by teachers, professors, students and advocacy groups, who argued the law violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Wingate's first restraining order contained inaccuracies, including wrongly listed plaintiff names and mistakes about the bill's language. At oral argument, Circuit Judge Jerry Smith asked whether the court could be confident those errors had not affected the judge's ultimate reasoning.

In the ruling, the court wrote that the district court, or perhaps its AI agent if one wanted to be charitable, had ignored and manipulated governing law, apparently to satisfy a policy agenda. Wingate acknowledged in a letter that a law clerk used the AI tool Perplexity as a drafting assistant, and said the version docketed on July 20, 2025 was an early draft that had not gone through the court's standard review process. He sent the letter to Robert Conrad, director of the Administrative Office of the Courts, in response to an inquiry from Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley. Lawyers for Mississippi, including Anthony Shults of the attorney general's office, argued the errors undermined confidence in the court's legal reasoning and urged reassignment.

Plaintiffs' attorneys, led by Robert McDuff of the Mississippi Center for Justice, called the AI use a regrettable shortcut that did not affect the constitutionality question, and asked that the case stay with Wingate. The panel sided with the state. With the injunction vacated, the dispute returns to the district court under a new judge, and the constitutional questions the plaintiffs raised remain unresolved. Grassley's office has also flagged AI-related problems in orders from staff for a second federal judge, which the senator described as error-ridden.
