stories.Headline: AI can write the thesis, but can it develop the scholar?
stories.Summary:
Generative AI is changing postgraduate research, and Aslam Fataar, a professor in Stellenbosch University's Faculty of Education, argues that the real test is whether AI helps students become capable scholars rather than just producing polished theses. He writes that a thesis produces both a research document and a developing scholar, and that AI can improve the document without strengthening its author's understanding. Fataar draws on Kamler and Thomson (2007), who describe doctoral writing as both text work and identity work, and on Gao and Zhang (2026), who warn of metacognitive miscalibration, where students overrate their grasp of material because an AI explanation sounds convincing. He also cites Zhao (2025) on how AI revisions can shift an author's stance toward greater certainty without any change in the evidence.

Fataar separates AI that assists a student's thinking from AI that substitutes for it. Assistance means a student uses AI to locate or approach difficult material and then reads and analyses it independently, while substitution means accepting an AI interpretation without examining its reasoning or evidence. To keep learning intact, he proposes recapitulation, a practice in which a researcher returns to AI-assisted work and rebuilds the reasoning until they can explain and defend it without the tool. He illustrates this with a doctoral student studying first-generation students' sense of belonging, who must check an AI's cultural capital explanation against the original interview transcripts before accepting it.

Fataar says universities should neither ban AI nor encourage dependence on it, and he recommends that recapitulation become routine in thesis supervision, with supervisors asking students why they accepted particular suggestions. He also suggests postgraduate programmes teach students to evaluate AI explanations and that students keep a brief research decision trail recording significant AI-assisted choices, intended as a tool for reflection rather than surveillance. He frames responsibility as shared among students, supervisors and institutions. He closes by offering three questions for AI-assisted thesis work: do I understand it, can I reconstruct it, and can I defend it.

stories.Headline: Allooloo Technologies Corp. Launches AI Agent Products for Financial Services Agents: Know Your Product and News
stories.Summary:
Allooloo Technologies Corp. launched AI agent products for financial services on October 23, 2026, announcing what it calls the zones of record, specialist datasets that agents read before a trade, a recommendation or an approval. The first two zones are now live: Know Your Product, which covers every listed issuer in eleven countries and is updated nightly, and News, which carries every filing and release as it lands. The company describes these as adjunct products meant for the AI agents that banks and dealers are adding to their desks. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire from Vancouver, British Columbia.

The company says the zones are designed to sit alongside existing terminal seats, market data and feeds, rather than replace or re-license them. The Know Your Product zone holds 28,462 listed companies on eleven exchanges and 2.4 million dated disclosures, with each fact signed and linked to the page it came from. The News zone, called Issuerwire.ai, covers 12,489 issuers in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, with 734,154 filings and releases, each headline traced to its source page. Agents can connect over the Model Context Protocol, with the Know Your Product zone at mcp.getissuer.ai and the News zone at mcp.issuerwire.ai, and the company says no account is needed to start. Usage is paid per question, with settlement handled inside each call.

The release is attributed to Matthew Keddy, chief executive of Allooloo Technologies Corp., who argued that agents carry a duty to show where a fact came from, which a human reader never had to prove. He said the company built the zones so agents can cite defensible facts under rules such as Know Your Product, Regulation Best Interest and product governance requirements. The release also lists groups it expects to be affected, including investment dealers and banks, listed issuers, investor-relations desks and newswires, auditors, and several AI laboratories whose models it says already read the zones. Allooloo describes itself as a Microsoft AI Cloud Partner that holds its data in Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services.

The release places the launch within a wider shift in which banks are reducing staffing while adding AI agents, citing JPMorgan Chase and HSBC as examples, and it cites industry estimates for fintech revenue and agentic finance growth. These figures come from the company's own citation of McKinsey and BCG, and the release does not describe any regulatory action or independent review of the products. The article does not say how many customers have adopted the zones or what pricing applies beyond per-question settlement. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
stories.Summary:
Ai2 released OlmoEarth v1.3, a satellite embedding model, on October 22, 2026, along with precomputed annual embeddings for the entire planet at 10-meter resolution in 64- and 128-dimension versions. The model turns a year of radar and multispectral satellite time series from Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and Landsat into one vector for each 10-meter pixel. Alongside it, the company introduced the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, a browser-based tool that lets people explore maps and find similar places without signing in. Until now, the main way to use OlmoEarth was fine-tuning in OlmoEarth Studio, which required GPU access and the ability to store imagery.

The release makes the model usable by a wider audience, since a small classifier trained on the embeddings can produce maps for tasks such as crop classification or change analysis. In evaluations across 27 tests on six continents, the 128-dimensional embeddings scored highest on 20 of them, and the 64-dimensional version led on 18. The company also introduced PLANTEUR, a crop-type benchmark for tropical farming. Training the release was cheaper than earlier versions, using 53% of the computing time of v1.2 and 18% of v1, with roughly $2,720 of rented H100 time for the final run. The weights, pretraining data and code are all open, and the embeddings cover 2025, 2024 and 2023 globally, with 2017 to 2022 covering select countries.

Ai2 is the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, which published the model and its technical report on Hugging Face and shared the embeddings through Source Cooperative. The company presented the release as a way for teams to test ideas in seconds rather than running fine-tuning jobs that take hours. Its illustrative example concerns illegal gold mining around La Pampa in Peru's Madre de Dios region, which peaked in 2017 and 2018 and was curbed by Operation Mercurio in February 2019. According to SiliconANGLE, the embeddings show a drop in significant change in the southern mining belt from 34 square kilometers for 2016 to 2020 to 9 square kilometers for 2020 to 2024. The Hugging Face article adds that mining resumed in pockets and that Peru sent navy patrols back into the reserve in August 2026.

stories.Headline: How to keep safe online in the wake of AI-supercharged hacking
stories.Summary:
Hackers have found a vulnerability in PHP, a coding language that underlies roughly 70% of all websites, and it can be used to take control of web servers. News of the flaw reached much of the world on Wednesday, and businesses and governments rushed to fix it. The article describes the weakness as sitting in the underlying code itself rather than in any single product. Attackers who exploit it could steal data, disrupt services or move through networks. The U.S. National Security Agency warned that the flaw could affect services that ordinary people rely on every day.

The article notes that because PHP is so widely used, the reach of the problem is large. Organizations running affected servers need to apply fixes quickly to close the gap. The article does not give a patch version number or a precise list of affected services. Experts quoted in the article say most of the responsibility falls on software providers and on the organizations that serve customers. They say those groups must find and repair the weakness in their systems.

Still, the article argues that individuals are not powerless and that there are basic steps everyone should take to protect themselves. Those steps are framed in the article as a practical response to a risk that is largely out of individual hands. The article places the flaw in a wider context of AI-supercharged hacking, in which automated tools make it easier to find and exploit weaknesses at scale. It does not say how long the fixes will take to reach every site. It also does not indicate whether any attacks have been confirmed, so readers should expect further updates as the situation develops.

Articles.Title: How to keep safe online in the wake of AI-supercharged hacking

stories.Headline: What Does an AI Agent Need a CPU For? Why Nvidia Wants In on the Business Dominated by AMD and Intel
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is moving into the market for central processing units, a business long led by AMD and Intel, as artificial intelligence shifts from answering questions to carrying out tasks on its own. The company is rolling out its Vera Rubin platform, which includes its first stand-alone CPU and is designed specifically for agentic AI. Nvidia says the chip delivers up to 1.5 times faster performance per core than CPUs built on the x86 architecture. The Motley Fool article describing the move was published on October 22, 2026, by Adria Cimino.

On the numbers, Nvidia is on track to generate $20 billion in stand-alone CPU revenue this year and puts the total market opportunity at $200 billion. For comparison, its data center revenue reached $89 billion in the second quarter, so the CPU figure equals only about three weeks of data center sales. The article notes that the $20 billion comes over just a few months, since the rollout began recently. AMD expects server CPU market growth of more than 35% annually, topping $120 billion by 2030, according to the market intelligence firm TrendForce. A separate report from IDC says Agentic Computer shipments in China will climb from 770,000 units in 2026 to 20.8 million units by 2030, roughly 27-fold growth, with Intel, AMD, Nvidia and Qualcomm all supplying platforms.

Executives at the two chip designers have described why agents need CPUs. Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said on an earnings call earlier this year that an agent is a harness built around an AI model, managing inputs and outputs, memory and tool use. That harness runs on CPUs, while GPUs power the model's thinking, and Huang predicts the world will eventually have billions of agents. AMD chief executive Lisa Su expects the CPU market to take off as well. She says CPUs were once paired with GPUs at a ratio of one to four or one to eight, but that the ratio is moving toward one to one.

The article cautions that Nvidia may not unseat the incumbents. AMD and Intel have decades of customer relationships and established leadership in CPUs. Customers running software designed for x86 chips may also be slow to switch to Nvidia, which uses a different architecture. Even so, the author argues Nvidia does not need to displace the leaders to win, since a growing agent market should leave room for all three companies. Investors are advised to watch how much CPU market share Nvidia captures and how that turns into revenue in the coming quarters.

stories.Headline: Wall Street prepares for AI's "day after"
stories.Summary:
Drops in artificial-intelligence stocks pulled markets lower around the world on Thursday, October 22, 2026, while oil prices climbed to their highest level since May on worries about the war with Iran. In New York, the S&P 500 fell 1.4 percent, moving toward its worst day since July, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.8 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down only 0.2 percent, or 113 points, by mid-afternoon, because most U.S. stocks actually rose. Asian markets fell first, with South Korea's Kospi down 3.5 percent, Hong Kong's Hang Seng off 3 percent and Japan's Nikkei 225 down 2.7 percent.

Investors have grown uneasy about the AI boom, which has been fueled by borrowing to build data centers and buy AI chips, and about share prices that rose sharply after years of enthusiasm. Companies in the sector are still reporting growth, but several results failed to lift their stocks. Lam Research posted summer profit and revenue slightly above expectations, yet its shares fell 11.6 percent after its forecast midpoint for the coming quarter came in a little below analysts' estimates. Meta Platforms dropped 7.9 percent after beating revenue expectations but missing on profit, and it said it would create a new class of stock to raise money for AI spending and other costs. Tesla slipped 2.6 percent despite a stronger-than-expected summer profit, because its revenue was weaker than forecast.

Nvidia, the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, fell 4.3 percent, making it the heaviest drag on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, which borrows money to buy Nvidia chips and rents them to customers, dropped 11 percent amid concerns about its debt. Oil was also a factor, as Brent crude rose 3.7 percent to $112.80 a barrel, its highest level in five months and well above the less than $97 it traded at at the start of the month. The article ties that rise to uncertainty about when the global energy industry can return to normal. In Europe, France's CAC 40 fell 1.4 percent, one of the sharpest losses on the continent, as French government bond yields climbed further amid worries about the country's debt and budget.

The U.S. Treasury market moved the other way, with the 10-year yield falling to 4.96 percent from 5.13 percent late Wednesday and from more than 5.30 percent earlier in October, which the article describes as a major move. That suggests investors were buying government bonds as a safer place to put money while AI stocks tumbled. A separate report showed fewer Americans filed new unemployment claims last week, a sign the economy may be stronger than economists expected and that layoffs remain low. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX also beat profit forecasts for the summer, and their gains helped cushion the broader market's losses. Procter & Gamble's chief executive, Shailesh Jejurikar, said the company expects geopolitical and economic challenges to continue, but it kept its full-year forecasts, and its stock rose 6 percent.

Articles.Title: Wall Street prepares for AI's "day after"
Worldwide drops for AI stocks send Wall Street toward its worst day since July

stories.Headline: Better Memory Stock: SK Hynix vs. Micron
stories.Summary:
Nvidia has reportedly asked Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to build the base dies for its new NVHBM memory using TSMC's 3nm process, according to a Seoul Economic Daily report that TrendForce cited on October 19, 2026. The request would bring two rival foundries, Samsung and TSMC, into closer cooperation, even though they compete for customers such as Qualcomm and Tesla. Nvidia's aim is to standardize production across its memory suppliers, which would keep HBM performance consistent and simplify product validation. Samsung's foundry division reportedly agreed to the requirements after an internal review.

The base die matters because NVHBM folds the memory controller, which normally sits in the GPU, into the memory stack itself, so it needs advanced logic technology. Industry estimates put TSMC's 3nm yields above 90 percent, against about 60 percent for Samsung Foundry's 2nm process, which helps explain the choice. Nvidia says the technology offers up to 30 percent more memory bandwidth, 15 percent lower HBM power consumption and 25 percent more XPU compute die area than standard HBM4E. Samsung and TSMC first worked together about four years ago on HBM compatibility with TSMC's GPU packaging, but this tie-up extends into HBM manufacturing for the first time. Samsung is also validating NVHBM base dies on its own 2nm process as a backup in case TSMC's 3nm capacity runs short.

TSMC has flagged tight 3nm capacity, which made up 33 percent of its third-quarter wafer sales, its largest share among all nodes, and its chairman C.C. Wei announced another 3nm fab in Tainan slated to begin mass production in the first half of 2028. Samsung will keep producing base dies in-house for its standard HBM lineup, with HBM4 and HBM4E using its 4nm process, and plans to keep its turnkey approach for custom HBM supplied to customers such as AMD. Separately, a Motley Fool article from October 23, 2026 said SK Hynix held a 50 percent share of the HBM market and Micron 18 percent in the second quarter, while the three big memory makers together control over 85 percent of DRAM. That same article said tight supply and surging AI demand have driven memory prices sharply higher, with conventional DRAM and NAND prices rising faster than HBM prices. The articles do not say how the base die arrangement will affect those market shares or prices.

stories.Headline: Stripe and Anthropic to support business operations within Claude Duet
stories.Summary:
Stripe announced on October 21, 2026 that its Link digital wallet and Stripe MCP tool have been connected to Anthropic's new AI agent app, Claude Duet. The Claude Duet research preview is initially open only to US subscribers on Claude Pro and Max plans through a waitlist, and it is designed to help small business owners and professionals track important matters and see through tasks they hand to the AI. Stripe, which provides programmable financial services, described the integration in a press release dated October 23, 2026. Anthropic introduced the agent as a tool that monitors work, prioritises tasks and carries out business activities in the background.

Through Link, business owners can ask Claude Duet to buy items such as digital advertising, business cards, team lunches and whiteboard markers from anywhere online. Each purchase requires the user's approval, after which Claude completes the transaction using a virtual card. Stripe MCP allows Claude Duet to send invoices and payment links, manage products and prices, analyse sales and process refunds. Separately, Anthropic said Duet requires approval before it sends messages, makes payments, signs documents or deletes information, and securities trading and transfers between accounts remain prohibited even with approval. The agent does not directly access users' passwords or sign-in tokens, and it uses safeguards to detect prompt injection and block requests for highly sensitive data such as credit card numbers.

Stripe's payments head, Kevin Miller, said that business leaders increasingly want AI agents to take on more work, and that combining Link's agent wallet with Stripe MCP lets Claude Duet handle many everyday tasks while users keep control. Anthropic's chief technology officer, Rahul Patil, said trust becomes more important once AI agents handle money, and that building payments into Claude Duet through Link keeps users in charge of every purchase. Anthropic has said it continues to develop its safeguards and acknowledged that Duet may misread conversations or misjudge urgency. Its capabilities for personal errands such as booking tickets remain less developed.

Stripe says Link already processes payments for more than 200 personal AI agents, including Meta's Muse, SpaceX's Grok Bot and Instinct. Stripe describes itself as a company that builds programmable financial services, and it reports processing more than $1.9 trillion a year, equal to about 1.6 percent of world GDP. Early testers have used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support and marketing, and one South Florida restaurant owner, Amin Ebrahimi, said it helped him work through invoices across his stores. Usage of the research preview shares limits with the rest of Claude, and background checks and complex tasks count toward those limits. The articles do not say when the preview will reach users outside the United States or when it will become generally available.

Articles.Title: Stripe and Anthropic to support business operations within Claude Duet

stories.Headline: AI-Native: Redesigning Automotive's Next Era
stories.Summary:
Two pieces of industry commentary, both dated October 2026, argue that automotive companies need to change how they adopt artificial intelligence. One, published by NTT DATA on October 23, says most organizations are still layering AI onto existing processes and functional structures, which produces pockets of efficiency without improving end-to-end results. The other, published by Cox Automotive on October 22 after a panel at the Automotive News Congress, focuses on how to scale AI across the enterprise in ways that create measurable business value. Neither piece describes a single event or a new regulation, so the story is one of industry direction rather than a dated incident.

NTT DATA's central recommendation is to redesign work around outcomes rather than tasks, processes or traditional functional boundaries. It says becoming AI-native means organizing people, software and AI agents into connected, end-to-end workflows that span multiple functions. The article lists four things readers will learn, including why applying AI to existing processes often yields only incremental gains and where automotive leaders should focus to move from isolated use cases to enterprise performance. The article does not provide figures, timelines or specific case results.

Cox Automotive's piece reports on a panel moderated by its President Steve Rowley, with Marianne Johnson, its Chief Product Officer, Oliver Parker of Google Cloud's Generative AI go-to-market team, and Jeff Rachor, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Automotive. Johnson argued that connected data matters most, because AI needs context and disconnected data simply automates wrong answers faster. Parker described agentic AI as systems that link reasoning, memory and action across multiple systems, and said this can free employees for higher-value work while cutting costs. Rachor stressed that deployments must be tied to business outcomes, that scaling requires governance, trusted partners, interoperability and a clear return on investment, and that the aim is to augment employees rather than eliminate them.

Both sources frame the current moment as a shift from early experimentation toward enterprise-wide scale. Cox Automotive describes the first phase as understanding what the technology could do and the next as connecting AI to trusted data, embedding it in business processes and extending its reach across the organization. The panel's speakers note that the pace of change is fast and that organizations are no longer asking whether AI belongs in their business. Neither article gives specific forecasts or next steps beyond these recommendations, and the NTT DATA piece is primarily a gated resource offering a download. Cox Automotive describes itself as the world's largest automotive services and technology provider, with more than 29,000 employees.

Articles.Title: AI-Native: Redesigning Automotive's Next Era

stories.Headline: Government of Canada expands support for artificial intelligence adoption and commercialization in the Prairie provinces
stories.Summary:
The Government of Canada has expanded its Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, with the announcement made on October 22, 2026, in Edmonton. The federal government says Canada, with Alberta playing a leading role, helped pioneer modern artificial intelligence, and the next step is to help businesses use the technology and help Canadian AI companies build, sell and scale their products. The expansion is aimed at making Prairie businesses and organizations more productive, competitive and resilient. Officials say the move builds on the region's existing strengths.

The expansion adds $500 million over five years, raising total federal funding for the initiative to $700 million. It forms part of AI for All, Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, and is delivered through Canada's regional development agencies. Adoption support will focus on five priority sectors named in the national strategy: health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing and robotics, while also reflecting regional priorities. The initiative will also help Canadian AI firms win customers, attract investment and scale their products, and it will support organizations that help small and medium-sized enterprises adopt or commercialize AI.

Support will also flow to incubators, accelerators and other not-for-profits. The announcement was made by the Honourable Eleanor Olszewski, Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience and the minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada (PrairiesCan). Her department is the agency delivering PrairiesCan's share of the program in the three provinces. The articles present her statements as describing the government's goals for the program rather than reporting any independent assessment of results.

No additional commitments beyond the funding figures and the stated priorities are described. Applications are open and will be accepted on a continuous basis until December 31, 2029, or until the funding has been fully committed, whichever comes first. Applicants are encouraged to submit expressions of interest as early as possible. The articles do not say how many projects will be funded or how the money will be divided among the three provinces.
Orgs: regional artificial intelligence initiative in alberta

Canada Boosts AI Adoption and Commercialization in Prairies

stories.Headline: OpenAI’s AI agents analyse a mouse brain gene atlas in 32 minutes
stories.Summary:
OpenAI, PerturbAI and Scripps Research used close to 2,000 AI agents to analyse a large mouse brain dataset in 32 minutes, and OpenAI published the work on Wednesday. The data came from a whole-brain CRISPR atlas built by PerturbAI, which switched off single genes in mice to show how each change affects different types of brain cells. The agents ran on GPT-Rosalind, a model built for life sciences research, and the results appear in a bioRxiv preprint that has not yet been peer-reviewed. The team estimates that researchers working by hand would need months to a year for the same analysis.

Each agent took one gene change, studied how the cells responded, searched the scientific literature and suggested possible explanations. The team then merged all the reports into a single reasoning atlas that links genes, cell effects, papers and likely mechanisms. The atlas covers 7.7 million mouse brain-cell nuclei and 1,947 disease-associated genes. According to OpenAI, the agents reproduced findings from earlier human analyses and also found new leads. In blinded tests, experts preferred the reports from the multi-agent approach 75% of the time, and at the largest workload the agents together cited more than 700 references compared with 11 for a single agent.

The analysis highlighted two leads for rare neurological disorders. Switching off Tsc2 changed dozens of genes tied to nerve-cell communication in the cerebellum, while switching off Tsc1 changed little, a gap that may matter for tuberous sclerosis. Switching off Dctn1, a gene linked to the rare brain disease Perry syndrome, raised the activity of genes that make cholesterol, and the agents suggested lab experiments to test whether this plays a part in nerve cell damage. Sarah Teichmann, chair in stem cell medicine at the University of Cambridge, said cell atlases let other scientists make discoveries no one has imagined yet.

The reasoning atlas is now available on GitHub, and the underlying dataset is on Hugging Face, so other researchers can inspect the framework. The articles stress that generating hypotheses is not the same as validating them, and the proposed disease connections still need laboratory work. Any treatment would be several stages of research away. The experiment shows how quickly AI can produce scientific leads, though not yet how quickly those leads can become medical advances.

Articles.Title: OpenAI’s AI agents analyse a mouse brain gene atlas in 32 minutes
OpenAI Ran Nearly 2,000 AI Agents on Brain Data: What They Found in 32 Minutes

stories.Headline: UMC, AP Memory advance AI chip power delivery with validated DTC silicon capacitors for advanced packaging
stories.Summary:
UMC and AP Memory announced on October 22, 2026, a technology and manufacturing collaboration to advance power delivery for AI and high-performance computing systems. The partnership pairs UMC's deep trench capacitor foundry technology and wafer manufacturing with AP Memory's silicon capacitor designs and system-level integration. The aim is to address the power efficiency problems facing next-generation data centers. Depending on system needs, these deep trench capacitors can be built into the interposer, substrate, or landside of an advanced package.

Rapid growth in AI workloads is putting heavy demands on power delivery inside computing systems. The articles describe a shift in data center design, moving power stabilization away from the circuit board and embedding capacitors directly into the interposer or substrate. This approach shortens the power delivery path, improves power integrity, and supports more efficient voltage regulation inside advanced packages. A key milestone came in the third quarter of 2026, when AP Memory completed tape-out and initial functional validation of its S-SiCap Gen2D discrete silicon capacitor designs. The next step is comprehensive system-level performance and reliability testing of these capacitors in substrate packages, targeting a range of capacitance and operating voltage requirements.

GC Hung, Senior Vice President of UMC, said the growth of AI and HPC is driving a shift toward vertical power integration at the chip level. He said UMC's DTC technology places high-density capacitance closer to the computing die for more stable power delivery, and that the partnership with AP Memory is meant to bring scalable solutions to market. Ivan Hong, President of AP Memory, said the successful tape-out and initial wafer validation of customized S-SiCap products built on DTC technology show the flexibility and manufacturability of AP Memory's design. He added that working with UMC lets the company offer customers a total solution, from product design through wafer manufacturing.

The articles say UMC's power delivery roadmap covers discrete and embedded silicon capacitors for different system architectures and extends to active components such as internal voltage regulators. The companies are also exploring extending the collaboration to capacitor-embedded interposers and landside capacitors. UMC, which has 12 fabs in production with combined capacity above 400,000 wafers per month, is further investing in new manufacturing capacity for power delivery and heterogeneous integration. The articles do not give a timeline for the system-level testing or for commercial availability of the products.

Articles.Title: UMC, AP Memory advance AI chip power delivery with validated DTC silicon capacitors for advanced packaging - digitimes
UMC and AP Memory Collaborate to Enable Advanced Power Delivery Solutions for AI and HPC Systems

stories.Headline: ASML's Hybrid Bonding Patents Reveal a Carousel Design Aimed at BESI's Turf
stories.Summary:
ASML has filed patents for a hybrid bonding tool that reverses the usual setup, according to SemiAnalysis analysts Howie and Sherry Zhang, who examined the filings. Instead of a robotic head picking up each die and placing it on a stationary wafer, the wafer rises to meet dies riding a conveyor track. The design borrows more from front-end lithography than from today's pick-and-place bonders, which could put ASML in direct competition with BESI. Hybrid bonding is becoming central to performance gains as transistor scaling slows, so the choice of tool stack matters to major logic customers.

In conventional die-to-wafer tools from BESI or ASMPT, the base wafer stays still while a bond head lifts, aligns and presses each die into place. ASML's design moves the dies on a carrier past measurement and plasma activation stations, with a chuck lifting the wafer to meet each die at the bonding station. The analysts say the track hardware comes from SuperTrak Conveyance, a startup they researched. Sherry Zhang said the timing is several years away but still worth discussing because the architecture differs sharply from current tools. Howie described ASML's overlay precision as far higher than pick-and-place systems, though the moving-track approach raises open questions about measurement accuracy and cleanliness across a track spanning several meters.

The analysts also restated their February 2024 view that HBM will not adopt die-to-wafer hybrid bonding before 2029, if at all, because the economics fail against thermo-compression bonding. For logic, they point to a Huawei phone chip, the 9050, as an early production example that runs up to 2.7 GHz without raising voltage or power. They are skeptical of vendor roadmaps, noting that ASML's earlier transistor-density projections never materialized and saying that claims about hybrid bonding in NAND and DRAM should be taken with a grain of salt. BESI's shares reportedly fell nearly 3% in Amsterdam when the research was published, while ASML rose.

Separately, the analysts describe how Huawei is pursuing full logic folding for data center accelerators by 2030, and how Chinese toolmakers including NAURA and AMEC are building hybrid bonding capability. Export controls could accelerate that localization, Sherry Zhang said, though she declined to predict policy. A related shift toward a 6x12 photomask, targeted for 2030, would restore full-reticle High-NA exposure and could feed into ASML's tool pricing, which management has said is value-based. Bits & Chips reports that BESI's hybrid-bonding orders in the first nine months of 2026 exceeded twice the total for all of 2025, with 23 customers and cumulative demand above 215 systems. CEO Richard Blickman said memory makers' interest is growing even as they delayed hybrid bonding in HBM.

Articles.Title: ASML's Hybrid Bonding Patents Reveal a Carousel Design Aimed at BESI's Turf - BigGo Finance
Besi sees increasing momentum for hybrid bonding - Bits&Chips

stories.Headline: Brazil Elections: How AI, Meta and Evangelicals Could Sway the Presidential Race for Bolsonaro
stories.Summary:
Brazil's presidential runoff is set for Sunday, October 25, between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, with polls showing a tight race. Ahead of the vote, The Intercept Brasil reported that Bolsonaro's campaign paid 600,000 reais, about $119,000, to Elytron, a U.S. company that sells election manipulation services. The reporting says it is unclear whether the campaign used those services, but it has fueled suspicion of outside interference. Lula's campaign has also asked the top electoral court to disqualify Bolsonaro over alleged interference by Meta.

The campaign's complaint centers on Meta's platforms, which include Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Lula's team says Meta limited the reach of his posts and suspended his campaign advertising account, and it submitted screenshots showing Meta AI assigning Bolsonaro's electoral number to fictional politicians. Brazil's electoral prosecutors have said Meta did not fully comply with court orders to treat both candidates equally. Meta denies favoring any candidate, calling the claims false and unfounded, and says Lula's account was suspended for one hour by mistake.

Lula's campaign has pressed the matter in several forums, including a request to the Federal Police to investigate the Elytron payments. Following a report on internal messages, the campaign also went to the electoral court and the Federal Prosecution Service, and prosecutors have asked federal courts to open a separate inquiry. A United Nations special rapporteur on freedom of expression has voiced concern about unequal reach across the campaigns. Independent researchers say they cannot determine whether the discrepancies were deliberate, because Meta's systems are opaque.

The race also reflects wider changes in how campaigns operate. This is Brazil's first general election since large language models became widely popular, and fact-checkers identified 920 pieces of AI-generated or manipulated election content before the first round, most of it unlabeled. Lula's supporters have run an intensive online effort, while Bolsonaro finished ahead in the first round and polls show the gap narrowing. Whether the courts act on the complaints before the runoff is not yet clear from the reporting.

Articles.Title: Brazil Elections: How AI, Meta and Evangelicals Could Sway the Presidential Race for Bolsonaro
Brazil presidential election dogged by alleged bias by Meta AI tools

stories.Headline: Meta Raises AI Spending Target Again as Cash Flow Turns Negative
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms shares fell sharply on October 22, 2026, after the company reported third-quarter results that showed negative free cash flow and a higher floor for its AI spending. Tech stocks broadly sold off that day, with the Nasdaq Composite down 2.60 percent, while Meta dropped about 6.98 percent in one report and roughly 6 percent in another. Investors were less concerned with the quarter's revenue, which reached $64.6 billion, than with how the company is funding its AI build-out. The sell-off spread to other AI-linked names, including Nvidia, Microsoft and Samsung-linked suppliers, as investors moved into U.S. Treasurys.

Meta's full-year capital expenditure forecast now runs from $135 billion to $145 billion, up from a previous range of $130 billion to $145 billion, which marks its third upward revision this year. Third-quarter free cash flow swung to a net outflow of $2.12 billion, and non-cancelable AI-related commitments reached $825 billion, up from $700 billion reported in July. To raise funds while keeping control in the hands of its leadership, Meta's board approved a new class of non-voting Class C common stock that takes effect January 19 next year. Holders of Class A and Class B shares will receive one Class C share for each share they own as a dividend.

Meta's management framed the results positively, with Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg saying the company hit major milestones in delivering personal superintelligence and that its investments are paying off. The company said its core business is strong and accelerating broadly. Meta also disclosed that it could face a $25 billion penalty in a New Mexico youth protection case, which it said it would appeal, arguing the amount should be no more than $3.4 billion. Credit markets showed concern as well, with the spread on Meta's five-year credit default swaps reaching an all-time high that day.

The sell-off came amid wider unease about AI-related debt, which had grown since October 14, when bonds issued by CoreWeave and other neocloud providers came under distress concerns. Reports noted that Tesla's own spending plans, released the following week, were below Wall Street estimates and that Tesla is being considered as an AI funding source for a possible merger with SpaceX. Analysts quoted in the coverage suggested that worries about Big Tech's rising AI capital spending are likely to persist while interest rates stay high. Until profitability is clearly demonstrated, investors may keep pressing on AI-exposed stocks, including major Korean chipmakers.

Articles.Title: Meta Raises AI Spending Target Again as Cash Flow Turns Negative - Seoul Economic Daily
Meta stock sinks 6% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative

stories.Headline: Why AI data centers are powering a boom in fuel-cell demand
stories.Summary:
On September 30, Hitachi, Brookfield Japan, Hartree Partners Singapore and Tokyo Gas signed a memorandum of understanding to work together on green data centers in Japan, and the companies announced it on October 23, 2026. The agreement builds on an earlier one among Hitachi, Brookfield and Hartree that was announced in July 2025, with Tokyo Gas now added as a fourth party. The companies want to design data centers that generate their own power, use it reliably and efficiently, and help cut emissions through green energy and related measures. As their first projects, they plan to build green data centers in the Kanto and Kyushu regions.

The four companies will draw up a basic concept for these power-integrated facilities and push toward a standardized model that can be rolled out flexibly. The design has four parts. First, on-site generation would be the main power source, combined with battery storage, grid power and other sources. Second, redundancy would be built into the whole infrastructure, including cooling and power distribution, so operations continue through equipment failures or swings in supply. Third, the group will set decarbonization requirements, covering carbon credits, environmental attributes and renewable energy, and fourth, major facilities such as buildings and on-site power plants would be standardized and modularized to shorten project lead times and allow scalable deployment.

The companies say the approach should reduce heavy reliance on the power grid, widen the choice of sites, encourage local production and consumption of energy, and speed up projects. They describe the effort as a way to combine their respective expertise to tackle securing power, keeping operations stable and decarbonizing AI data centers. Their release points to Japan's surge in data center construction, especially in urban areas, which is raising electricity demand and stretching the time needed to secure power capacity because of grid limits. It also notes that the Japanese government, as part of its Green Transformation initiatives, has promoted sustainable infrastructure and spreading data centers across regions.

The same pressure is visible in the United States, where data centers took 4.4% of electricity use in 2024, according to the Department of Energy. Penn State's Institute of Energy and the Environment says consumption could triple by 2028, and a Bloomberg analysis projects data centers could use as much as 20% of US electricity production by 2035. Andrew Denis of the energy technology firm ZON said roughly half of the data center projects due online in 2026 face delays tied to power availability, and Britt Burt of Industrial Info Resources said the old focus on location has given way to speed to power. Burt estimated about $6 trillion is eyed for new data centers worldwide, with about $4 trillion of it in the US, while Denis said communities near big clusters in Virginia, Texas and Georgia have reportedly seen electricity rates rise 8 to 15%.

stories.Headline: Crusoe Partners with Araico on AI Cloud in Paraguay
stories.Summary:
Crusoe, the AI factory company, announced on October 22, 2026 a strategic partnership with Paraguayan energy and infrastructure developer Araico to build AI compute infrastructure powered by the Itaipú Hydroelectric Dam. The initiative is Crusoe's first dedicated AI Cloud deployment in Latin America and follows its strategy of placing computing near abundant energy sources. Under the agreement, Crusoe plans an initial deployment online in mid-2027, with a path to 106 MW of IT capacity and long-term options to reach about 280 MW in total. The facility will sit next to the Itaipú substation, drawing on one of the most reliable 100% renewable hydroelectric sources in the world. It will serve U.S. cloud customers and growing demand across Latin America through Crusoe Cloud.

Paraguay's President Santiago Peña said the partnership unlocks new value from the country's natural resources and brings jobs, investment, and technology. He described it as a chance for Paraguay to become a regional leader in AI infrastructure. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, who was leading a U.S. business delegation when the deal was signed, called it historic and said it could become the largest private foreign investment in Paraguayan history. Crusoe co-founder Cully Cavness said the company was built to develop digital infrastructure where power is abundant and environmentally aligned. Araico CEO Alejandro Zuccolillo said the deal would turn Paraguay's energy abundance into industrial growth, local jobs, and digital innovation.

Under the division of work, Araico will lead local development and site infrastructure beside the Itaipú substation. Crusoe will manage, operate, and deliver the physical compute for Crusoe Cloud. Crusoe's statement said the project extends its energy-aligned AI infrastructure across North America, Europe, and now Latin America. The companies described the agreement as a step toward deeper digital infrastructure ties throughout the Western Hemisphere. The articles do not give a project cost or describe any further steps beyond the planned 2027 deployment and the scaling options.

stories.Headline: Sam George Outlines $270m Ghana AI Investment And Warns Against Foreign Data Risks
stories.Summary:
Communication Minister Samuel Nartey George announced on October 22, 2026, that Ghana plans a $270 million investment in artificial intelligence, speaking at the Joy News Digital Economy Forum. He also warned that feeding government data into foreign AI models carries risks. The forum covered the country's digital transformation, technological development and data security. The minister described the investment as a way to use new technology to improve public services and grow the digital economy. His concerns suggest that any adoption of AI needs safeguards to protect sensitive government information.

Public institutions handle confidential records about citizens, public finances, national security and administration, and the reports say sending that material to external AI platforms without adequate protection could expose it to unauthorised access. Uncertainty about how such data is stored and used adds to the problem. The concerns point to the need for clear policies, including stronger data protection standards, secure digital infrastructure and rules on how external technology providers handle government information. The reports note that the $270 million investment also raises questions about how Ghana will build its own AI capacity while protecting national interests. Developing local expertise, supporting domestic technology developers and strengthening local digital infrastructure could reduce reliance on foreign systems.

A separate report from theindependentghana.com adds detail on the infrastructure side. Sam George, the Ningo-Prampram Member of Parliament, said Ghana's first AI data centre would be established within two years, with Phase I providing computing infrastructure for local researchers, universities and businesses that currently buy capacity abroad. He said the government is working through procurement with the Public Procurement Authority to secure the equipment. He also said the centre is only a first step and would not meet all of Ghana's AI needs within the current administration's term. The report notes that Ghana opened a National Data Centre in Accra in January 2016, run by the National Information Technology Agency, while a specialised facility existed at the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission from 2010 for nuclear-test monitoring.

The reports make clear that the new centre would be a specialised AI facility rather than a general government data centre, and they leave open how the $270 million will be divided among projects. They do not say what specific data protection rules the government will adopt. Ghana's challenge, as the reports frame it, is to deliver practical benefits to citizens while protecting government information and strengthening digital independence. Whether the infrastructure and safeguards arrive on the stated timeline remains to be seen as procurement proceeds.

stories.Headline: Idaho Fish and Game website powers down as AI discovers global flaws
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, the Idaho Fish and Game website was replaced with a minimal page that is not working at full capacity. The agency made the switch to a static site to reduce the risk of a security vulnerability. The change came shortly after Scripps News reported that artificial intelligence had found two serious flaws in a programming language used by about 70 percent of the world's websites. In the aftermath of that discovery, many sites around the globe went offline while companies raced to patch the problems.

The agency has not said whether its move was tied to those broader concerns. Officials also said there is no timeline for when the full website will return. Still, the temporary page keeps key information available for hunters and anglers. That includes seasons and rules brochures, public comment opportunities, access to the licensing website, hunter education opportunities, and agency contact information. Anyone who cannot find a specific item on the temporary site is directed to contact a Fish and Game office.

The Idaho Fish and Game agency is responsible for the decision, and its officials announced the change without tying it directly to the global flaws. Scripps News is the outlet that reported the artificial intelligence discovery. The agency's stated reason was the need to minimize potential security vulnerability on its site. Its statement described the move as a precaution. No further explanation of the agency's reasoning appears in the reporting.

The story sits within a wider moment in which the discovery of serious flaws in widely used web software has prompted many organizations to take their sites offline. The articles do not say how long the global patching effort will take or when the Idaho site will be restored. The only concrete next step reported is that the full website remains offline with no set return date. Readers seeking routine information in the meantime can use the temporary page or call a regional office.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Sued By Texas Attorney General Over Deceptive Practices And AI Chatbot Dangers
stories.Summary:
The Texas Attorney General, Ken Paxton, filed a lawsuit on a Friday against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and its chief executive, Sam Altman. The filing, reported on October 23, 2026, accuses the company of deceptive trade practices that expose consumers, including children, to harm. According to the complaint, OpenAI misled the public by presenting its flagship software as dependable and safe while failing to put adequate safeguards in place to prevent harmful output. The suit is filed under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act and asks a court to enforce compliance and hold the company and its leadership accountable.

The complaint's central claim is that OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a non-profit meant to advance digital intelligence for the public good without financial constraints, but has since become a high-valuation commercial business. Paxton argues that in chasing market leadership and growth, the company released ChatGPT without adequately training it or disclosing its operational risks. The state points out that large language models generate output based on patterns in user input, so unmonitored use can produce inaccurate or dangerous statements, and users may receive no meaningful warning. The lawsuit, in effect, asks the court to require clearer disclosure and stricter oversight of how the product is deployed.

The filing lists a range of harms it ties to people's reliance on the chatbot. It says the tool has helped people carry out violence, encouraged self-harm and suicide, caused professionals public embarrassment, eroded users' critical thinking, and drawn minors into dependence while collecting their data without parental oversight. The complaint blames these outcomes on OpenAI's misrepresentations about its products and its careless rollout of ChatGPT in Texas and elsewhere. It further claims the company's push to win the AI race and build large fortunes drove these risks even though it knew of the dangers.

State enforcement officials, in announcing the filing, said that companies advancing AI quickly remain bound by existing consumer protection laws. They stressed that such firms must tell users clearly about the limits and risks of their systems. The articles do not describe any response from OpenAI or any ruling in the case. They also report that retail sentiment about OpenAI on the Stocktwits platform was "bullish" at the time of writing, with high message volume.

stories.Headline: Wall Street regulator to focus on AI, private assets in corporate exams
stories.Summary:
The US Securities and Exchange Commission said on Friday, October 23, 2026, that the use of artificial intelligence, private assets and tokenized securities would be key areas of focus in its examinations of Wall Street firms during the current fiscal year. The statement was reported by Reuters and carried by WTVB. The agency said that for the federal government's 2027 fiscal year, which began October 1, examiners would prioritize private funds and private credit. It also plans to look closely at artificial intelligence and other technology that may affect market operations, compliance, fraud prevention and investor protection.

The announcement follows a move by the Trump administration to expand access to private assets for retirement savers and retail investors, which could offer higher returns but also expose everyday Americans to more risk. The SEC last month unveiled a five-year exemption allowing companies to offer blockchain-based or tokenized stocks. The agency's examinations division inspects firms such as investment advisers, broker-dealers and stock exchanges, and it can refer findings of wrongdoing to the enforcement division. Critics quoted in the report say ordinary investors may not see the higher returns they expect from these assets, may not understand the fees involved, and may find that the assets are hard to price and cannot be quickly turned into cash.

The SEC's statement described the planned focus areas but the article does not name a specific official who spoke on the matter beyond the agency itself. The article attributes the critical view of private assets to unnamed critics rather than to any named individual or group. It also notes that the agency last year de-emphasized scrutiny of the cryptocurrency sector, which provides context for the renewed attention to tokenization. The article does not say what enforcement actions, if any, will follow from these examinations or when the agency will report its findings.

Articles.Title: Wall Street regulator to focus on AI, private assets in corporate exams

stories.Headline: Famous Billionaire Calls AI a Bubble — But That Is Not What His Money Says
stories.Summary:
Ken Griffin, founder of the hedge fund Citadel, said on October 20, 2026, at the firm's Future of Global Markets Conference that artificial intelligence is almost certainly in a speculative bubble. He told Bloomberg that economic transformations often bring bubbles with them. His worry centers on the huge sums flowing into AI infrastructure without a clear sense of future demand. Citing UBS, the articles note that hyperscalers are projected to spend $4.1 trillion on AI infrastructure between 2026 and 2028, nearly triple their spending over the previous six years.

Griffin compared the graphics processing units that power AI systems to airline seats, arguing that once capacity exceeds demand, operators may cut prices because serving another customer costs relatively little. He drew a parallel to the fiber-optic boom around 2000, when telecom companies built far more capacity than the market needed and prices collapsed. He also questioned whether businesses were getting enough value from expensive AI models to justify the cost. Even so, he acknowledged that revolutionary technologies often produce lasting winners, and he said he wished he had kept his Amazon stock during the internet era.

The articles point out that Citadel's own holdings suggest it has not walked away from the sector. According to an amended filing for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, which was submitted on September 2, Citadel Advisors held about $8.6 billion across five AI-linked companies: Amazon at $2.59 billion, Nvidia at $2.36 billion, Microsoft at $1.41 billion, Broadcom at $1.1 billion, and Alphabet at $1.1 billion. During that quarter the firm raised its Amazon share count by 34% and its Microsoft share count by 43%, while cutting Nvidia shares by roughly 37%. The filing also disclosed call and put options on companies including Nvidia and Micron Technology, which can serve as hedges, and the articles caution that the figures are only a snapshot from June.

The articles argue that Griffin's views are not necessarily contradictory, since excess investment can destroy shareholder wealth while also building the foundation for major businesses. They note that Amazon survived the dot-com collapse to become a dominant cloud provider, and that Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Oracle together hold $2.3 trillion in cloud backlog. Griffin also said AI agents have cut some sophisticated Citadel research tasks from weeks to hours. The articles conclude that Griffin is not telling investors to abandon AI but to avoid mistaking a remarkable technology for an investment worth any price.

Articles.Title: Famous Billionaire Calls AI a Bubble — But That Is Not What His Money Says

stories.Headline: As AI fears rise, a composer puts it on stage at Symphony Hall
stories.Summary:
Tod Machover, the composer and faculty director of the MIT Media Lab, has written a new classical work called "already and not yet" that premieres Thursday with the Boston Symphony Orchestra at Symphony Hall. During the piece, an AI system listens to the players through microphones and improvises its own music, which is broadcast over a bank of surround-sound speakers. The performance runs through Saturday under the baton of Kent Nagano and is part of the orchestra's week of "Technology and Our Humanity" programming. The article, written by A.Z. Madonna and published October 22, 2026, reports the story as coverage of the premiere. The system was designed by MIT Media Lab PhD researcher Manaswi Mishra, who will control the AI on stage during performances.

Graduate student Ana Schon will mix the sound in the hall. Machover explained that the system can be shaped to stay close to what the musicians play or to make variations and connections between different parts of the sound. Even so, the output is not fully predictable, since Machover knows the general kind of thing it will do but expects it to differ every time. The article notes that Machover, Mishra, and Schon tested the system with BSO musicians at Symphony Hall the week before, and that the players were open and inquisitive.

Machover has said he is not trying to show that human musicians can be replaced by machines. He wants to demonstrate that the technology many people fear can be musical and shaped by and for people. He acknowledged that even saying the word AI to musicians can be frightening, though he described the reaction of the BSO players as encouraging. In his personal life he uses almost no AI tools, does not use chatbots, and manages his own calendar by hand.

He has said that he values attention to detail and dislikes automating most of his work, a view he traces to childhood lessons with his mother, a piano teacher. The article places the premiere within a broader moment of public unease about artificial intelligence, and it presents the work as an effort to model a different relationship between people and the technology. It also points to other recent projects connected to Machover, including a symphony that uses AI and a related reflection on democracy that the BSO is presenting this week. The article does not describe any plans beyond the Thursday-through-Saturday run at Symphony Hall.

Articles.Title: As AI fears rise, a composer puts it on stage at Symphony Hall

stories.Headline: U.S residents favor AI training for workers, Northeastern survey finds
stories.Summary:
A Northeastern University survey report, released Friday, October 23, 2026, finds that many Democrats and Republicans favor retraining programs focused on artificial intelligence for workers, along with ongoing lessons. The report, published by the university's news site, draws on responses from 38,000 people across all fifty states, polled from June to August 2026. Researchers say the findings reflect growing agreement on the need for worker protections and training. The report is the first of several expected from the Northeastern team.

Sixty-four percent of Republican respondents and 63 percent of Democratic respondents support job retraining meant to build the skills needed for AI-heavy work, and the researchers say this could cover both blue collar and white collar jobs. Many respondents also backed tax-advantaged savings accounts that workers could use to pay for training and education. Fifty-seven percent of Republicans and 56 percent of Democrats supported "worker-owned retraining accounts" that people could keep as they move between jobs. The survey does not describe any enacted law or policy, only public preferences. The results point to a possible area of bipartisan agreement on how the government should respond to AI's effects on employment.

The report's lead researcher, David Lazer, a distinguished professor at Northeastern, said the responses show a growing consensus that the government should protect people from the disruption AI could bring. He called this the single most surprising result, while noting a widening partisan gap in trust. Ata Aydin Usulu, a doctoral researcher on the survey, said men on average viewed AI more positively than women and that higher education correlated with greater trust. He attributed part of that to people with more education having more exposure to AI tools. Usulu also said young people's distrust stems in part from fears that AI is replacing entry-level jobs.

The survey comes amid growing public opposition to AI, including demonstrations this week in more than 50 U.S. cities and campuses calling for a pause on AI development, according to media reports. Concerns about data centers center on environmental impact and energy costs, and one IT company cited in the article says a single large AI data center can draw more than 100 megawatts a year, enough to power 800,000 homes. Only 22 percent of respondents said they would support an AI data center in their community, while 54 percent said they would not and 23 percent had no opinion. Lazer described opposition to data centers as vast and said it has become a hot-button issue in the country.

Articles.Title: U.S residents favor AI training for workers, Northeastern survey finds

stories.Headline: Discerning AI CoP hosts screening of ‘Ghost in the Machine’, Oct. 27
stories.Summary:
The Discerning AI Community of Practice, based at the Center for Data Ethics, will host a screening and panel discussion of the 2026 documentary "Ghost in the Machine" on Tuesday, Oct. 27. The event runs from 6 to 7:30 p.m. in The Commons Theater. Food will be provided, and attendees do not need to register. The announcement appeared on Marquette Today on Oct. 23, 2026.

The film, directed by Valerie Veatch, is described as an investigative documentary about the buried history of artificial intelligence. According to the article, it presents AI not as a neutral system of algorithms but as a technology shaped by racism, misogyny, eugenics and entrenched structures of power. The film rejects the idea that AI is inevitable or objective. It traces how myths of progress and efficiency have hidden political and cultural agendas behind modern AI systems. The article frames the film as being about power, asking who builds AI, who benefits from it and who bears the cost.

The articles do not name a specific person as responsible for the screening beyond the sponsoring group, the Discerning AI Community of Practice, which is based at the Center for Data Ethics. The announcement does not include a quotation from any organizer or panelist. It also does not identify the panelists or describe the panel's topics. The piece presents the film's themes in its own words rather than attributing claims to a speaker.

The screening is part of the community's broader focus on the ethics of data and artificial intelligence, though the article does not spell out that program in detail. The announcement does not say whether the event will be repeated or what follow-up activities are planned. It was published on the university's news site, which lists the event among its campus news and calendar items. No further developments are reported in the articles provided.

stories.Headline: Is training AI on copyrighted works fair use? Scholars say "market dilution" theory still lacks evidence
stories.Summary:
Three scholars, Abhishek Nagaraj of UC Berkeley Haas, Pamela Samuelson of UC Berkeley Law, and Christopher Jon Sprigman of New York University, argue in a policy article in the journal Science that it is still unknown whether AI-generated books, images, or music are diluting the market for works made by people. Their article was published in October 2026 and questions a legal theory called "market dilution," which holds that machine-made works could flood the market and weaken incentives for human creators. The theory gained attention after a federal judge, in a June 2025 ruling in Kadrey v. Meta, suggested that it could prevail if authors showed it was actually happening. The judge still sided with Meta because the authors had not offered persuasive evidence of market harm.

The scholars say the theory lacks a clear definition, and early studies are hard to interpret because researchers have not agreed on what counts as dilution. They also note that the U.S. Copyright Office mentioned market dilution in a May 2025 report on generative AI training but offered no analysis showing the harm was likely. The authors argue that the theory may conflict with copyright law's main concern, which is market substitution, where someone copies protected expression and displaces demand for a specific work. A narrower version of the theory, concerning an AI system trained on one entity's works with outputs that compete with that entity's licensing markets, is at issue in cases Getty Images has brought against Stability AI in the U.S. and the U.K. Nagaraj, Samuelson, and Sprigman also say that many new works are hybrids of human and AI contribution, which makes it hard to decide what counts as AI-generated.

They argue that hybrid works with considerable human input should not automatically be treated as diluting a market just because AI was used. Their article adds that future studies must separate new market entrants from established creators who adopt AI. The researchers say that if market dilution is shown to exist in certain cases, legislatures may be better suited than courts to address market-wide harms. Nagaraj said the idea could redraw the boundaries of fair use for AI developers, with consequences for creators and end users. More than 100 copyright lawsuits over AI training are moving through U.S. courts, and two federal courts have so far ruled that such training is fair use.

Articles.Title: Is training AI on copyrighted works fair use? Scholars say "market dilution" theory still lacks evidence

stories.Headline: The Roles and Missions of Church-Related Institutions in the Era of AI: Humanistic Approaches
stories.Summary:
St. John's University announced a conference titled "The Roles and Missions of Church-Related Institutions in the Era of AI: Humanistic Approaches," to be held on Saturday, October 24, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. in the D'Angelo Center Ballroom on its Queens, New York campus. The event is presented by The Lilly Network of Church-Related Colleges and Universities in partnership with The School of Education. The announcement was posted on the university's website on October 22, 2026.

Attendees were invited to register through an RSVP link on the page. The keynote speakers include Dr. Edmondson, Associate Provost for Continued Learning and founding director of the Learning and Development Initiative at the New Jersey Institute of Technology. His initiative focuses on AI literacy, digital opportunity and workforce capability, and he has delivered more than 100 presentations on artificial intelligence and higher education. He is also the author of ten books, the most recent of which is Remaining Human in the Age of AI, published in 2026.

The second speaker, Dr. Elmoudden, is a professor of communication studies at St. John's whose research examines AI bias, particularly as it relates to culture, minoritized religion and disability. Dr. Elmoudden co-wrote The Future is Now: Empowering Society Through AI Literacy with Jason S. Wrench of SUNY New Paltz. The textbook explains core AI concepts and argues that AI literacy requires ethical awareness and critical thinking alongside technical knowledge. The page presents this material as the basis for the conference's human-centered framing, though it does not describe any formal requirements or policy changes arising from the event.

The speakers' prior appearances in an online video about AI and mental health are also noted on the page. The announcement does not describe any policy change, requirement or new institutional commitment tied to the conference. It frames the event within the broader discussion of how faith-affiliated colleges and universities should respond to artificial intelligence, and it lists the university's other recent education news as context. The page does not say whether additional sessions, publications or follow-up events are planned beyond the October 24 gathering.
