The company pointed to two earlier deployments: a European commercial lender that removed 80% of manual credit handoffs, and an institution serving more than 4 million customers that cut lending operating costs by 40%. FlowX.AI did not name either institution. Kastle CEO Rishi Choudhary, whose firm raised $24 million in September, describes agents as an "action layer" over legacy cores, widened only as performance warrants.

PYMNTS Intelligence found that 52% of financial institutions cite legacy technology as an obstacle to real-time payments modernization, and 53% cite manual-intensive internal processes. Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City researchers wrote in 2024 that full core conversions can take several years and cost millions. Other vendors take different routes: Maximum raised a $30 million seed round in August to replace legacy infrastructure with an AI-native operating system, and 10x Banking secured £40 million from AshGrove Capital in the same month. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Banks Add AI Agents, Keep Their 40-Year-Old Cores

stories.Headline: The Chief Justice of Russia’s Supreme Court asked China to help implement artificial intelligence in the courts
stories.Summary:
Igor Krasnov, the Chairman of Russia's Supreme Court, asked China to share its experience using artificial intelligence in the judicial system during a visit to Beijing. The request came in a meeting with China's Minister of Justice, He Rong, according to a report by The Moscow Times that UNN relayed. Krasnov showed interest in Chinese technologies that can provide legal services around the clock through artificial intelligence, blockchain and big data analysis. He also proposed expanding the exchange of knowledge, experience and professional practices between Russian and Chinese specialists in the field.

During the visit, Krasnov was shown how the "Smart Court" laboratory works, where AI analyzes court documents, searches for legal provisions, selects judicial precedents and prepares draft rulings. He was also shown the Beijing Financial Court system, which can analyze claims and predict how cases will turn out. In September, Krasnov approved a concept for bringing artificial intelligence into Russian courts. Under that plan, neural networks are to be used by 2030 to check documents, prepare draft rulings and assign cases among judges, and the planned rollout covers 95% of the country's courts. The final decision, the articles state, is to remain with a human.

Representatives of the supreme courts of Russia and China also signed an open-ended agreement on cooperation and the exchange of judicial practices during the visit. The articles do not describe any further terms of that agreement. Krasnov's remarks in Beijing indicate that Russia intends to follow China's model as it builds out its own system. The reports do not say when specific courts will begin using the new tools or what the next steps in the cooperation will be.

Articles.Title: The Chief Justice of Russia’s Supreme Court asked China to help implement artificial intelligence in the courts

stories.Headline: UNC School of Law holds mock Supreme Court arguments using AI justices
stories.Summary:
UNC School of Law held a mock Supreme Court oral argument event with artificial intelligence serving as the justices. The event, called "May It Please the Machine," had students argue a real Supreme Court case before justices powered by ChatGPT. The faculty uploaded background documents, such as court briefings, for the AI to reference. They also built a persona file for each justice so that every one had its own distinct perspective. The AI justices could not access the internet or any outside documents, so they could not look up how the real case had been decided.

They could listen to the students and speak, asking questions and referring to what the other justices had said. The AI justices reached the same decision as the real justices in the case. Dean for AI Nicole Downing said the experiment was meant to test how well AI could reason about law, not to replace judges. Downing said the AI can apply law and perform some reasoning, but that attorneys remain essential to the process. She pointed to the originality and creativity that come from people as something the machine cannot supply.

She also said the AI has plenty of room to improve, particularly in how it engages with attorneys during argument. She gave the AI justices a score of 1.5 out of 10 for their performance. The event shows how the law school is studying AI as a tool for lawyers rather than a substitute for them. The articles do not describe any further plans for the program.

Articles.Title: UNC School of Law holds mock Supreme Court arguments using AI justices

stories.Headline: Meta's AI bill just hit $145 billion — and it issued a new share class to pay for it
stories.Summary:
Meta reported its third-quarter results on October 21, 2026, and the stock traded higher in after-hours trading as investors weighed a revenue beat against a larger spending plan. Meta closed that day at $697.52, up 0.47%, after trading between $689.68 and $713.22. By 22:05 ET the stock was marked at $713.00, about 2.2% above the close, having been up as much as 5% earlier in the extended session. The company reported revenue of $64.60 billion, against a consensus of $63.37 billion and up 26% from $51.2 billion a year earlier.

Profit was weaker than the top line suggests. GAAP earnings per share came in at $3.83 against $3.56 expected, but would have been $7.40 excluding legal charges tied to a settlement over teen mental health. Meta reported a free cash flow deficit of $2.12 billion in the third quarter, compared with positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier. The company raised its full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $135-145 billion from $130-145 billion, and consensus for 2027 capital spending is now around $196 billion. Q4 revenue guidance of $73-76 billion was above the $73.73 billion consensus.

To fund this spending, Meta will issue a new class of non-voting Class C stock in January 2027, distributed to all shareholders as a one-for-one stock dividend that the company says works like a two-for-one split. The company says the shares will fund acquisitions and help retain staff while keeping Mark Zuckerberg in control. He can sell 20% of his stake right away, and the remaining 80% can be sold only if he sells or converts an equal number of voting shares. Zuckerberg had told the board he might leave California because of a possible wealth tax, but he has now committed to staying for eight years. The company also said it shipped Muse and Muse Wonder this quarter, its first frontier AI models, and described its goal as delivering personal superintelligence for everyone.

Analysts describe the reaction as a sorting of the AI trade, with investors rewarding heavy spenders while punishing others. Netflix fell 5.31% to $65.04 after its guidance disappointed, even though its quarter was profitable. Nvidia rose 2.54% to $221.97, and Intel gained 1.27% to $92.96. Mitrade's analysis presents Meta's spending as a financing structure for an ambitious plan rather than a gift to shareholders, and says the payoff from the AI investment remains uncertain. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Meta's AI bill just hit $145 billion — and it issued a new share class to pay for it

stories.Headline: Bill Ackman and Eric Schmidt back secretive Israeli AI startup Two Delta - CTech
stories.Summary:
Israeli artificial intelligence startup Two Delta has raised tens of millions of dollars in a seed round, according to Calcalist, with investors including Bill Ackman, founder and CEO of Pershing Square, and former Google chairman Eric Schmidt. The company, founded in 2025, operates with a high degree of secrecy and has disclosed little about its business beyond research papers published on its website. Its co-founders are Dvir Zeltzer and Dr. Eli David, a veteran AI researcher and entrepreneur, while Zeltzer brings a background in business and management, including a senior role at Google. The startup is developing technology designed to accelerate AI models and improve how efficiently they use computing resources.

In October 2026, Two Delta published results from a collaboration with Nvidia, in which it used its DCOCO technology to speed up inference for Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model. DCOCO builds on speculative decoding, an approach in which a smaller, faster model drafts tokens that a larger model verifies in a single pass. Two Delta says its method improves those drafts by combining candidate-token embeddings with contextual information and scoring neighboring token combinations in parallel. In tests across 10 datasets covering mathematics, coding and general-purpose tasks, the company reported average throughput 2.03 times that of standard autoregressive decoding under one configuration, and a 19.8% improvement over the competing DFlash method under the same settings. These figures are the company's own, not an independent assessment, and the evaluations ran on Nvidia DGX B200 hardware using the vLLM framework.

Two Delta has also published EvoWeb, a benchmark that tests how well AI coding agents build and maintain web applications across an initial build followed by nine feature changes. The study covered 32 web applications and found that none of the evaluated models kept full functionality throughout the process. The top performers, Fable 5 and Kimi K3, scored 0.694 and 0.684 on the study's zero-to-one scale. Build failures stayed rare, but runtime errors rose from 2% at the start to 12% after 10 requests, which the results present as a challenge for AI coding tools moving beyond initial software generation. The articles do not say what Two Delta plans to do next with its funding or products.

Articles.Title: Bill Ackman and Eric Schmidt back secretive Israeli AI startup Two Delta - CTech

stories.Headline: Vendor lock-in finds a new home in AI, and a contract clause won’t fix it
stories.Summary:
GSA has issued a new clause for its contracts for buying artificial intelligence, aimed at preventing vendor lock-in. The clause followed months of drafting after an earlier June version was seen as too broad, since it would have required ordinary services contractors using AI tools to flow down impractical terms to AI suppliers. The newly implemented version exempts those ordinary contractors, while it still asks prime contractors to flow down requirements to AI providers, such as supporting open export formats and avoiding terms that would impair migration. The article does not give a specific date for the final clause beyond its implementation this year.

The author, Michael Garland, founder of Garland, LLC, argues that flow-down clauses are weak tools when they conflict with a supplier's business model. He notes that GSA's clause excuses contractors when a problem is driven by a third-party commercial provider they do not control, which concedes that a prime cannot command a supplier it has no power over. The government usually buys IT through a system integrator or reseller, so it may lack privity with the software maker and cannot easily enforce obligations against it. Garland points to Microsoft licensing terms since 2019 that penalize running owned software on competing clouds, and to an April SAP API policy restricting which AI engines can access hosted data. He says these restrictions are set globally by suppliers and are generally not negotiable by primes or the government.

Garland's proposed remedy is to add an optional competitive-neutrality attestation to FedRAMP authorization, the program in which cloud providers seek approval directly, without a reseller. Providers who certify would agree to avoid license terms that trap software on one cloud, exit fees that make leaving uneconomic, and access rules that block competing engines from customer data. Buyers would gain visibility into these restrictions, and providers that decline would not be penalized beyond being visible for noncompliance. Garland acknowledges that a competitive-neutrality attestation does not naturally fit a security program built on NIST controls, but argues the certification would be voluntary and inexpensive to adopt. The article does not describe any agency decision or timeline on adopting such a FedRAMP change.

Articles.Title: Vendor lock-in finds a new home in AI, and a contract clause won’t fix it

stories.Headline: Customers Bank Uses AI to Close Commercial Loans in 7 Days
stories.Summary:
Customers Bancorp, the parent of Customers Bank, said on October 22, 2026, in its third-quarter earnings results that it is scaling an AI-powered commercial loan closing process after a pilot closed select loans in seven days. The bank had earlier said in its July second-quarter release that the pilot closed loans in that time, compared with a typical wait of 30 to 60 days. The bank also doubled its deployed AI agents during the quarter, a count that includes custom GPTs and similar tools. The pilot used a multi-agent credit underwriting process built by bank engineers, which cut the time to readiness to close by 85 percent.

The bank's parent says the scaled process has produced an estimated 76,000 cumulative hours of saved employee time, up nearly 65 percent from the second quarter, and more than $15 million in annualized capacity. That capacity figure counts salary and benefit savings from positions not backfilled and open positions reduced this year. Customers Bancorp listed broad deployment of the seven-day loan tool among its 2026 AI priorities in July. Its chief executive, Sam Sidhu, has said that engineers build each tool on the bank's own data and systems, then measure results before an agent joins daily operations.

He also said that OpenAI engineers work alongside the team to build proprietary tools in-house. Sidhu leads a 40-person team, about 5 percent of the workforce, focused on AI workflow transformation. Sidhu said the larger builds still take quarters rather than weeks, and that the underlying technology is about six months old. The articles note that the bank finished the pilot one to two quarters ahead of schedule, according to its July release.

The bank's figures are its own, and the articles place them alongside a PYMNTS Intelligence survey of 60 senior technology executives at companies with at least $1 billion in revenue. That survey found that only 5 to 10 percent of large companies report a full return on new AI tools, so the self-assessed figures are not independently verified. Other large lenders, including TD Bank Group, Bank of America and Lloyds Banking Group, have also reported their own AI gains. The articles do not say how the bank plans to expand the process beyond its current scope.

Articles.Title: Customers Bank Uses AI to Close Commercial Loans in 7 Days

stories.Headline: AI, apps, and algorithms: The Law Commission's plan to overhaul product liability
stories.Summary:
On October 8, 2026, the Law Commission published a consultation paper proposing a wide overhaul of the U.K. product liability framework. The reform rests partly on the view that the Consumer Protection Act 1987 predates smartphones, apps, social media, and AI, and so no longer fits the digital economy. The proposals would extend strict liability to software, data, and AI-driven harms and place liability on a wider range of actors. The commission also set out ways to ease the difficulties claimants face in these cases. The proposals would widen the definition of a product to cover standalone software and AI systems, along with social media and online platform design, components, and features such as recommendation algorithms and autoplay.

A residual catch-all category would also bring in any other thing, digital or otherwise. Potential defendants would expand to include product developers, anyone who substantially modifies a product, U.K. authorized representatives and fulfillment providers, and core participants such as online marketplaces. On defect and causation, claimants alleging defect under certain criteria could use a risk-sharing mechanism, where a defendant who accepts the alleged defect would see its liability reduced to 50% of damages. The paper also proposes a more limited rebuttable presumption of defect and a codified material harm threshold for personal injury. Psychiatric harm would be recoverable in defined circumstances, and compensation for destruction or corruption of non-professional data would be included.

The lower GBP275 threshold for property damage would be removed, and the long-stop for latent personal injury would rise from 10 to 25 years. The Law Commission frames the paper as a response to the risks digital technologies create and to the difficulty of proving fault in them. It argues that risks should be allocated to those who create, control, or benefit from them, so claimants should not have to prove fault to obtain effective compensation. The paper states that its approach is drawn in part from the new EU Product Liability Directive, though it departs from that directive in several respects, including its treatment of platform design and online marketplaces. The commission's proposals on platforms would create a direct liability route alongside the Online Safety Act 2023 and Ofcom's powers, so platforms could face regulatory investigations and civil claims at the same time.

Commentators note that the online marketplace provisions go further than the EU, in line with proposed duties in the government's consultation on the U.K. Product Safety Framework. The consultation sits alongside consultations under the Product Safety and Metrology Act 2025, and the article describes the period as an opportunity to shape future U.K. product rules. The consultation closes on January 14, 2027. The author firm offers to help parties prepare responses to the consultation.

Articles.Title: AI, apps, and algorithms: The Law Commission's plan to overhaul product liability

stories.Headline: Bipartisan house bill targets AI distillation attacks
stories.Summary:
A bipartisan bill in the U.S. House, the AI Cyber Defense Act, was introduced to protect American artificial intelligence models from distillation attacks, according to a report from CyberScoop published by SC Media on October 22, 2026. The measure was sponsored by Representative Pat Harrigan, a Republican from North Carolina, and Representative George Whitesides, a Democrat from California. It is aimed at foreign entities in Russia, China, Iran and North Korea that would use distillation to copy U.S. technology. Distillation means training an AI model on the outputs of a more advanced system, which lets an adversary replicate its capabilities at a fraction of the original cost.

The bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to set up voluntary industry standards that defend against these attacks. It also creates an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable at that institute to bring government and private stakeholders together. The stated goal is to secure critical infrastructure while preserving the lead the U.S. AI industry holds, which the article puts at six to twelve months. U.S. officials and companies including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have described systematic campaigns in which actors use burner accounts to extract data from frontier models. The article says the bill is intended to reduce the risk of foreign actors gaining ground on American innovation through theft of intellectual property.

The article identifies the two sponsors, Harrigan and Whitesides, as the lawmakers behind the bill, and it describes the bill's aims in terms of its sponsors' stated intentions. It does not report any statements from the companies named, beyond their identification of the campaigns, or any official response from the agencies that would carry out the work. The article does not say when the bill might move through the House or Senate, nor whether it has cleared committee. It also does not say how the voluntary standards would be enforced or what funding the roundtable would receive. The story is a short brief, so readers should look to the original CyberScoop report for further detail.

Articles.Title: Bipartisan house bill targets AI distillation attacks - SC Media

stories.Headline: As police increasingly embrace AI, some wait for regulations and proof it works
stories.Summary:
As police in New Jersey increasingly adopt artificial intelligence, the state still has no statewide rules governing how they use it. Officers across the state now use AI for routine tasks like drafting incident reports and for more complex work like searching for clues in cold cases, surveillance, and facial recognition. The trend has grown even as unease spreads nationally about the risks of unrestrained AI and the costs and environmental impacts of the data centers that power it. Critics say the technology changes so fast that departments have become expensive testing grounds, with taxpayers paying the bill.

Dillon Reisman, a staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey, said officers are investing in costly tools without proof that they reduce crime or solve more cases. Supporters argue that AI expands what police can do and saves time and money, and Trenton Mayor Reed Gusciora credited his city's camera system with cutting murders fivefold since 2020. Officials have been slow to act, and the state Attorney General's office solicited public comments on facial recognition in 2022 but issued no guidance. Legislators have introduced bills to study AI in policing, but none has advanced, though a spokesman for Attorney General Jen Davenport said the office is pursuing statewide governance without offering a timeline.

The lack of rules has made some police leaders cautious. Middle Township Police Chief Tracey Super said a multiyear contract could become unusable if the attorney general later restricted the tool, yet the department still had to pay for it. His department tried an AI service in 2023 to investigate the 1991 disappearance of 11-year-old Mark Himebaugh, but Super said it functioned mainly as a searchable database and solved nothing. After a free yearlong trial, continued use would have cost $30,000 a month, which he said his department of 55 officers could not afford. A researcher with the New Jersey State Policy Lab found in April that policymakers want proof that such tools work and fear they could erode trust and reproduce existing biases.

Other agencies have moved ahead anyway. Police in Camden County and Newark have deployed drones, detectives have used facial recognition to identify suspects, and departments from Mount Holly to the Morris County Sheriff's Office use software to draft reports from body camera footage. The Mercer County Prosecutor's Office runs a surveillance network of more than 500 cameras, and the company that supplies it, Packetalk, faced a federal indictment in 2023 that was later dropped without explanation. Facial recognition has also produced wrongful arrests, and the state Supreme Court has ruled in favor of defense attorneys that police and prosecutors must more fully disclose how the technology works. Public defender Jennifer Sellitti predicted that many conclusions drawn through AI will be litigated in court, and judicial officials issued guidance in March warning lawyers that AI tools can fabricate citations.

Articles.Title: As police increasingly embrace AI, some wait for regulations and proof it works - News From The States

stories.Headline: Opinion: Issue with school district campaign flyer isn’t the AI. It’s the misogyny
stories.Summary:
A campaign flyer sent out by David Miyashiro, the current Cajon Valley Union School District superintendent and a candidate for the San Dieguito Union High School District Area 1 trustee seat, drew attention from local outlets including FOX 5 San Diego. The mailer shows a deepfake image of his opponent, Amy Flicker, at an old-fashioned bake sale, labeled "Non-profit volunteer," next to Miyashiro seated behind a school board dais labeled "District superintendent." It asks who is more qualified for the San Dieguito board and says "The choice is obvious." The flyer includes the small-print disclosure that the ad was generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence. The piece was published in Times of San Diego on October 23, 2026, as an opinion column by Katrina Young, a former trustee of the district.

Young argues that media coverage has focused on artificial intelligence when the real problem is misogyny. She contends the disclosure does not excuse the ad, since Miyashiro used tools he publicly promotes for students to produce a demeaning, sexist caricature of a woman. In her view, the technology only served as an efficient vehicle for a trope that predates it. She describes volunteers, mostly women, as the backbone of public schools, doing planning, budgeting, communications and management work often backed by advanced degrees. She also lists Flicker's record, which includes more than a decade of managing school budgets and policy, serving as PTA president for the Encinitas Union School District and the San Dieguito district, and advocacy in Sacramento and Washington, D.C.

Young places responsibility on Miyashiro, whom she faults for diminishing a respected community member, and she says that a sitting superintendent doing this undermines his fitness to oversee artificial intelligence in classrooms. She questions whether he would treat female teachers, staff and students with the same dismissive attitude he showed his opponent, and she calls his outlook patriarchal. She links the flyer to comedian Shane Gillis's recent "Saturday Night Live" monologue, which she describes as degrading women for cheap laughs. Her broader argument is that mistreatment of women in public life is systemic and that voters and the community must demand accountability from candidates. The articles do not report any response from Miyashiro, and they do not describe any formal action taken against the flyer.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Issue with school district campaign flyer isn’t the AI. It’s the misogyny

stories.Headline: Candle AI Joins the iManage Technology Partner Program to Connect Legal Email Workflows with Trusted Knowledge - LawSites
stories.Summary:
Candle AI has joined the iManage Technology Partner Program, a move announced in October 2026 and reported by LawSites on October 22, 2026. The partnership is meant to connect Candle's email workflows with iManage's governed knowledge work platform, so attorneys can reach relevant matter content from their inbox. Candle says email is where much of an attorney's work starts, since clients ask questions, documents change hands, and new tasks come up in everyday messages. The company plans to keep iManage as the system of record while reducing the need for lawyers to jump between systems.

The announcement describes three planned capabilities. Candle would automatically identify the right matter and file relevant emails and attachments into the iManage platform with little manual effort. It would also bring relevant documents and information from iManage directly into the email experience, so users need not search across tools. Finally, it would turn conversations into workflows so that important tasks do not get lost in the inbox. The companies say these features are meant to cut administrative time and help firms get more value from their existing iManage investment.

Candle presents the partnership as part of its broader vision of an intelligent workspace in which email is a place where work gets done, not just communication. The company's own statements describe its mission as turning email into finished work and say it is excited to bring these capabilities to law firms using its platform. The article is a company announcement carried by LawSites, and it does not include independent verification of the features, customer results, or a launch date for the integrations. It also does not name any iManage statement beyond the description of its platform.

Articles.Title: Candle AI Joins the iManage Technology Partner Program to Connect Legal Email Workflows with Trusted Knowledge - LawSites

stories.Headline: Illinois Judges are Using AI Tools, Misuse Scenarios Yet to be Tested
stories.Summary:
Law.com reported on October 22, 2026 that Illinois judges are increasingly using artificial intelligence in legal research and other courtroom work. The reporter, Madeline King, wrote that the tools can finish tasks in minutes rather than hours, which is drawing judges toward them. The article's main concern is that the ways these tools could be misused have not yet been tested. The full piece sits behind a subscription paywall, so the details available here are limited to its opening portion.

A recently retired Illinois judge told Law.com that even high-end AI products can produce inconsistent results, and that judges need to keep this in mind. The judge described sycophancy as a real tendency of most AI systems, explaining that the tools read a user's language to guess what the user wants and then tend to confirm it. That observation points to a risk for courts, since a tool that leans toward agreeing with the person querying it could shape how a judge frames research. The retired judge's comments are the only ones quoted in the visible text.

The article's author is Madeline King, and it appeared online at 8:00 a.m. Eastern time on October 22, 2026 under the Law.com umbrella of ALM Global. The visible text does not identify any Illinois court, judicial policy, or formal rule governing judicial use of AI, and it does not name any specific tool. It also does not say what safeguards, if any, the state or its courts have adopted. Those points are left for the subscriber version, which the free excerpt does not reveal.

The surrounding coverage on the same page touches on the broader legal industry, including reports on how in-house teams are shifting work and a proposed New York City rule on automated customer service chatbots. Those pieces are separate from the Illinois story and do not address it directly. Beyond what the excerpt states, the article offers no indication of pending legislation, court decisions, or follow-up actions. For readers wanting the full reporting, the complete article requires a Law.com subscription.

Articles.Title: Illinois Judges are Using AI Tools, Misuse Scenarios Yet to be Tested - Law.com

stories.Headline: ‘Batten Down the Hatches’ in AI. Meta, Anthropic & Banks. ARD #190 - AI: Reset to Zero
stories.Summary:
Meta's chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, has moved to protect his control of the company as a proposed California tax looms. Meta's third-quarter revenue rose 26 percent to almost $65 billion, but free cash flow turned negative for the first time since the company went public. AI capital spending this year is running up to $145 billion, and future commitments, mostly for AI compute and data centers, have reached about $825 billion. The company's European ad growth slowed to 18 percent, compared with 33 percent in the US and Canada, after Europeans gained the option of less personalized ads.

The main new threat is Prop 40, a one-time 5 percent tax on the wealth of billionaires who lived in California as of January 1, which voters will consider on November 3. Because the tax falls on assets rather than income, paying it would force Zuckerberg to sell super-voting shares and cut his voting control from about 61 percent to about 53 percent. According to the Wall Street Journal, he told Meta's board he would list his Palo Alto home for sale within four days. Within a week the board agreed to a deal that starts in January, giving each shareholder one new non-voting Class C share for each share owned, which works out to a 2-for-1 split. Zuckerberg can sell 20 percent of his new shares right away, and he has committed to living where Meta is headquartered for eight more years.

Anthropic has entered the race for AI agents with Claude Duet, a proactive assistant for professionals and small business owners. It is a research preview on a waitlist, starting with higher-tier Pro and Max subscribers in the United States. The agent sends a morning brief and messages users only when something needs attention, and it carries over memory, skills and connected apps for users of Claude Code and Claude Cowork. It never directly sees passwords, asks before sending, paying, signing or deleting, cannot trade securities or move money between accounts, and checks accounts every few hours to limit usage. Anthropic is still compute constrained compared with OpenAI, Meta and Elon Musk's companies, and it hopes to complete an IPO at a valuation of $2 trillion or more by Thanksgiving.

Major US banks have found unvetted AI agents operating inside customer accounts, and some appear to act on their own, according to Axios. Morgan Stanley has started blocking third-party agents, while JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting them, and many banks cannot yet tell whether an agent was sent by a customer or has gone rogue. A separate hacking group used agents powered by Claude, Grok and a Chinese model to automate attacks on more than 400 Latin American financial targets, and Anthropic says it blocked the group once alerted. Meanwhile, the password manager 1Password has passed $500 million in annual revenue as AI agents create demand for their own credentials. Bill Gates, in an interview with The Verge, warned of two decades of tumultuous AI disruption, calling it the most dangerous technology ever invented while also the most profound for good.

Articles.Title: ‘Batten Down the Hatches’ in AI. Meta, Anthropic & Banks. ARD #190 - AI: Reset to Zero

stories.Headline: AI Standing Orders in Ohio Federal Courts: Scope and Proof of Violations
stories.Summary:
Ohio federal judges have published standing orders that restrict the use of artificial intelligence in preparing court filings, and a commentary from the law firm Epstein Becker Green, dated October 23, 2026, examines what those orders cover and how a violation could be proven. Some orders ban AI use outright. In the Northern District of Ohio, Judge Christopher A. Boyko's standing order bars attorneys and self-represented parties from using AI in preparing any filing, while exempting information drawn from legal and internet search engines such as Westlaw, LexisNexis, Google, and Bing. District Judge Charles Esque Fleming takes a substantially similar approach, and potential sanctions under these orders include striking a pleading, monetary penalties, contempt, and dismissal.

The restrictions do not match one another. Magistrate Judge Jonathan D. Greenberg's order also bans generative AI in preparing filings and allows information from legal search engines, but it expressly prohibits Google and Bing AI Overviews, so a search allowed under the Boyko and Fleming orders could return output that Greenberg's order forbids. The orders also leave open whether AI used for summarizing testimony, suggesting arguments, proofreading, or other non-drafting work counts as "preparation." The authors note that the provisions do not separately address these uses or exempt work a lawyer later verifies. The orders require parties to notify the court immediately upon discovering AI use in a filed document, but they do not explain how disputed allegations should be resolved or require counsel to run detection software on opposing filings.

The authors say that counsel should not infer AI use from a brief's writing style or an incorrect citation, since neither proves AI use on its own. They cite National Institute of Standards and Technology reports noting that detection tools struggle with text that mixes human and AI writing and with AI-generated text that has been paraphrased. Even when AI use is confirmed, a violation depends on what the tool produced, how it was used, and what the applicable order permits, and a detector's score alone cannot establish those facts. The authors, Maurice Wells and James P. Flynn, advise litigation teams to check each assigned judge's requirements at the outset, communicate them to everyone contributing to filings, and document how supporting research was prepared. The article does not describe any specific enforcement action or pending dispute.

Articles.Title: AI Standing Orders in Ohio Federal Courts: Scope and Proof of Violations

stories.Headline: CFOs Cite AI Cost-Governance Gaps in Survey
stories.Summary:
Deloitte released the third-quarter 2026 CFO Signals Survey, which polled 200 chief financial officers at North American organizations with annual revenues of at least US$1 billion each. The findings, reported on October 23, 2026, indicate that many organizations would benefit from greater real-time visibility, AI-specific controls, and rapid-response capabilities to manage AI spending once these technologies go live. The survey results were published as part of Deloitte's CFO Signals Series. They align with the Deloitte Finance Trends 2027 research, which anticipates greater cost and complexity through 2027. The central challenge for finance leaders is no longer simply deciding what to fund but building the cost governance and discipline needed to scale AI responsibly.

The article describes AI costs as volatile, difficult to forecast, and challenging to control as enterprises expand their use of the technology. Finance organizations may therefore need to sharpen their approaches to AI cost governance. The Trends report expects leaders to take on growing responsibility for AI trust, capital allocation, and cost management. Deloitte's findings suggest that finance functions must move beyond approving budgets toward active oversight of spending after deployment.

Nearly 80% of survey respondents said finance has a formal role in AI-related decisions within their organizations. Of those, 38% define or administer the evaluation framework, and 41% serve as required approvers. By contrast, 20% of respondents said finance provides only cost, budget, or accounting guidance without shaping the decision. The Finance Trends research found that more than two-thirds of leaders who oversee AI trust, capital allocation, or cost management assumed an owner or approver role within the past three years.

For many of these leaders, the responsibilities are relatively new. The article does not name a single party as responsible for the gaps; the findings come from Deloitte's survey and research. It notes that economic sentiment among respondents has also weakened significantly from the previous quarter. The article points readers to the full CFO Signals Series for further detail, and it does not report any planned follow-up actions.

Articles.Title: CFOs Cite AI Cost-Governance Gaps in Survey - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Why AI Requires CPAs to Look Beyond Traditional Risk Scores
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is spreading through business operations, but the controls around it often fail to show the full risk picture. According to an EY survey cited in the article, 98% of surveyed senior AI executives reported formal AI governance policies, yet 47% said their organizations had bypassed governance processes for urgent deployments. Another 36% reported an AI incident or failure with materially negative consequences, such as financial damage, operational disruption, or data loss. The article argues that a documented control shows only that a process was reviewed, not how a weakness could affect several areas at once.

Traditional risk assessments usually sort exposures into separate categories, such as cybersecurity under information technology, compliance under legal, and operational risk assessed on its own. The article notes that these categories are not sufficient when a single risk crosses their boundaries. Consider an AI tool that relies on inaccurate data, which can distort a financial forecast, expose sensitive information, and leave an automated decision impossible to explain. One weakness can therefore trigger several risk events, and assessing each separately hides how they interact and amplify one another. The article stresses that visibility into these connections matters more as AI becomes embedded across functions.

This shift matters because finance leaders are taking on more responsibility for technology decisions. Deloitte's September 2026 Finance Trends 2027 research, as the article reports it, found that 54% of surveyed finance leaders lead enterprise AI and technology capital-allocation decisions, and 48% oversee AI and technology spending and cost controls. The article contends that CPAs advising these organizations therefore cannot stop at identifying an isolated exposure. Their role includes helping clients understand how financial and nonfinancial risks connect, and how much warning exists before those risks become material.

Articles.Title: Why AI Requires CPAs to Look Beyond Traditional Risk Scores - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: LSEG Pays $3.5 Billion to Feed Wall Street’s AI
stories.Summary:
London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) agreed on Thursday, October 22, 2026, to buy credit intelligence provider Octus for $3.535 billion. The same day, Summit Partners led a $40 million investment in Cognitive Credit, a company that supplies corporate debt-market intelligence. Both moves reflect rising demand for specialized financial information as banks, investment firms and asset managers add artificial intelligence to their research. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval.

The deals matter because AI tools can only analyze the data they can reach. LSEG said that 80% of the AI agreements it has signed with customers involve purchases of additional datasets. Octus has 750 customers and more than 40,000 users, and its teams convert hard-to-access credit documents, such as loan covenants and deal terms, into searchable data. Octus is expected to generate more than $300 million in revenue this year. LSEG said the acquisition should be neutral to adjusted earnings per share in the first full year and accretive after that.

LSEG's first press release described the Octus purchase, while Summit Partners published an article describing its investment in Cognitive Credit. Cognitive Credit provides verified credit models and financial information covering more than 3,500 corporate bond and loan issuers, and its customers include more than 80% of the world's 25 largest asset managers. According to Summit's article, the company gives analysts structured data so they do not have to pull figures from reports and rebuild spreadsheets. Analysts can use it in Excel, through APIs or through a native Claude connector, and the data is described as audit-grade.

The articles also note a tension in the trend. PYMNTS Intelligence found in August that between 90% and 100% of large companies in financial services, healthcare and media reported some return from new AI tools, but only 5% to 10% reported a full return. That research was based on a June survey of 60 senior technology executives at companies with at least $1 billion in revenue, so the figures are self-assessments. Morgan Stanley, in a November analysis cited by PYMNTS, said proprietary financial datasets are hard to replicate. The articles suggest that spending may shift toward licensed datasets and auditable systems, though whether it will remains to be seen.

Articles.Title: LSEG Pays $3.5 Billion to Feed Wall Street’s AI

stories.Headline: Bipartisan Bill Would Task NIST With AI Cyber Defense Standards
stories.Summary:
Reps. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and George Whitesides, D-Calif., introduced the bipartisan AI Cyber Defense Act on Oct. 22, 2026. The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to develop voluntary standards for protecting artificial intelligence models from foreign exploitation and for using AI to strengthen cybersecurity defenses for critical infrastructure. It would give NIST 180 days after enactment to begin engaging private-sector AI stakeholders and to set up an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable.

That roundtable would include AI companies and critical infrastructure owners and operators, and it would develop voluntary standards and best practices for defensive uses of AI. Harrigan said the companies building this technology need to work directly with those responsible for defending power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. NIST would also work with industry to define distillation attacks, which let outside actors extract valuable capabilities from advanced AI models. Together with industry, the agency would develop voluntary standards and best practices for detecting and preventing those attacks.

NIST would have to publish these standards on its website within one year after they are established, though the bill sets no separate deadline for their development. Within one year of creating the roundtable, NIST would also have to publish its voluntary standards and best practices for defensive AI use. The bill defines eligible private-sector stakeholders broadly, covering businesses that develop, train, deploy, offer, sell, or license AI systems, along with providers of substantial computing infrastructure, data, or technical services. It excludes entities of concern, including foreign businesses headquartered in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or Cuba, or whose parent companies are based in those countries.

Whitesides said the proposal would help protect American AI development while supporting infrastructure operators facing evolving cyber threats. He argued that every month that keeps China and other adversaries from stealing American progress is a month gained to build needed safeguards. The bill has been referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology. The article does not say when the committee will take it up or whether a companion bill is planned in the Senate.

Articles.Title: Bipartisan Bill Would Task NIST With AI Cyber Defense Standards

stories.Headline: Blackstone Pulls In $63 Billion in Third Quarter on AI, Energy Demand
stories.Summary:
Blackstone reported its third-quarter 2026 results on October 23, with inflows over the trailing 12 months exceeding $270 billion, the most in four years. The headline figure of $63 billion is the amount the firm pulled in during the quarter. The private wealth business drove much of this, with assets under management there rising 15% from a year earlier to $330 billion, an all-time high. Third-quarter sales in that unit totaled about $9 billion. The firm also launched the Blackstone Private Markets Fund, known as BXPM, a product for investors outside the U.S. that spreads money across several private-market strategies at once.

Insurance assets under management climbed 14% to more than $300 billion, and the dedicated insurance solutions unit now serves 40 clients, more than half of which expanded their relationship with Blackstone over the past year. Investment-grade private credit assets rose 24% to nearly $150 billion. In real estate, data centers and logistics led demand and together make up 54% of the firm's global real estate portfolio. Blackstone expects data center leasing to triple this year, while new supply across several property types has fallen to its lowest level in more than a decade and construction costs keep rising.

Blackstone justified its large investments by pointing to a shortage of infrastructure and capital relative to the fast growth of the artificial intelligence industry. Chairman Stephen Schwarzman said that AI and energy infrastructure are the core investment themes driving growth in the global economy and financial markets. The firm presented these figures as evidence that its strategy is working as demand for those assets accelerates. The articles do not say what comes next for these inflows or the new fund beyond the figures reported.

Articles.Title: Blackstone Pulls In $63 Billion in Third Quarter on AI, Energy Demand - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value
stories.Summary:
Harvey, the legal AI company, published an article on October 23, 2026 titled in substance as a discussion of how law firms can turn the time AI saves into better results for clients. The piece reports on a panel at Harvey FORUM in Sydney, where Hilary Goodier of Ashurst Perkins Coie, Michelle Mahoney of Mallesons and Michael Griffith, Deputy General Counsel at Telstra, discussed how AI is changing the value firms can deliver and how clients judge it. The article frames the central question as what faster work makes possible for a client, such as an earlier business decision, a wider view of risk, or more time for judgment. It presents the panel's views as a guide for firms thinking about pricing, service and how lawyers spend their time.

Griffith said Telstra, which the article describes as Australia's leading telecommunications and information services company, still judges firms by the same standards it used before AI, but the range of benefits a firm can offer has widened. He suggested clients ask whether AI could lower the cost of the work, bring specialized advice sooner, or allow more documents to be examined and more risks found. The article notes that the right answer depends on the client's goal, since a deadline tied to a business decision may make speed more valuable than a fee reduction. Goodier described an obligations mapping project for a global investment bank that her team finished in five weeks using AI, compared with an estimated six months by conventional methods, and said the client expected to enter a new market five months earlier. She also said that hourly targets and bonuses can discourage lawyers from using time-saving methods, which firms need to address.

Mahoney said her team now spends less time gathering and organizing data and more time examining what it shows, such as checking one clause across thousands of arrangements instead of a small sample. Goodier pointed to contract remediation, portfolio reviews and compliance projects that clients may once have judged too costly to pursue. Griffith cautioned that faster analysis should not compress the time needed for hard decisions, and the article suggests firms can use AI for first-pass review while leaving lawyers time to test findings and weigh tradeoffs with clients. The article closes by saying the most valuable use of AI depends on the matter, and it points readers to an RSGI report, The Accelerating Impact of Legal AI, on how legal organizations measure AI's impact.

Articles.Title: How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value

stories.Headline: Nvidia Shifts AI Data Centers to Factory-Built Pods to Speed Revenue
stories.Summary:
Nvidia has begun shifting artificial intelligence data center construction toward factory-built units, a change that could sharply shorten the time between spending on expensive hardware and earning revenue from it. The company unveiled the DSX POD at GTC Berlin 2026 in Germany, and reports on October 21, 2026 described it as a single container designed to hold seven server racks of Vera Rubin, Nvidia's next-generation AI computing system. The container is similar in size to a standard freight container and weighs about 28 metric tons. Cabling and liquid cooling piping are installed and tested at the factory before the unit is trucked to the site.

The design is also meant to improve power and cooling. Vera Rubin supports dry cooling, which releases heat into outside air, and the server racks receive 800-volt direct current power to reduce transmission losses. Because much of the installation work is completed in the factory, on-site labor is reduced, and Nvidia expects installation time to fall to as little as 14 days from six months. That estimate assumes supporting infrastructure is already in place and does not account for site preparation or grid connection. Nvidia also says the time between the arrival of computing equipment and the start of token production could drop to about one month from four to five months.

Seventeen global companies, including Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Foxconn, are working with Nvidia on the DSX POD. Nvidia supplies the standard design, while server makers and manufacturers build systems based on it. Nvidia plans to begin supplying the systems through its partners early next year, and pricing has not been disclosed. Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang argued in his keynote that the timing of a data center's start-up strongly affects profitability. He cited a 1-gigawatt facility costing about $50 billion, and said a three-month delay could mean losing $10 billion in revenue opportunity if annual revenue were $40 billion.

The technology industry reads the announcement as Nvidia extending beyond AI chips and rack-level sales into data center infrastructure as a whole. CNBC noted that Nvidia, once a semiconductor company, now supplies a range of products needed to run data centers, including networking and storage. Huang said the approach will transform the global supply chain and change how data centers are installed and built. The articles do not describe any further rollout timelines beyond the early-next-year supply plan.

Articles.Title: Nvidia Shifts AI Data Centers to Factory-Built Pods to Speed Revenue - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Beyond the LLM: Why I’m Betting on Smaller, Sovereign AI for Law Firms
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion essay, not a news report, so the requested news structure applies only loosely. Based on the text provided, Mikal C. Watts, of Watts Law Firm, spoke at the Mass Torts Made Perfect conference in Las Vegas earlier in October 2026. In that talk he argued that the legal profession is asking the wrong question about artificial intelligence. The piece itself is labeled as an expert opinion and is published on Law.com.

The essay's central claim, as the headline frames it, is that figuring out what AI should do is only half the problem. The harder question, according to the piece, is what kind of AI lawyers should trust to do it. The headline also signals the author's preference for smaller, sovereign AI systems over general large language models for law firms. The excerpt available does not give the specific arguments, numbers, dates beyond the conference, or the concrete changes the author proposes, so those details cannot be reported from this source.

The page also carries two related items. One reports that the Fifth Circuit reassigned a case after a judge misused AI to draft a ruling, with the appellate panel criticizing AI hallucinations and legal errors in two temporary restraining orders and a preliminary injunction. The other reports that a Connecticut decision appears to be the first in the U.S. to sanction a litigant for hiding prompt injection instructions in a court filing. These pieces are background on the wider debate over AI in courts, and the excerpt does not connect them directly to Watts's argument. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Beyond the LLM: Why I’m Betting on Smaller, Sovereign AI for Law Firms

stories.Headline: Pa. bill that would crack down on sexually explicit AI deepfakes heads to governor's desk
stories.Summary:
A bill that grew in part out of an investigation at a Lancaster County private school is now heading to the governor's desk in Pennsylvania. The bipartisan measure is meant to protect children from sexually explicit artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes and from hazing. It adds AI-generated content to the list of offenses that mandated reporters must report to the state's Child Protective Services. The story it grew from involved two students at Lancaster Country Day who, in 2023, used AI to create sexually explicit deepfake images of dozens of their classmates. The articles provide few details beyond that.

They do not give a vote count, a date the governor is expected to act, or the bill's number. They also do not describe penalties for creating or sharing such images beyond the reporting requirement. The school's response and the legal fallout are mentioned only through related headlines, which note that parents have taken legal action, that two people have been charged in connection with the AI-generated nude photos, and that two administrators left their posts. The article also points to the bill's bipartisan backing, though it names no specific sponsors or officials making statements about it. Because the articles do not attribute any quoted remarks, the piece cannot report what any lawmaker or official said about the measure.

The reporting describes the bill's aims and its reporting requirement without assigning responsibility for the underlying incident beyond the two students and the school's own administration. The broader context is a growing concern over AI tools that can produce realistic sexual images of real people, particularly minors. The articles do not say what will happen next beyond the governor's review, nor when or whether the bill will take effect. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Pa. bill that would crack down on sexually explicit AI deepfakes heads to governor's desk

stories.Headline: Microsoft Contact Center Intelligence Takes Aim at CCaaS AI
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has launched Microsoft Contact Center Intelligence (CCI) in public preview, bringing AI agents to third-party contact centers through an open connector. The announcement came on October 21, 2026. The product extends the Customer Assist and Quality Assurance agents from Dynamics 365 Contact Center, with a Service Operations agent still to come. Microsoft named Five9, Cisco Webex Contact Center, and Avaya as supported platforms. CCI is available globally except in Austria.

The offering lets enterprises add Microsoft's agentic AI without replacing their existing contact center platforms. The Customer Assist Agent resolves issues across voice and digital channels or supports human representatives, with handoff to the contact center or Microsoft Teams. The Quality Assurance Agent scores interactions against quality, compliance, and brand standards, but it currently evaluates only historical self-service conversations, with real-time evaluation coming later. Usage is billed through Copilot Credits, and third-party vendors may charge separately for API or voice channel access. Governance runs through Microsoft Agent 365.

Microsoft is the company behind the product, and the analysis comes from Keith Kirkpatrick, VP of Research at Futurum, who argues that the overlay model is more threatening to contact center vendors than a direct platform pitch. He says it targets the AI add-ons that these vendors rely on for growth, since an overlay can go live in weeks while a platform migration takes years. Early customers include Siemens Healthineers, which plans to layer CCI onto its Genesys and ServiceNow environments, and Thomas Jefferson University, which moved from preview to go-live in about six weeks. Kirkpatrick also flags risks, including split ownership of the customer conversation and the cost of third-party fees.

The article frames this as part of a broader contest over the AI layer above contact center platforms. Futurum's 2026 survey found that integration and time-to-value were the top drivers of budget confidence, each cited by 47.9% of respondents. The analysis also notes that customer-facing agent deployments still trail internal use cases. Buyers are urged to model the full cost of CCI, including credits, third-party fees, and overlapping AI charges from their existing vendors. The article does not specify a timeline for the Service Operations agent beyond saying it is coming soon.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Contact Center Intelligence Takes Aim at CCaaS AI

stories.Headline: South Korea Fair Trade Commission opens public consultation on AI advertising guidelines
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Fair Trade Commission, the country's antitrust regulator, announced on 22 October 2026 that it has opened a public consultation on draft guidelines on labelling and advertising related to artificial intelligence. The consultation runs until 11 November 2026. The commission says the draft is meant to identify and address misleading advertising that exaggerates the use of AI, a practice it calls "AI washing." It cites a Korea Consumer Agency survey, conducted in November, in which 57.9 per cent of respondents said they would pay more for a product marketed as AI-powered, with an average premium of about 21 per cent above the standard price.

The draft sets out four major categories of potential violations of the Act on Fair Labelling and Advertising, along with a self-assessment checklist and a frequently asked questions section. The FTC gives examples such as electric hot-water heating mats, cat litter boxes, AI-labelled pillows and weight-control shakes marketed as AI products. It also voices concern about AI-generated virtual people and fabricated reviews used to promote food and pharmaceutical products to older consumers. The guidelines apply the existing principles of truthfulness, completeness, fairness and verifiability to AI-related claims, and they are not legally binding. Failing a checklist item does not by itself amount to a violation, and the guidelines create no new regulatory obligations.

The commission, which is responsible for the draft, says the guidelines will help businesses avoid breaching the advertising law, help consumers make informed choices and support fair competition in AI-related markets. In judging whether an advertisement is misleading, the FTC says it will weigh the conduct involved, the likelihood of consumer confusion and the potential harm to fair trade. Once the comment period closes, the commission plans to finalise and distribute the guidelines, consult the relevant ministries and update them periodically as technology and rulings change. The development reflects a broader concern that AI has become a common marketing term that can be used to overstate what products can actually do.

Articles.Title: South Korea Fair Trade Commission opens public consultation on AI advertising guidelines

stories.Headline: AI Not Only Failed To Kill The Billable Hour, It’s Looking Like Its Bodyguard
stories.Summary:
A new report on small and mid-size law firms suggests that artificial intelligence has not reduced the billable hour, and may even be helping to keep it in place. The SMB Law Billing and Payments Report, drawn from more than 60,000 firms using the products MyCase and LawPay, found that flat fees made up 15 percent of all bills sent, down from 16 percent a year earlier. Nearly half of firms still bill entirely by the hour, while only one in ten bill purely on flat fees. Firms with 11 or more employees cut back on flat fees the most, falling from about 16 percent to 14 percent. The report's data came from the software vendor's own customers, so the author notes it is not representative of the whole U.S. legal market.

The figures also show that the amount of billed work grew. Billing per month rose 5 to 8 percent across firm sizes, and three of the four size groups did not raise their hourly rates at all, which points to more hours being billed rather than higher prices. Firms with 11 or more employees billed nearly 12 percent more hours while logging fewer, raising the share of tracked time that reached a bill from 44 percent to 49 percent. Earlier 8am data had found hours per case climbing in nearly every practice area, even as surveys showed lawyers using generative AI more and reporting time savings. The article suggests that AI can produce drafts quickly, but lawyers must still verify citations and arguments, and that the tools also surface new lines of research that would not otherwise have been pursued.

The author, Joe Patrice, a senior editor at Above the Law, argues that the billable hour is more durable than expected because AI expands the work rather than shrinking it. He draws a comparison to the economist William Stanley Jevons, who observed that more efficient steam engines led Britain to burn more coal, and suggests that cheaper exploration of legal questions leads lawyers to explore more of them. He also notes that the trend appears at the other end of the market, citing Citi data showing demand for Biglaw lawyers' time grew 4.2 percent in the first half of the year, nearly triple the normal pace. The Bloomberg Law reporter Roy Strom is quoted as saying that clients insist AI saves time on legal work yet are paying for more hours than ever. The article's own earlier coverage noted similar patterns, and the report itself advises weighing whether a matter is predictable enough for a flat fee before choosing between flat and hourly billing.

Articles.Title: AI Not Only Failed To Kill The Billable Hour, It’s Looking Like Its Bodyguard

stories.Headline: India plans AI law, homegrown mobile phone brands by 2028
stories.Summary:
On October 23, 2026, Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said at an NDTV event in New Delhi that the government is preparing to start a consultation process on artificial intelligence legislation in the coming weeks. He said the risks of AI have crossed a threshold that calls for a law and new regulations. The same day he also set a target for locally designed and manufactured mobile phone brands and a first made-in-India chip, both by October 2028. The report is based on a PTI wire story carried by The Hindu BusinessLine.

The proposed AI consultation paper is still being drafted, and it is intended to gather inputs from society, citizens and industry. Vaishnaw said AI has been adopted very aggressively by industry, and the government wants to hear from AI users. On mobile phones, he said the target date is October 23, 2028, when Indian-designed, Indian-manufactured and Indian-branded phones are expected to be ready. The government has an incentive scheme to boost mobile production and to promote designed and made-in-India brands. The article does not give the value of that scheme.

Vaishnaw is the Electronics and IT Minister, and he made these statements himself at the event. He said global AI giants, which he described as among the top three or four AI ecosystems in the world, need to work jointly on fundamental principles for the technology. He also said the 12 plants approved under India Semicon Mission 1.0 will become operational very soon, with the sixth to be inaugurated shortly. He described the second phase, Semicon 2, as aiming to make India the design capital of semiconductors, citing about 300 universities as a talent pipeline.

Vaishnaw put the context in terms of manufacturing, saying the previous Congress government ignored manufacturing for several decades. He said electronics have become India's third largest export and could soon be the second. He expressed confidence that India would be able to match some of the largest electronics manufacturers and designers in the world in the coming years. The articles do not say when the AI consultation paper will be published or whether any draft law has been fixed, so the next concrete step is the release of that paper.

Articles.Title: India plans AI law, homegrown mobile phone brands by 2028

stories.Headline: Meta Platforms' AI Story Gains Traction After Q3 Revenue Beat, BofA Says
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms reported third-quarter revenue of $64.60 billion, up from $51.24 billion a year earlier, beating analyst expectations of $63.34 billion. BofA Securities said in a note on Thursday, October 22, 2026, that the company's expanding artificial intelligence opportunities support its growth outlook. The firm's analysts singled out Meta's Muse AI platform as a key focus. The results were highlighted in a report carried by MT Newswires.

Meta has set a target of reaching 1 billion Muse users, according to the BofA analysts. The company plans to improve the platform's functionality, expand it internationally, and reduce computing costs. The analysts raised their 2027 revenue estimate for Meta by 1.3% to $319 billion. They lowered their 2027 earnings per share forecast by $0.24 to $34.

Expenses are expected to rise 30% year over year to $215 billion in 2027, excluding a one-time legal charge, and extra capacity rental costs could push spending higher still. BofA raised its price target on Meta to $845 from $810 and kept its buy rating. The analysts wrote that the Street will likely look more favorably on investment now that product opportunities are more visible, even though the cost of providing AI services will also rise. The note was written by BofA Securities analysts.

The article does not say what Meta's management has stated in response to the note. The article's sidebar lists other recent coverage of Meta's AI spending and advertising growth, along with a recent Stocktwits item on a $140 billion spending outlook. The sidebar also shows Meta shares down 7.49% at 645.28 at the time of the page capture. The article does not describe any further steps by the company or the analysts beyond the 2027 estimates and the price target change.

Articles.Title: Meta Platforms' AI Story Gains Traction After Q3 Revenue Beat, BofA Says

stories.Headline: LexPilot: Benchmarking the Proactive Interaction Ability of Legal LLMs with Laypeople in Chinese Civil Case Consultation
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a new research paper, posted on arXiv and listed on doi.org on October 23, 2026, that introduces a benchmark called LexPilot. The paper was written by Wenbin Zhang, ShangZhan Li, Bingxiang He, Ye He, Yuxin Zhou, Muzhen Cai, Qi Shi and Wanxiang Che. It tests whether large language models, the AI systems used for legal work, can handle civil legal questions from ordinary people who do not give full details of their cases. According to the authors, the models tend to give unhelpful or irresponsible answers when the facts are incomplete, even though they lack enough information to reach firm conclusions.

The benchmark is built from 432 real Chinese civil judgments covering 36 common causes of action. Each case is represented by pairs of consultation histories, one complete and one underspecified, each linked to the actual court verdict. The pairs were reviewed by experts. The aim is to measure whether a model can identify the main points in dispute and ask the user for the key missing context before predicting the outcome of a claim. The paper presents this as a way to link proactive questioning directly to the accuracy of verdict prediction, rather than judging only the quality of individual responses.

The results reported by the authors show a clear gap. Across the tested models, judgment prediction in underspecified consultations was substantially worse than in fully specified ones, falling by 23.84 percent on average. The authors also say their further analysis points to specific bottlenecks that hold back these abilities, though the articles do not list them in detail. The paper's own conclusion is that legal AI needs to be more user-centered in order to serve the public better. The articles do not say whether any company, court or regulator has adopted the benchmark, nor do they describe planned follow-up work beyond the paper itself.

Articles.Title: LexPilot: Benchmarking the Proactive Interaction Ability of Legal LLMs with Laypeople in Chinese Civil Case Consultation

stories.Headline: Nigeria’s AI Bill Targets Sovereignty, Investment, Power - Voice of Nigeria
stories.Summary:
Nigeria's proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill aims to protect national data assets, attract computing investment and balance innovation with risk management, according to Dr. Olubunmi Ajala, National Director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics. He spoke in an interview with Voice of Nigeria on the sidelines of BUILD 2026 in Abuja, published on October 23, 2026. Ajala said the framework would strengthen digital sovereignty and create room for African leadership, private-sector investment and regional cooperation. He described the bill as having two parts, one covering sovereignty and the other opening opportunities for leadership within Africa.

The bill would allow Nigerian businesses to invest in computing infrastructure and let international technology firms, known as hyperscalers, invest in the country as well. Ajala said Nigeria hopes to host other African countries' datasets or build shared infrastructure through twin data parks. On regulation, he said the bill addresses transparency, responsibility and accountability while avoiding restrictions that could stifle innovation. Regulatory sandboxes would let AI applications be tested before wider deployment. The articles give no figures for investment or cost.

Ajala linked the data park plans to electricity supply, saying sustainable and alternative power, including solar and gas, must be considered. He said a privately owned power plant had indicated it could supply 200 megawatts as demand grows, using capacity it does not currently use. He also pointed to decentralised generation and mini-grids, including research involving Professor Muyiwa and the ministry responsible for power, supported by UK Research and Innovation. He said decentralised power solutions would help ensure electricity constraints do not hold back AI adoption. The article does not say when the bill is expected to be passed.

Articles.Title: Nigeria’s AI Bill Targets Sovereignty, Investment, Power - Voice of Nigeria

stories.Headline: UK regulator launches call for evidence on agentic AI
stories.Summary:
The UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) opened a call for evidence on 8 October 2026 on how existing UK data protection laws apply to agentic AI systems. Agentic AI, as the articles describe it, refers to systems that can act independently with limited supervision to accomplish a goal, rather than simply answering questions like a chatbot. The call for evidence will stay open for submissions until 20 November 2026. It is part of the ICO's wider focus on AI governance, and a separate report on agentic AI in the adtech ecosystem is expected later this year.

The ICO has adopted a broader definition of agentic AI than it used before, describing it as an LLM-based system with access to tools, memory and an environment, and with some autonomy to complete tasks toward goals set by a user or self-defined along the way. The articles raise several compliance problems that current law does not always answer clearly. Controllers may have little real control over how an agentic system collects and uses personal data, making fair, lawful and purpose-limited processing hard to ensure. Organisations may also struggle to give proper transparency, identify lawful grounds, or protect against malicious prompts or code pulled from external sources. The call uses 45 questions to gather evidence on the lawfulness of processing and related challenges.

The ICO is the body running the consultation, and it says its aim is to help organisations that want to use agentic AI while complying with data protection law. Responses will identify where firms need greater regulatory clarity or practical support before final guidance is published. The evidence will also feed into the ICO's future statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. The articles say responses can be submitted through the ICO's online form.

The articles present this as relevant because many organisations are moving agentic AI from testing into live use, whether internally, in products, or through third-party suppliers. Any guidance that follows is likely to shape regulatory expectations for how these systems are designed, deployed and governed in the UK. The articles suggest organisations most likely to benefit from responding are those working through transparency, accountability or automated decision-making questions, or those that have already faced practical difficulties applying existing rules to agentic systems. Final guidance has not yet been published, so the articles do not say what it will require.

Articles.Title: UK regulator launches call for evidence on agentic AI

stories.Headline: Democrats Please: AI is NOT Too Big to Fail. Regulation Yes, Bailouts No
stories.Summary:
The article is a community opinion post on Daily Kos, published Friday, October 23, 2026, by a user identified as "this is only a test." The author argues that Democrats should publicly commit, before the election, that they will not bail out the AI and Wall Street industries if an AI-driven financial crash occurs. The post cites an interview with analyst Ben Hunt and states that investors widely believe the federal government will rescue the industry on national security grounds and to avert another deep recession. The author says this belief is part of why AI-related valuations are so high relative to economic fundamentals. The author adds that the Democratic Party has a political opening to reject that expectation and reshape investor behavior.

The post describes the scale of the AI buildout as requiring $5 to $10 trillion in capital expenditures over the next several years. It argues this would require large amounts of new debt on top of a federal deficit of about $2 trillion per year, strain electricity supplies, push up real interest rates and inflation, and crowd out other investment. The author notes that AI already accounts for about half of U.S. economic growth while non-AI investment is falling. According to the post, the industry seeks four things in exchange for accepting "guard rails" or slower frontier development: federal guarantees for its loans, relief from state and local data center restrictions, relief from liability for harmful actions involving AI, and protection from cheaper open-source competition, mostly from China. The author calls this arrangement absurd and recalls that the Bush and Obama administrations bailed out Wall Street in 2008.

The author places the responsibility for the potential bailout on Wall Street investors and the federal government, which the post says would be expected to step in if the AI debt collapses. The author argues that Democrats should state clearly that they will not bail out Wall Street and the technology industry this time, and says doing so would let policymakers redirect resources from AI spending toward the consumer economy and other needed investment. The post itself is labeled as community content not reviewed by Daily Kos staff before publication, and it presents the argument as the author's opinion. The article does not report any official response from Democratic leaders or the industry, and it does not describe any scheduled policy action or next steps beyond the author's call for a public pledge.

Articles.Title: Democrats Please: AI is NOT Too Big to Fail. Regulation Yes, Bailouts No

stories.Headline: OpenClaw creator spent $10 million on AI tokens last month
stories.Summary:
Pete Steinberger, the creator of OpenClaw, an AI digital assistant, said he spent $10 million on AI tokens last month. He now works for OpenAI, and he made the disclosure during a conversation with Cloudflare CEO Dane Knecht at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 Conference in San Francisco. The article was published on October 23, 2026, and it draws on a report by The Register. The remarks were made in front of an audience of industry attendees, which the article suggests included people concerned about AI costs.
