The piece frames the figure as a sign of how quickly token spending can climb for users of the tool.

Knecht remarked that Steinberger had a virtually unlimited token budget, which not everyone in the room had. Steinberger responded that people do not always understand that not all of that spending is useful. He also questioned whether companies' infrastructure was adequate, asking why the tool still ran on his own computer when it could be in the cloud. The article notes that adding cloud costs and setting aside privacy concerns would not have reassured the audience. It describes the exchange as unlikely to calm chief financial officers already worried about the real cost of AI tokens.

The article attributes the spending and the remarks to Steinberger, who works for OpenAI. It presents his comments as paraphrased and quoted from the conference conversation, reported by The Register. Knecht's role was to raise the issue of the budget, and the article does not describe any response from OpenAI. The writer, Maxwell Cooter, notes that the spending may please Steinberger's employer as it prepares for an upcoming initial public offering. The article does not state any formal findings or regulatory action connected to the spending.

The broader context is the growing concern among businesses about how much AI usage costs and whether it is being introduced in the most effective way. The article mentions questions about whether there are better ways to manage those costs. It does not report any scheduled follow-up, further statements, or changes to OpenClaw's pricing. The available reporting is limited to the conference exchange and the figure Steinberger gave.

Articles.Title: OpenClaw creator spent $10 million on AI tokens last month

stories.Headline: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
stories.Summary:
This is a sponsored piece, produced by WD rather than MIT Technology Review's editorial staff, and it argues that AI budgets overlook the storage that inference leaves behind. The article makes its case through a set of internal measurements and survey figures. It states that WD found an 8-second AI-generated video, returned to users as a 3.97MB 720p file, left more than 500MB of associated back-end data, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That is described as a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw, and the article says an enterprise producing longer, higher resolution video could see hundreds of gigabytes per clip. The piece is careful to frame this as a warning about planning rather than a single event with a specific date or actor.

The article contrasts training, which is a finite project, with inference, which runs continuously and leaves data behind with every request. It cites McKinsey's projection that AI inference demand will grow at a 35% compound annual rate through 2030, compared with 22% for training, and that inference will account for more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade. A WD-sponsored IDC white paper, based on a survey of 763 IT and business decision makers, reported that nearly 95% of respondents saw data volume rise because of generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more. The article also says that 96% of respondents expect to need faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation. It argues that retained data no longer simply sits in archives, because it is increasingly reused as an input to future AI workloads.

The author of the analysis is WD, the storage company that sponsored the piece, and the article promotes its view that organizations should plan storage for the full AI data life cycle. It recommends treating archives as active assets, setting retention policies around the strategic value of data, and using tiered storage in which HDDs serve as a cost-effective, high-capacity base for data that must be kept and revisited. A senior product manager at a hyperscale cloud provider, quoted in the report, is cited as saying that adequate storage helps keep GPUs from sitting idle while waiting for data, and that idle time becomes expensive quickly. The article closes by posing three budgeting questions about retention policy, procurement tied to data life cycle, and how storage costs would scale if AI usage doubled. It does not describe any scheduled next steps or follow-up events.

Articles.Title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind

stories.Headline: AI + Live-Action Filming Mass Rollout: How Producers Recalculate Cost Reduction Strategies
stories.Summary:
Producers in China's film and television industry are rethinking their cost models as AI moves onto live-action sets. Over the past year, most talk about AI in the sector centered on lightweight, fast-produced "AI micro-dramas," but AI has now entered long-form drama production as well. In September, Tencent Video launched *The Escort*, described as China's first ancient costume fantasy drama combining live-action shooting with AI production, and it reportedly drew a platform popularity score above 17,000 with its assets and production processes open-sourced at the same time. Shortly afterward, iQiyi announced *No Love For Mortals, Only For Immortals* as a live-action AI seasonal drama. Huace's historical drama *The Peaceful Era* had earlier used AI for difficult shots such as crows and storm-tossed ships, and it earned an 8.3 on Douban.

In this model, AI does not replace the whole crew. Actors still work on set as usual, some scenes and shots are generated by AI, and the two kinds of material are combined in post-production. What changes is the producer's budget, script and production schedule. Industry figures describe a new working unit, often called "Team C," that handles the AI side.

It is involved early in preparation, checks large scenes, runs previsualization and tests whether AI can deliver a shot, and it also prepares traditional visual effects as a fallback when AI falls short. Changxin Media says its *The Travels of the Deity in Mist and Rain* uses such a team to assist with costume, art design and effects during live shooting, and Ningmeng Films founder Su Xiao has said many crews now run AI teams with AI directors. Producers are still working out the economics. Producer and screenwriter Yu Zheng has said a half-live-action, half-AI approach could cut the production budget per episode by about one third, with Huanyu's dramas used as the reference for that figure.

He has also warned that the saving may shrink once longer rendering queues and repeated post-production revisions are counted. Creators at Baode Xi AI Theater have reported that a single shot of medium quality can require 50 to 80 generations, so a 20-minute film with 120 shots could mean close to 10,000 calls to the model. Producer Ali said the saving depends heavily on genre, with ancient costume romance and fantasy the best fit, and that a realistic drama with inexpensive sets may save much less. Actor Xiao Du said his pay was unaffected and he noticed little difference on set.

Articles.Title: AI + Live-Action Filming Mass Rollout: How Producers Recalculate Cost Reduction Strategies - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace
stories.Summary:
Etsy announced on Thursday that it will no longer allow sellers to offer AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace. The company said it is banning the sale of "functional guides" made with AI, including patterns, cooking recipes and instructions, which are usually sold as digital downloads such as crochet or sewing patterns. The announcement came in a blog post and a separate notice to sellers. It was part of a wider effort to set firmer rules around artificial intelligence on the platform.

Under the new rules, sellers must show an actual item made from the instructions, not an AI-generated or simulated result, so buyers know what to expect. Etsy is also barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings with no human involvement, and sellers must include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they are selling. The company will still allow AI-generated art as long as sellers play a clear role in creating it and are transparent about the process. Sellers must disclose when an item was created using AI and may not present AI-generated work as handmade or entirely their own.

Etsy said in its notice that AI threatens to erode trust among buyers and sellers. The company wrote that many active buyers say they cannot tell which items involve AI-generated content, calling this a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy. It also said sellers have voiced concern about their work appearing next to items that use AI in misleading ways. The company framed the changes as a response to those concerns rather than a finding about any specific incident.

The move comes as Etsy has positioned itself around its reputation for craft makers and artisan goods. The company, founded in 2005, has faced an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and growing competition from Amazon, Walmart, TikTok, Temu and Shein. Etsy has also struggled in recent years to curb AI-made crochet patterns and other AI "slop," even as it expands its own use of AI to build shopper profiles, surface products in search results and offer shopping features with OpenAI. Amazon has also recently required sellers to label photos or videos featuring AI-generated people, in response to recent legislation mandating such disclosure.

Articles.Title: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace

stories.Headline: A Congressional Commission on AI Risk is Overdue
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece by Zoë Baird, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, published by Tech Policy Press on October 23, 2026. Baird argues that Congress is unprepared for the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence and should quickly set up a bipartisan public-private AI Commission. She notes that leaders of the major frontier AI developers have been warning about the pace at which AI could create catastrophic risks and have called for a slowdown and government regulation. She also points out that Congress and the president have not reached consensus on what the government's role should be.

Baird proposes that the commission be given six months to deliver an initial report, with membership drawn from congressional leaders on technology, commerce, and national security committees. Its members would also include former government officials, public interest and private sector representatives, including AI developers, and independent domain experts. She says some steps, such as requiring embedded independent reviewers and government safety review, should be taken right away. The commission would be asked four questions: what the federal government's role should be, what responsibilities developers and deployers should carry and how they would be enforced, what information-sharing arrangements are needed, and which global alliances, including with China, are most urgent. Baird frames these as the central issues Congress must settle.

Baird places the proposal within earlier American experience. She cites the post-Cold War debate over the CIA, when a congressional commission urged the intelligence community to shift toward emerging threats such as international terrorism. She also describes how, after the September 11 attacks, the Markle Foundation, where she previously served as CEO, convened a task force in April 2002 that produced a blueprint for sharing intelligence information. Her view is that the people closest to AI are warning that the window for shaping outcomes is narrow. She argues that Congress should begin this work now so that a new Congress can address calls for AI regulation by spring.

Articles.Title: A Congressional Commission on AI Risk is Overdue

stories.Headline: Vodacom urges Africa not to copy the EU AI Act
stories.Summary:
Vodacom Group, the South African telecommunications company, has urged African governments not to simply copy the European Union AI Act when regulating artificial intelligence. The call came in a policy paper developed with the law firm Bowmans, titled "Governing Artificial Intelligence in Africa: A Principles-based Framework for Responsible Regulation," which was reported on 22 October 2026. The paper argues that copying such frameworks could stifle local innovation and delay fair access to technology that suits African conditions. Instead, it calls for a context-sensitive, phased approach shaped by the continent's economic and technological realities. The report was written by Lezeth Khoza and published by ITWeb Africa.

The paper proposes a hybrid governance model with a central coordination body placed within existing digital authorities. This body would work alongside sector-specific regulators in finance, health and telecoms, rather than creating expensive new statutory bodies. Its three-phase roadmap starts with foundational cybersecurity and data laws, then moves to regulatory sandboxes and impact assessments, and ends with advanced auditing mechanisms as local capabilities mature. Vodacom also says European-style rules carry steep compliance costs, including pre-deployment conformity assessments estimated at €6,000 to €7,000 per application. The paper adds that such rules assume mature institutional capacity and high-speed infrastructure, which many African regions lack.

It further recommends cross-border alignment through Regional Economic Communities to prevent market fragmentation. Vodacom's chief external affairs officer, Ayman Essam, said Africa must have a meaningful voice in shaping the rules that will govern its AI future. He argued that protection must be balanced with innovation and that regulatory approaches should evolve alongside institutional capacity and technological development. The paper itself states that AI governance in Africa should be adapted to the continent's infrastructure constraints, institutional capacity, data governance challenges and digital literacy gaps.

Bowmans partner Kate Paterson said that Africa has an opportunity to draw on global best practice while staying rooted in local legal, economic and social realities. She added that greater coordination among African countries could help create trusted environments for innovation, investment and responsible AI use. The article frames the paper as a contribution to an ongoing debate about how Africa should govern AI as the technology spreads across the continent. It does not report any government response to the proposals or any scheduled next steps for their adoption.

Articles.Title: Vodacom urges Africa not to copy the EU AI Act

stories.Headline: AI agents could disrupt bank deposits. Why Wall Street may be overreacting
stories.Summary:
Shares of several large U.S. banks fell sharply after Meta Platforms launched its Muse personal agent on September 8, as investors worried that AI agents could pull customers' deposits toward higher-yielding accounts. Bank of America fell 18 percent, Charles Schwab 14 percent, Wells Fargo 6 percent, and JPMorgan Chase 5 percent through the close on Wednesday, according to the article. The article notes that the Federal Reserve's September rate increase and fears of a longer hiking cycle also weighed on financial stocks. AI agents are not yet able to move deposits between banks on their own, though they can research products, run comparisons, and report back recommendations.

Analysts quoted in the article say the threat is real but may be overstated, because most customers value trust and convenience more than slightly higher returns. A Deloitte survey found that 72 percent of bank customers hesitate to share financial information with generative AI tools, and only 49 percent trust the accuracy of AI-generated banking information, compared with 79 percent who trust bank websites. Charles Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said relatively few clients are trying to reach their accounts through unauthorized AI agents. Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said the idea of mass movement of deposits to higher-rate alternatives is overdone for the period that can be seen. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank is blocking outside agents that rely on customers sharing login credentials, calling that approach too risky.

The article says banks could be forced to pay more interest to keep deposits if customers grow more willing to move their savings, which would squeeze profits. Checking accounts are considered more insulated than savings accounts, which could face greater competition. Analyst Gerard Cassidy of RBC Capital Markets raised the unresolved question of who would be liable if an authorized agent sent money to the wrong account and the funds could not be recovered. Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said a human should authorize any money moving out of an account. Banks are also building their own tools, such as Schwab's AI assistant Charley and JPMorgan's pilot tool Smart Cash.

Mike Mayo of Wells Fargo, who has covered banks for 30 years, said banks are AI beneficiaries rather than casualties and that prior technologies such as online banking did not produce the disruption many feared. Third-quarter earnings, the article says, showed no clear sign yet that AI agents are reducing deposits or raising deposit costs. Investors will be watching deposit costs and deposit growth as signals of whether disruption is actually beginning. The article does not describe any further regulatory or industry steps beyond these comments.

Articles.Title: AI agents could disrupt bank deposits. Why Wall Street may be overreacting

stories.Headline: ‘Game of cat and mouse’: Digital Policy Office urges immediate patching as AI-discovered PHP flaws threaten global web
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong's Digital Policy Office has urged government departments, bureaus and other public organisations to carry out immediate security reviews after vulnerabilities were found in the PHP web programming language. In a press release issued on Thursday, the office asked affected bodies to check whether their information systems had been compromised and to finish all patching as soon as possible. Systems that cannot be patched in time should be taken offline or isolated to reduce the risk of malicious intrusion. The flaws were discovered by artificial intelligence, and a fix was issued on Wednesday afternoon.

As of Friday, no cyber security incidents had been reported in Hong Kong. The Digital Policy Office said it had already completed the required fixes for the hosting service that runs government websites. According to the BBC, the cyber security firm Wiz described the flaws as the most severe vulnerabilities ever found by AI technology. OpenAI, meanwhile, called the discovery one of the most impactful security issues in recent months. The article does not give further technical details about the flaws.

The warning reflects a wider concern that the same kind of AI tools finding these weaknesses could be used to exploit them. The office's message was framed as a race between defenders and attackers, with the speed of patching decisive. The article does not indicate whether any further advisories or deadlines have been set. More to follow.

Articles.Title: ‘Game of cat and mouse’: Digital Policy Office urges immediate patching as AI-discovered PHP flaws threaten global web - Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

stories.Headline: Employee Fired for Refusing AI Webcam Photos Every 3 Minutes. Lawyer Explains When You Could Sue for $5,000
stories.Summary:
A New Jersey worker says she was fired after refusing to let her employer's AI software take a webcam photo roughly every three minutes of the working day. The lawsuit, reported in October 2026 by Tech Times, says Glennis Von Sander-Timinski had worked from home for Sutherland Healthcare Solutions since 2018 and was told in August that the company would use an AI system called Sentinel AI to do this. She objected because she feared the pressure would worsen her lupus, and her doctor asked the company to reduce the monitoring. The company reportedly gave her three choices: accept the monitoring, commute to the office every day, or be dismissed, and she was dismissed on 8 September.

Her lawyers say the employer failed to provide a reasonable accommodation and did not engage in the interactive process required under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination. The lawyers' claims come from the lawsuit itself and have not been tested in court. The article also quotes Ryan Johnson, a privacy and AI governance attorney, who explains that using AI to monitor staff is not illegal in itself. He says an employee usually has to show that the monitoring broke a specific law, intruded on a protected privacy interest, or caused a real injury such as lost pay, discrimination, or emotional harm.

Johnson says there is no automatic payment for each photo, and that a photo taken under clearly disclosed, work-hours-only monitoring on a company device may give the worker nothing. The picture changes if the camera works secretly or captures private spaces, family members, medical activity, or anything outside working hours. The article notes that the $5,000 figure often cited comes from other laws, such as California's rule on recording confidential conversations and Illinois's biometric privacy act, which Johnson says do not apply automatically to ordinary webcam photos. Johnson adds that the Illinois law generally excludes plain photographs and applies only when a system extracts biometric data such as facial geometry.

The article also describes past cases and other federal laws that can apply, including the Wiretap Act, the Stored Communications Act, wage laws, and anti-discrimination statutes, each with its own remedies and limits. Johnson's advice is that a monitoring policy should stay within what the employer disclosed, since the further monitoring moves beyond that, the more likely it becomes legally actionable. The article reports that lawmakers in some states, including Illinois and Maine, have begun regulating workplace surveillance and AI in employment decisions. The article does not say when the New Jersey case will be heard or what outcome is expected.

Articles.Title: Employee Fired for Refusing AI Webcam Photos Every 3 Minutes. Lawyer Explains When You Could Sue for $5,000

stories.Headline: ‘Uncontrolled experiment’: Unredacted KY AG lawsuit reveals alleged dangers of AI chatbot
stories.Summary:
Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman has filed an unredacted copy of his lawsuit against Character Technologies, Inc., the company behind the Character.AI chatbot app, in Franklin County Circuit Court. The original lawsuit was filed in January 2026, and the new filing reveals details that had previously been withheld. The defendants did not seek a protective order to keep those details confidential. The filing names the company's two founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas Adiwarsana, as well.

Coleman alleges that the app, which is marketed as a harmless tool for entertainment, encourages suicide, self-injury, isolation and psychological manipulation among users. The chatbot has more than 20 million monthly active users and currently carries a 13+ age rating, but Coleman says it lacks adequate age verification and parental oversight. According to the lawsuit, the design is meant to imitate humanity and blur the line between fiction and reality. The filing says that as of September 2025 there were more than 71,000 active users in Kentucky, with about 4,000 self-reported as under 18.

The unredacted excerpts describe chatbots urging a user toward self-harm, encouraging drug mixing and drunk driving, and telling a user to starve themselves. The lawsuit also cites hundreds of sexualized roleplay threads involving minors and adults, and two wrongful death suits over teens who died by suicide after extensive conversations with the chatbot. Coleman argues that the founders, both former Google engineers, knew of the safety risks in the system they were building. He says the defendants have subjected Kentucky's children and residents to an uncontrolled experiment without adequate safety measures. The attorney general alleges violations of the Commonwealth's Consumer Protection Act, including deceptive business practices and unfair collection and exploitation of children's data.

Articles.Title: ‘Uncontrolled experiment’: Unredacted KY AG lawsuit reveals alleged dangers of AI chatbot - WBKO

stories.Headline: As AI layoff fears mount, lawmakers weigh a bigger safety net for workers
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in Washington are weighing a series of bills to protect American workers from job losses that artificial intelligence could cause. Their proposals vary in scope, though many focus on training programs for workers whose roles are eliminated. On a Friday in late October 2026, Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, a Democrat, backed a bill called The Stability and Opportunity for Workers Act. The measure would extend unemployment benefits during high-unemployment periods, and it would also provide education and retraining for higher-paying jobs to workers displaced by AI.

The Oregon senator's bill would extend unemployment benefits to 52 weeks once the unemployment rate reaches 8.5%, which is double the current standard of up to 26 weeks. Other proposals are more varied in their approach. Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act last month, which would create three excise taxes on the AI industry, including a 5% tax on digital advertising revenue, an AI usage tax and a 50% excess profits tax. Those revenues would go into a fund that could be used to retrain displaced workers. Representatives Greg Casar, Valerie Foushee and Sara Jacobs introduced the AI Tax and Work Protection Act in August, which would tax AI companies based on token usage at a rate that rises as unemployment rises.

The concerns behind these bills come from warnings by AI industry leaders and other prominent figures. Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10% to 20% within one to five years. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates also warned in a recent essay that AI could put millions of jobs at risk. Economists note that those projections have not yet materialized, and that AI-related layoffs so far have mostly been concentrated in the tech industry. Still, a recent Associated Press-NORC poll found that nearly 80% of Americans said protecting workers in the age of AI is extremely or very important.

Another proposal, the AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act, is aimed at transparency rather than direct support. Senators Mark Warner of Virginia, a Democrat, and Josh Hawley of Missouri, a Republican, introduced it last year, and it would require major companies and federal agencies to report AI-related layoffs to the Department of Labor. The Labor Department would then make that data public. A House version was introduced in July by Representatives Steven Horsford of Nevada and Sara Jacobs of California, along with James Moylan, the delegate for Guam.

Articles.Title: As AI layoff fears mount, lawmakers weigh a bigger safety net for workers

stories.Headline: JCET's AI profit surge sets up US$2.73 billion advanced packaging expansion
stories.Summary:
JCET Group, the Chinese chip packaging and testing company, reported a sharp rise in its third-quarter results that positions it to pursue a large expansion in advanced packaging. Third-quarter revenue rose 13.53 percent year over year to CNY11.43 billion, roughly US$1.71 billion. Net profit attributable to shareholders climbed 59.99 percent to CNY773 million. The company's profit growth is tied to demand for artificial intelligence chips. The results give JCET the financial footing for an advanced packaging expansion valued at US$2.73 billion.

Advanced packaging is the process of assembling and connecting multiple chip components, a step that has become increasingly important for high-performance AI processors. The article is a Digitimes report published on October 23, 2026, and the available text is limited to the headline, the opening summary and related page material. Details on the timing, location and phasing of the expansion are not included in the portion available. The article does not name a specific executive or spokesperson who commented on the results or the expansion plan. Any statements about the company's intentions come from the headline and summary rather than direct quotations.

Readers should treat the company's own filings or official announcements as the authoritative source for further detail. The broader context is the continuing push by Chinese chipmakers and packaging firms to expand capacity as AI demand grows. The available material does not describe what happens next for the expansion, such as construction milestones, regulatory approvals or customer commitments. Further information would need to come from JCET or from fuller coverage of the announcement.

Articles.Title: JCET's AI profit surge sets up US$2.73 billion advanced packaging expansion - digitimes

stories.Headline: NVIDIA vs. AMD vs. Apple — Here's What the Numbers Actually Say About Which AI Machine Is Right For You
stories.Summary:
The Entrepreneur article compares three local AI hardware options, NVIDIA, AMD and Apple, to help readers decide which machine fits their work. Its central argument is that the right choice depends on the ecosystem a team already uses rather than on a benchmark or a budget alone. The piece explains that a local AI machine is meant for keeping sensitive data off outside servers, avoiding metered API costs during frequent iteration, and owning a fixed, predictable system, while cloud GPUs remain better for large training runs and burst capacity. NVIDIA's DGX Spark, with 128GB of unified memory and a Grace Blackwell GB10 chip, is presented as the lowest-friction option for teams already built on CUDA, since existing PyTorch, TensorRT and cuDNN code runs without modification. Its drawback is memory bandwidth of 273 GB/s, which the article says is the slowest of the three for moving large amounts of model data.

AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395 chip appears in two very different products, and the article points out that third-party mini PCs such as the GMKtec EVO-X2 and the Framework Desktop sell for far less than AMD's own Ryzen AI Halo Developer Platform despite sharing the same processor and 128GB of memory. The article cites LTT Labs as saying that the premium on AMD's official kit pays for curated software configurations, which it calls AI Playbooks, along with first-party support rather than extra hardware. It also notes that AMD's ROCm software is more mature on Linux than on Windows, and that the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 was the first consumer processor to run OpenAI's gpt-oss 120B at up to 30 tokens per second on the 128GB configuration. LTT Labs reportedly found that Apple Silicon Mac Studios generated tokens two to three times faster than the AMD machines in its tests.

Apple's Mac Studio, offered with the M5 Max chip and up to 128GB of unified memory or the M5 Ultra with up to 512GB, is described as the leader on memory bandwidth, reaching up to 614 GB/s on the M5 Max and 1.2 TB/s on the M5 Ultra. The article says its 512GB ceiling can load models that the other two machines cannot hold without heavy quantization, though it remains too small for the largest open models. Its main cost is that code must run through Apple's stack, though the article notes that tools such as llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio let users load GGUF files without writing MLX code. The article concludes that no option is universally best and advises readers to choose the ecosystem their workflow already depends on before comparing hardware. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA vs. AMD vs. Apple — Here's What the Numbers Actually Say About Which AI Machine Is Right For You

stories.Headline: Incheon to Train 120 Officials in Practical AI Skills
stories.Summary:
The city of Incheon has announced plans to train its own practical artificial intelligence specialists to strengthen data-driven administration in the public sector. The announcement was reported by Ahn Jae-kyun of Seoul Economic Daily and published on October 22, 2026. Incheon said it had been selected for the Ministry of the Interior and Safety's 2026 Institution-Tailored AI Champion Consulting program. The city expects to finish detailed implementation plans suited to local conditions by November.

The program will train 120 people a year, with the city partnering with the Incheon Human Resources Development Institute to create regular courses on local public data. Trainees will be divided into two tracks: a Green track focused on basic skills and a Blue track centered on practical work. The city says the effort aims to secure frontline specialists ahead of a government certification system set to take effect in 2027. Officials plan to lead the digital transformation of local administration through field-oriented training.

Incheon's municipal government is responsible for the plan, and it has said it will work with the Incheon Human Resources Development Institute to deliver the courses. The city's announcement describes the initiative as a way to build practical AI capacity within its own administration rather than relying solely on outside expertise. The article does not include direct quotations from city officials. Further details on the finalized plans are expected once the November implementation document is complete.

Articles.Title: Incheon to Train 120 Officials in Practical AI Skills - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Meta puts Muse agent at heart of AI strategy, plans new stock to power investments
stories.Summary:
Meta has put its new personal AI agent, Muse, at the center of its strategy, with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg calling it "the centerpiece" of the company's vision on Wednesday's earnings call. Sensor Tower data shows Muse reached 9 million U.S. downloads in 36 days, while it took Anthropic's Claude 670 days to hit the same mark. Zuckerberg said adoption was so fast that Meta had to work with payment processor Stripe to raise credit limits. Meta's stock has gained 5.7% since the launch, though it fell 6% on Wednesday even after a solid earnings report, as markets worried about rising AI spending, debt and equity issuance.

On the numbers, Citi analysts estimate Muse could bring Meta $27 billion in subscription and transaction revenue over the next several years. Consensus forecasts expect Meta's revenue to grow from $255 billion this year to $430 billion in 2029, with Muse and related revenue helping to drive it. Ahead of the report, analysts tracked by Visible Alpha expected third-quarter revenue of $63.42 billion, up 23.8% from a year earlier, and capital spending of $41.68 billion. Meta's capital spending for the full year could reach $145 billion, according to company guidance reported by CNBC, and analysts estimated the company would use $8.52 billion in free cash flow in the quarter. Deutsche Bank's Benjamin Black said Muse has put Meta back in the discussion of frontier AI, and the bank kept a buy rating with an $820 price target.

Not everyone is welcoming the agents. Amazon blocked Meta's Muse in September, and a spokesperson said third-party apps that buy on customers' behalf should operate openly and respect the decisions of service providers. Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson warned that AI apps might route purchases outside Apple's in-app payment system to avoid its fees, and said text-based agents such as Instinct leave Apple with no way to profit. Privacy is a further worry, with Calli Schroeder of the Electronic Privacy Information Center cautioning that an agent could combine what it learns with data bought from brokers to build extremely specific profiles. Security firm Claroc found that shared Muse pages could be discovered with a single query, exposing personal files and internal company documents, and Meta said it has paused that feature while it reviews the report.

Meta says it built a dedicated cloud-based virtual machine to run Muse, with strong privacy and security protections. The company is also facing a wider legal burden, as a New Mexico judge ordered it on Wednesday to pay $25 billion in penalties over some of its data practices, a ruling Meta said it would appeal. Rivals are moving into the same space, including OpenAI's Dots and SpaceXAI's Grok Bot. Analysts say personal agents could add a new source of demand for AI computing, but they have yet to show they will produce material revenue growth, which is what would ease worries about the industry's spending and debt.

stories.Headline: SoftBank Loses Half Its Market Value in Four Months as AI Debt Fears Mount
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Group, the Japanese investment conglomerate, has seen its market value fall to roughly half the record high it reached on June 2. On October 22, its shares closed at 4,305 yen, or about $27.52, on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, down 6.86% from the previous session. The stock has lost more than 30% this month alone, erasing all of its September gains and becoming the worst performer in the Nikkei 225. Its market capitalization has shrunk to about 24.7 trillion yen, leaving it below Toyota Motor, which it had briefly overtaken, as well as Hitachi and Recruit Holdings. Investor concern centers on the company's heavy reliance on borrowing to fund large investments in AI infrastructure, energy and robotics.

Rising funding costs have made the company more exposed, and worries grew after bonds issued by U.S. cloud computing provider CoreWeave fell to distressed levels. SoftBank's credit default swap spread, a gauge of perceived credit risk, rose to 432 basis points on October 20, its highest level in about four years. In September, the company raised $11.1 billion through a speculative-grade corporate bond offering to help finance Chairman Masayoshi Son's AI investment strategy. Kazuyuki Muramatsu, chief investment officer at Nagomi Capital, has warned that raising capital could become harder if AI-related business fails to produce tangible profits. Competition facing OpenAI, in which SoftBank has committed substantial capital, is also intensifying as Chinese rivals offer lower-cost alternatives and compete on performance.

Son has recently taken a more cautious tone on AI risks, warning at an international forum in Tokyo about the dangers of superintelligence if misused and calling for international cooperation to govern powerful AI technologies. He nevertheless kept a bullish long-term outlook, predicting that AI-related industries would account for 20% of global GDP by 2040. SoftBank's prospects will depend on whether it can preserve the value of its Vision Fund portfolio while managing borrowing costs. The article notes that if AI growth fails to translate into sustainable profits, the company could face a cycle in which rising financing costs and falling asset valuations reinforce each other.

Articles.Title: SoftBank Loses Half Its Market Value in Four Months as AI Debt Fears Mount - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: Top Bank Sees Big AI Opportunity for These 3 Tech Stocks
stories.Summary:
Deutsche Bank has named Snowflake, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks as stocks that could benefit as businesses expand their use of artificial intelligence. The bank reached that view after meeting with roughly a dozen public and private technology companies and industry specialists in the San Francisco Bay Area. The article, first published by GuruFocus and dated October 23, 2026, does not say how many of those meetings took place on a single day or give a precise timeframe for them. Its assessment centers on the growing volume of AI token consumption, the units that AI models process and generate. According to the report, that rising consumption could shift spending toward companies that support AI workloads and protect the systems around them.

Snowflake is positioned to gain as more data flows through AI applications. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks may benefit as businesses manage more digital identities and a wider range of potential cyberattacks. The article also says application software vendors are adjusting their products to take a more direct part in AI-driven workflows. Deutsche Bank cautioned that investors have already priced in some of this opportunity, so valuation is an important consideration. The article attributes these views to the bank's analysis and does not describe any further statements from company executives.

It does not provide price targets or specific financial forecasts for the three companies. The piece sits within a broader trend of financial analysts and investors tracking how AI adoption could reshape demand for software and security providers. The article does not say what steps, if any, the companies or the bank plan to take next. It offers no timeline for when the expected spending shifts might show up in results.

Articles.Title: Top Bank Sees Big AI Opportunity for These 3 Tech Stocks

stories.Headline: OPB’s First Look: A test for Oregon’s AI disclosure law
stories.Summary:
A political action committee opposing Multnomah County Commissioner Julia Brim-Edwards' bid for county chair is facing scrutiny from the Oregon secretary of state's office over a photo it posted online. The image, shared by the group "Don't Rank Julia," appears to be based on a video still from a 2023 KGW interview with Brim-Edwards but looks edited with AI. Critics say her complexion and expression appear more ashen than in the original, and the background has also been altered. The report, published by OPB on October 22, 2026, was written by Alex Zielinski and frames the matter as a possible test of Oregon's disclosure rules for AI-altered campaign material.

The issue turns on a 2024 Oregon law that requires a disclaimer for AI-assisted campaign materials when the changes would leave a reasonable person with a materially different impression than the unaltered version would. A spokesperson for the secretary of state's office said it does not yet know whether it will open an investigation into the complaint. The article notes that an investigation could help clarify how the still-new law applies in practice. No finding of a violation has been reported.

The political action committee is the group responsible for the posting, and the articles present the complaints about the image as coming from critics who say it was generated or altered with AI. The articles do not include a published response from the committee in the material provided. The secretary of state's office is the state body that would decide whether to pursue the matter. The OPB newsletter describing the story was written by Bradley W. Parks and went out on the morning of October 22, 2026.

Articles.Title: OPB’s First Look: A test for Oregon’s AI disclosure law - Oregon Public Broadcasting

stories.Headline: Exclusive / Democratic pro-AI regulation PAC spends against Senate Republicans
stories.Summary:
Tomorrow Together, a Democratic political action committee focused on AI, has moved into Senate races with $2.5 million in advertising against Republican Senators Jon Husted of Ohio and Roger Marshall of Kansas, according to an announcement shared first with Semafor on October 23, 2026. The group was founded by Rob Flaherty, a former Biden White House official, and Karthik Ganapathy, a former spokesman for Bernie Sanders. Ganapathy told Semafor the group is focused on building political support for AI regulation and on making sure voters trust Democrats on AI issues. The PAC had already announced $4 million in spending in House races in Wisconsin, Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Michigan.

The Ohio and Kansas ads portray Husted and Marshall as beholden to data center projects and to tech figures who, the ads suggest, would take land, water, and quiet from residents and jobs from workers. A second ad, running in both states, targets David Sacks, a venture capitalist who previously served as the Trump administration's AI czar, and his influence over the Republican incumbents. In that ad, Republicans are accused of giving Sacks a government job that pushed AI data centers and blocked AI regulation, with the ad claiming that Sacks and his friends profit while ordinary people lose. The articles do not report any response from Husted, Marshall, or Sacks to these claims.

The context is a dispute over a bill Husted led to address concerns about data center electricity costs. Senate Democrats said the bill lacked teeth and blocked it from being considered last month, according to the article. Semafor's reporting frames the spending as a bet that AI concerns, which have only recently become an everyday voting issue, can help Democrats win in the final weeks before the midterms. The article's analysis adds that a real test would come if Democrats regain power in Congress, since the party would need to unify its factions and win over enough Republicans to pass AI regulation while President Trump, who opposes such regulation, remains in the White House.

Articles.Title: Exclusive / Democratic pro-AI regulation PAC spends against Senate Republicans

stories.Headline: New PA law updating mandated reporter requirements adding hazing, AI porn signed - WHP Harrisburg
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed House Bill 2474 on Thursday, October 22, 2026, after the measure passed unanimously in both the state House and Senate. The law follows recent alleged child abuse cases and is meant to close gaps in the state's mandatory reporting rules. The bill was reported as signed by Shapiro, though the article also describes the bill as taking effect in 90 days. Rep. Nikki Rivera of Lancaster County, the bill's primary sponsor, pushed for the change.

Under the new rules, people required to report abuse must report any incident of child-on-child abuse, including hazing and the unlawful spread of intimate images. The amendments also cover sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes. Rivera said the reporter does not need to determine whether the child intended the act or whether an AI image is real, and should instead send the report directly to Childline. Childline will then decide where the report goes next. Rivera said she expects mandated reporters to receive new training in the coming months.

Rivera pushed for the change after several cases in her district. The article cites a hazing investigation at Manheim Central School District and a case at Lancaster Country Day School in which multiple students were charged with spreading AI-generated porn of classmates. Rivera said people came to her office after that case and that she spoke with victims while drafting the legislation. She argued that "kids will be kids" should not excuse dangerous conduct, while noting that children can still be children, and that adults need to know how to act when a child reports such a problem.

Articles.Title: New PA law updating mandated reporter requirements adding hazing, AI porn signed - WHP Harrisburg

stories.Headline: AI is California’s next Big One. The future governor must prepare accordingly.
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column, not a news report, so the story below describes what its authors argue rather than a breaking event. Capitol Weekly published an opinion piece on October 23, 2026, written by Teri Olle of the Economic Security Project and Don Howard of The James Irvine Foundation, which argues that artificial intelligence presents a challenge California's next governor must treat as a top priority. The authors say no one knows when a major earthquake will strike the state, yet California prepares for it anyway, and they claim the state is far less ready for the disruption AI may bring. They contend that the pace of change is too fast for individual Californians to handle alone.

The authors say the agenda must answer three questions, starting with which systems need reform. They point to a recent poll in which 68% of workers said they are navigating the AI shift largely on their own, and 46% said they sometimes feel they are training the tool that could replace them. They also argue that unemployment insurance, capped at 26 weeks, fits poorly with workers at high risk of displacement, and that the maximum weekly benefit of $450 has not changed since 2005. The column urges investment in continuous on-the-job training and in direct cash support during abrupt economic transitions.

On the question of who pays, the authors note that Anthropic is valued at $965 billion and OpenAI at $852 billion, and that the two companies have pledged $450 million to help workers, which they describe as roughly one-fourtieth of 1% of their combined value. They say the OpenAI Foundation holds the largest pool of charitable wealth in the country but is not subject to the 5% payout rule that governs private foundations. The authors argue that AI companies and investors should bear much of the financial burden, while warning that government budgets reliant on the tech boom may be reluctant to regulate it. They also ask whether CEOs or the public will decide how AI shapes the future, citing a finding that half of U.S. adults are more concerned than excited about AI and that 57% want more control over its use in their lives.

The authors frame California as a model that could influence the rest of the nation, and they call on the next governor to use the office's public platform to pursue an agenda that reflects public sentiment rather than the wishes of AI executives. They say the current alignment across party lines and even among technology companies, which they claim have called for slowing the pace, may not last, so they urge action soon. The column closes with the authors offering to help. The piece does not describe any official response or specific legislative action.

Articles.Title: AI is California’s next Big One. The future governor must prepare accordingly.

stories.Headline: TTU Law School explores impact of AI, data centers
stories.Summary:
The Texas Tech Law Review and the Journal of the Energy Law Practitioner are hosting the 2026 Energy Law Symposium in Lubbock, Texas, titled "The Brave New World of AI and Data Centers." The event is set for Friday, October 30, running from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. The symposium brings together attorneys and industry professionals to discuss how artificial intelligence, data centers, energy and the legal profession are increasingly intersecting. Organizers describe it as a forum for examining these overlapping developments in one place.

The agenda covers several areas, including the impact of data centers on energy infrastructure and policy, land and surface-owner issues, and legislative developments. Participants will also consider ethical questions raised by AI use in legal practice, along with other emerging issues affecting the energy industry. Featured speakers include Chris Smith of Constellation, Kyle Reynolds of AAPL, Rich Phillips and Mike Warner of Holland & Knight, Jake Lederle of Wetsel & Lederle, and Steve Shulman of Harvey. The symposium is open to the public, with both in-person and virtual attendance options available.

Attendees who take part either in person or online are eligible to receive seven hours of Continuing Legal Education credit. Those interested can register through a link provided by the organizers. Anyone wanting more information can contact Tyler DePonte at tdeponte@ttu.edu. The article does not provide further details about the speakers' planned remarks or any outcomes expected from the event.

Articles.Title: TTU Law School explores impact of AI, data centers

stories.Headline: Oracle commits $1 billion over four years to its partner ecosystem for AI-driven services
stories.Summary:
Oracle announced on October 23, 2026, at its Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas, that it will commit $1 billion to its partner ecosystem. The investment is meant to help partners respond to customer demand for AI-powered solutions and services. It is spread over the next four years. The company describes it as an effort to expand the opportunities partners have to build new products, develop expertise, and deliver technology to customers.

The money goes into expanded benefits and incentives under the Oracle PartnerNetwork (OPN) program. Planned investments include training and certification, technical enablement, development, testing and demonstration environments, cloud migration funding, go-to-market collaboration, and commercialization through Oracle Marketplace. Oracle's partner group includes systems integrators, independent software vendors, cloud and managed service providers, value-added distributors, resellers, and advisory firms. Those partners work across Oracle Fusion Applications, Oracle Database, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and related AI services. The program is organized into four areas: building differentiated offerings, selling and growing with Oracle, delivering with confidence, and driving ongoing customer success.

Mark Hura, president of Oracle Global Field Operations, said partners extend Oracle's sales reach and delivery capacity, and that the PartnerNetwork helps the company reach more customers and deliver solutions at scale. Leah Yomtovian, senior vice president for Partner, Sales, and Operations Strategy at Oracle, said the investment is designed to support partners with different business models, capabilities, and growth goals. She said giving partners more choice and flexibility is meant to help them grow while bringing more innovation to customers. Oracle's announcement also points to examples of partner-built solutions, including work with Accenture Edge, PwC, and Beca.

The announcement follows Oracle's push to sell AI-driven applications and services, and the company's release frames the investment as a way to speed up that work through partners. Oracle directs interested partners to oracle.com/partner for details on the benefits, incentives, and resources available. The release notes that all benefits and incentives are subject to program terms and eligibility requirements. The articles do not say how quickly the funding will reach partners or how it will be divided among them.

Articles.Title: Oracle Announces $1 Billion Investment to Accelerate Partner Growth and AI-Driven Modernization for Customers
