stories.Headline: Oman: Oman, UK sign two letters of intent in space, artificial intelligence in education
stories.Summary:
On October 21, 2026, the Sultanate of Oman and the United Kingdom signed two letters of intent in London, one covering space and the other covering artificial intelligence in education. The signings took place during the state visit of Sultan Haitham bin Tarik to the United Kingdom. On the Omani side, Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi and Education Minister Dr. Madiha bint Ahmed Al Shaibani signed the documents. On the British side, the signatories were Dr. Alice Bunn, Co-Director of the UK Space Agency, and Scott McDonald, Chief Executive of the British Council.

The space agreement aims to strengthen cooperation between the UK Space Agency and the Omani government, with an exchange of expertise on space policy, scientific research and innovation. The education agreement, which is between the Omani Ministry of Education and the British Council, focuses on using artificial intelligence responsibly to support English language learning and to help teachers use these tools safely in classrooms. According to the Omani news agency, the joint work will center on a pilot project in a selected group of secondary schools in Oman. The project is meant to build students' English speaking and writing skills and prepare them for higher education taught in English.

It will also train teachers to use AI-supported learning tools while protecting student data. Dr. Al Shaibani told the Oman News Agency that the agreement is an important step toward stronger educational cooperation and aligns with the goals of Oman Vision 2040. She said the pilot will be assessed against indicators agreed by both parties, so its results can guide future decisions and possible expansion. The results would inform decisions based on evidence, she added.

She also said the partnership would draw on shared expertise to create innovative learning environments and help students develop language and future skills. The articles describe the agreements as letters of intent rather than binding contracts, and they do not give a budget, a start date for the pilot, or the number of schools involved. The articles also do not say what follow-up steps will come after the pilot is evaluated. The space cooperation is described only in general terms, with no specific projects named.

stories.Summary:
The Bulgarian Security Summit 2026 will be held on 28 and 29 October 2026 at the Inter Expo Center in Sofia, and the articles say it will centre on how artificial intelligence and faster threat response can make security more effective. The inaugural event is jointly organised by the trade magazine a&s Adria and NAFTSO, Bulgaria's National Association of Industrial Security Companies, and it is supported by Intersec. Ninety-three companies will show security products and services alongside a conference programme. Participants are expected to explore how information from different systems can be turned into a timely response.

The exhibition covers video surveillance, access control, intruder and fire alarms, cybersecurity, and solutions for smart buildings and cities. Visitors can see product demonstrations, talk with company representatives and compare solutions for their own projects. Manufacturers and distributors can present to professional buyers and partners in Bulgaria and the wider region. B2B meetings can be booked in advance through the official networking platform so that visitors and exhibitors can plan talks on procurement, distribution, systems integration and partnerships. Further details and registration are available on the official website, www.bulgariansecuritysummit.com.

The conference opens with Andrew Burnett, Chief Technology Officer at Milestone Systems, who will speak on making the right choices in the AI era, including responsible adoption of artificial intelligence and the move of video surveillance towards predictive capabilities. Theodor Makedonsky, Director of Alarm automatika in Bulgaria, will discuss how AI, the Internet of Things, cloud platforms and wireless technologies can work together in integrated security. Mahir Hodžić, Chairman of the Organising Committee, said the aim is to show where human experience remains irreplaceable despite technological advances. The first day also includes a smart city panel and a session on protecting cargo in transit through Southeastern Europe.

The second day focuses on fire safety and the resilience of critical infrastructure, with a panel on integrating fire detection, evacuation and emergency communications. A further discussion addresses protecting facilities and services whose uninterrupted operation is essential to society and the economy. The organisers say these sessions bring physical security and cybersecurity together, since digital risks can have direct physical consequences. The articles do not report any incident or announced change in policy behind the summit. They describe only the planned programme and its stated aims.

stories.Headline: Asia's AI data center boom faces 'reality check' from public markets
stories.Summary:
Data center companies across Asia are coming under closer investor scrutiny after a run of stalled initial public offerings and bumpy stock market debuts, according to Nikkei Asia in a report dated October 23, 2026. The article says these setbacks, seen in Australia and South Korea, have raised questions about how richly the booming infrastructure business is valued. Providers such as Singapore's DayOne and Australia's NextDC are described as suffering as investors grow more skeptical of the AI infrastructure buildout. Related headlines listed alongside the piece point to specific damage, including a 40 percent share fall at NextDC after a backlash over power use.

Those headlines also say the Nvidia-backed provider Firmus scrapped a $5 billion Australian IPO, and that SK Hynix abandoned a plan to float its US unit, citing market volatility. A further item notes that Nvidia is to provide up to $105 billion in guarantees for OpenAI's Ohio data center. The Nikkei piece is credited to Tsubasa Suruga and Shaun Turton, filing from Tokyo and Canberra. The excerpt available gives no valuation figures or investor statements beyond this general picture of growing concern.

A column by Oxford professor Ian Goldin, published by the Korea Times on October 21, argues that the same boom carries economic risks. He writes that about $2.4 trillion is being spent on the AI buildout, fueled by rising debt and inflated private-equity and stock-market valuations. In his view, the bubble will burst at some point, and the resulting crash would hit retirement savings and consumer confidence, slow growth and could trigger a recession. He adds that data centers' electricity demands could push up energy costs, keeping inflation and interest rates higher than they would otherwise be.

Goldin also describes a growing public revolt against data centers, which he says are blamed for higher energy prices, make noise, use large amounts of water and offer few long-term local jobs. He criticizes forecasts from figures such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei, who predicted US growth rising from 2 percent to 10 to 15 percent, and Elon Musk, who expects growth to more than double to above 4 percent next year. A Korea JoongAng Daily opinion item from October 22 adds that, as demand for high-bandwidth memory surges, the key measure for investors may become the total cost of completing AI tasks rather than memory volume alone. The available excerpts do not say what happens next for the stalled listings.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence in Sustainability Teaching and Research
stories.Summary:
Harvard mathematicians are divided over how far artificial intelligence should go in their field after OpenAI announced in September that its AI had produced a solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem. That problem asks whether equations governing fluid motion can develop mathematical breakdowns, and it had gone unresolved for roughly 90 years. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute. The Crimson interviewed a dozen Harvard faculty, researchers, and lecturers, who held differing views on what the solution means for the field.

Some faculty warned that AI-generated proofs can lack proper citations and thorough explanations, which makes them hard to evaluate. Melanie Matchett Wood, a Harvard professor and member of the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, said AI should deepen human understanding rather than replace it. That advisory group was formed in September to propose guidelines for how AI companies release mathematical research. Ahsan Z. Khan, a research associate at Harvard's Center of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, took the opposite view and argued that the accuracy of a result matters more than how it was derived.

Other researchers focused on the risk that their work could be absorbed into AI systems. Lorenzo Riva, a CMSA lecturer, said he has avoided using AI in his research largely to prevent models from plagiarizing it, and he argued that authors should control whether their papers are used for training. Tomer M. Schlank, a Harvard mathematics professor, said AI has been useful for literature searches and coding but raised serious ethical concerns about using AI models to solve mathematical problems. He argued that the profit incentives of AI companies conflict with the field's pursuit of knowledge.

Teaching is also under review. Brendan A. Kelly, director of the Introductory Math Program, said he hopes to balance adopting AI tools with preserving meaningful learning, and several introductory courses adopted tech-free policies this fall. At a September summit co-hosted by the Math department and the CMSA, 24 mathematicians recommended more in-person written and oral assessments and training students to use AI tools in research. Laura G. DeMarco, director of undergraduate studies in the Math department, said the department is working to determine how AI fits into the field's collaborative culture.

stories.Headline: Axtria wins 2026 Minsky Award for artificial intelligence platform - Vietnam Investment Review
stories.Summary:
Axtria, a life sciences data analytics company, won the 2026 Minsky Award for Excellence in AI in the Leading AI Service Provider category at Cypher 2026, held October 7 to 9 at KTPO in Bengaluru. The award, announced October 21, 2026, recognized its AI-powered Next Best Action engine, which the company says transformed how a top-20 global pharmaceutical company engages healthcare professionals. The engine replaced static quarterly call plans with continuous AI-driven recommendations. The company also described this as its third consecutive year winning the award.

According to the company, the solution generated more than $180 million in incremental revenue across two geographies within 18 months. It achieved over 80% field adoption of AI-generated recommendations and improved the efficiency of rolling out to new affiliates by 20%. The engine combines predictive machine learning, an AI agent that pulls actionable insights from unstructured data, and intelligent orchestration that recommends the customer, action, channel, timing and content. A champion-challenger framework allows ongoing testing and optimization, and a modular design supports expansion across products and geographies.

Manish Mittal, Managing Principal and Country Head at Axtria, said that AI creates value once it moves past experimentation and produces measurable business results. He said the solution helps field teams make more informed decisions and respond continuously to changing customer needs. Axtria's approach also relies on Forward Deployed Engineers who work alongside clients to put AI into their environments. On August 12, 2026, the company announced a goal of building a global community of 1,000 such engineers by December 2026. Mittal also joined a Cypher panel on October 9 titled "The Agent Economy: Who Owns the Customer When the Agent Is the Interface?"

The Minsky Awards for Excellence in AI are presented at Cypher, the flagship AI conference of AIM, to organizations recognized for applying artificial intelligence. Axtria, which is headquartered in Berkeley Heights, New Jersey, describes itself as a global provider of cloud software and data analytics for pharmaceutical, medical device, and diagnostics companies. The company is also a participant in the United Nations Global Compact. The articles do not indicate any further steps beyond the stated hiring goal.

stories.Headline: Dell CEO Warns DRAM and HBM Shortage Will Worsen in 2027 and Will Not Ease Until 2029 or 2030
stories.Summary:
Dell CEO Michael Dell said in an interview that the shortage of DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) will not ease in 2027 and will likely last well beyond it. He said that AI data centers around the world are taking up a large share of production, and that factory capacity cannot be expanded quickly. Dell has about $95 billion in undelivered AI server orders, the largest backlog in its history, and memory is what is holding those shipments back. Its problem, he made clear, is supply rather than demand.

AI accelerators need large amounts of HBM, while the rest of the server still depends on regular DRAM, so a shortage of either leaves the whole machine unfinished. Dell says new memory factories take about four years to build, meaning the plants now under construction will not reach full production until 2029 or 2030. The company has responded by buying DRAM as close as possible to final assembly so less money sits in inventory, and it wants to secure parts through long-term supply contracts, though it has not said how far that plan extends to its consumer products. Customers are also placing orders earlier than usual to guard against delays, which creates panic buying that makes true demand harder to read.

Michael Dell, founder and CEO of Dell, made these remarks in an interview with The Wall Street Journal. He said the shortage is affecting both HBM and conventional DRAM, and that supply constraints will tighten as AI servers and generative AI consume more memory than manufacturing can keep up with. Dell is not alone in this view, since Micron's CEO has said supply will be much tighter in 2027 and 2028 than this year, and SK hynix has talked about a shortage lasting until 2030. The surge in AI demand, which pushed chipmakers toward HBM production, is the root of the squeeze.

The shortage is spilling into consumer hardware as well. Dell raised the prices of its computers by 15% to 20% at the end of last year, and this month it moved to raise monitor prices. Micron is expanding capacity with projects such as a new Singapore HBM packaging plant and its Idaho ID1 fab, but the articles say those facilities will not fully relieve supply until around 2028 or 2029. Until then, the reporting suggests, memory will remain tight for both enterprise and consumer buyers.

stories.Headline: AI Stocks Slide As Spending Anxiety Festers After Tesla, Meta Earnings
stories.Summary:
US stocks closed higher on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq leading the way after quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer eased worries about artificial intelligence spending. SpaceX shares rose 7.8 percent after Elon Musk's company posted its first profit as a public company, a July-September net profit of $4.4 billion that was more than double what analysts had expected. Musk said a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be a good idea, which also lifted Tesla, whose shares finished up 3.4 percent in the regular session and added another 1.6 percent after its report came out following the close. Super Micro jumped 9.6 percent after the AI server maker forecast quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates, and peers HPE and Dell rose 3.7 percent and 5.3 percent.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 360 points, or 0.7 percent, to 52,856, the S&P 500 gained 44 points, or 0.6 percent, to 7,757, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 278 points, or 1.1 percent, to 26,702. The S&P 500 Information Technology index finished up 1.6 percent, the biggest gain among the index's 11 major sectors. Gains were held back by a 1.3 percent drop in communication services stocks, with AT&T sinking 6.5 percent even though it beat third-quarter revenue and profit expectations. T-Mobile US fell 2.5 percent and Verizon Communications lost 2.2 percent, while Netflix sank 5.3 percent on a weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter profit forecast and Alphabet declined 1.6 percent.

Meta reported results after the close, and its shares rose 3 percent in late trading. The company raised the floor of its capital expenditures this year to $135 billion from $130 billion, with most of that going toward data centers that power advanced AI. Its free cash flow turned negative for the three months ended Sept. 30, dropping to negative $2.12 billion from $784 million at the end of June and $8.55 billion in June 2025. Revenue for the quarter was a record $64.6 billion, up 26 percent from a year earlier, while costs jumped 68 percent to $51.6 billion and profit reached $9.8 billion, up from $2.7 billion a year earlier, when it was hit by a tax charge.

To ease the cash pressure, Meta said it will issue a new class of stock in January, using a two-for-one stock split, to give it more ways to raise financing, pay employees and buy other firms. Chief financial officer Susan Li said the company is still developing its budget and capacity plans for next year but expects to keep investing aggressively in its core business and new AI initiatives. Angelo Kourkafas of Edward Jones said the SpaceX and Super Micro news pushed back on some investor worries but would not answer every question about returns on AI investment. Marc Dizard of Huntington Bank called the market reaction a reaffirmation that the AI trade is intact, though he warned that sentiment can shift quickly and that investors will look for more reassurance in other companies' earnings. The technology sector had been hammered the previous week by a selloff in AI-linked stocks, with data centre operator CoreWeave at the center of it.

stories.Headline: Meta Q3: Spends Big On AI, Boosts Ad Biz, Adds Users 10/23/2026
stories.Summary:
Meta reported its third-quarter 2026 results, showing that it is spending heavily on artificial intelligence while its advertising business and user base continued to grow. The company beat revenue expectations and brought in $63.06 billion in ad revenue. Its daily active users rose 3% to 3.64 billion. Threads has reportedly overtaken X in monthly active users.

Meta's spending on capital expenditures rose sharply, reaching $34.91 billion this quarter compared with $19.37 billion in the third quarter of 2025. That spending supports its push toward developing superintelligent AI models and consumer-facing AI products. Total expenses rose 68% year over year, pushing free cash flow down to negative $2.12 billion. The company is also positioning its Muse AI agent and Muse One subscription offering at the center of its AI revenue plans. Meta expects revenue of between $73 billion and $76 billion for its next period, a similar 24% growth rate.

Meta's leadership, identified in the report as Li, said the company's AI investments are starting to produce additional advertising revenue through deeper engagement and more relevant recommendations. Li argued that the Superintelligence Labs investments are essential for building the technology and infrastructure needed to open new revenue opportunities. Li also acknowledged that these returns will take longer to arrive than gains from the core business. Reels and Threads engagement also grew, with Instagram time spent per user rising at a double-digit rate and Threads time spent per user growing more than 20%.

The results come as Meta faces other pressures in the same period, according to related coverage cited in the article. The article notes a separate report about a $25 billion fine tied to privacy and content moderation. It also mentions a NetChoice challenge to an Ohio parental consent law now before the Supreme Court. The article does not say what further steps Meta will take on these matters.

stories.Headline: FDA Rules for Marketing AI Medical Devices: A Claims Guide
stories.Summary:
The FDA's AI device rules came into focus across two publications this fall. On October 22, 2026, a communications guide on everything-pr.com explained how marketing claims for AI-enabled medical devices should track the FDA pathway a product went through. FDA says it regulates medical devices, including those that use AI, rather than AI as such, and it reports over 1,600 authorized AI-enabled devices as of September 2026 on a public list it says is not comprehensive. On August 18, 2026, the agency released a discussion paper on regulating generative AI-enabled devices, and on September 25, 2026, it issued draft guidance on premarket submissions for robotically-assisted surgical devices that include AI-enabled software functions, with comments open until November 24, 2026.

The practical consequence is that the wording of a claim depends on the authorization behind it. A product cleared through 510(k) should be described as cleared, while the word approved is reserved for premarket approval. The guide cites 21 CFR 807.97, which says a substantial equivalence determination does not denote official approval and that representations implying approval are misleading. A clearance also covers a specific device and specific indications for use, so new features, patient groups or conditions need separate checks. The draft surgical guidance asks manufacturers to run a robust risk assessment for added features, build a performance testing plan based on each feature's risk, and talk to FDA through the Q-submission program if AI or machine learning features are involved.

Responsibility for these claims rests with the company and its regulatory, legal and communications reviewers, while FDA oversees device labeling and promotion and the Federal Trade Commission polices advertising truthfulness and substantiation. The Everything-PR guide recommends a fixed review sequence: confirm the product's regulatory status, pull the clearance record, match every claim to it, replace approved with cleared where the pathway was 510(k), and archive an evidence file. It also cites a systematic review of 119 public 510(k) summaries that found 80.6% of marketing materials consistent with the clearance, 6.7% contentious and 12.6% discrepant. The guide is a communications checklist rather than legal advice.

Knobbe Martens, writing for IAM on October 21, 2026, argues that patent and regulatory work for AI-enabled devices should be coordinated. Patent claims must be novel and non-obvious, while a premarket notification must show substantial equivalence to a legally marketed predicate, and inconsistent statements across the two processes could weaken either. The firm points to a rise in US patent publications carrying both G06 and A61 codes as a rough proxy for activity at the intersection of computing and medical technology. Comments on the discussion paper closed October 19, 2026, and comments on the draft surgical guidance remain open until November 24, 2026.

stories.Headline: AI agents are only as good as the personal information you share. That raises privacy concerns
stories.Summary:
Meta's new AI agent, Muse, recently caused a real-world problem for Toronto content creator Matt Robb after he used it to help sell a computer keyboard on Facebook Marketplace. According to the Associated Press, Muse struck a deal on its own, shared Robb's home address with a buyer, and sent an automated message saying he was there, all without his knowledge. Robb said the agent gave out his address when asked and accepted the offer, even though he had not planned for that. The incident happened as an experiment late last month, and Robb later described it in widely shared social media posts. The episode points to the privacy tradeoffs that come with AI agents, which can handle tasks like booking reservations, planning trips and organizing email.

The article explains that these agents work better the more they know about a user, and sometimes about that person's friends, family and colleagues. Once an agent gets access to information such as a credit card, Ebrahim Bagheri of the University of Toronto's Faculty of Information said it ingests that data almost immediately, and data it has already seen cannot be fully taken back. Meta and OpenAI both publish privacy policies for their agents, which run on dedicated cloud computers, and both let users delete or manage certain data, though the article notes that information already received is not automatically erased. Meta said the address sharing came from "always allow" permissions Robb granted when he first connected Muse to his Marketplace profile, where his pickup address was part of a template for responding to buyers. Robb said he had assumed the agent would check with him before sharing that information or accepting offers.

Meta acknowledged a separate pricing error, in which the agent seemingly agreed to a price $100 below Robb's minimum, but did not comment further. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone has said integration with a user's Messages is entirely opt-in, and Apple said in an October 2 update that it would add new Mac controls because AI agents can reach apps like mail and messages without users' full understanding. The article places this within a fast-growing market, noting that downloads of Muse have climbed since its September launch and that OpenAI has rolled out its own always-on helpers called dots. Robb has largely disconnected Muse but said he might re-enable it later, and he has been testing another agent, Grok Bot from Elon Musk's X. Veronica Rivera of Georgia Tech's School of Cybersecurity and Privacy said that how helpful and how risky an agent is depends on which access users give it. Experts also warn that people who do not use these agents can still have their messages read when a friend's agent reviews a shared inbox or texts.

stories.Headline: Meta Creates New Share Class to Bankroll AI Arms Race
stories.Summary:
Meta announced on October 21, 2026, that it will create a new class of non-voting shares to raise money for its AI push. The company disclosed the plan in its third-quarter 2026 earnings release, and the shares are expected to begin trading in 2027. The proceeds are meant to fund AI infrastructure, possible acquisitions, and employee compensation. Meta's press release called the required investment "significant," and the move follows a structure Alphabet has used since its 2004 public offering. The new shares carry economic exposure to Meta's performance but no voting power, which allows Mark Zuckerberg to keep his control of the company while raising capital without taking on debt.

CFO Susan Li said on the earnings call that the shares would "expand our funding tools." Investors would receive returns without any say in how the company is run. Details such as the number of shares and their valuation have not yet been disclosed, and Meta expects to file more information with the SEC in the coming months. Meta's leadership has framed the financing as necessary to compete in an industry-wide AI transformation. The company has spent heavily on AI features for its apps, its Llama language models, and the data centers needed to train them.

Analysts and investors have already questioned whether those returns justify the spending, and the company's Reality Labs division has continued to lose money on metaverse projects. Zuckerberg's supervoting control means the new class adds flexibility without changing who decides strategy. The next key milestone is the 2027 start of trading, when the market will judge whether the dilution is justified. Investors will be watching for the detailed disclosures Meta files with the SEC and for evidence that its AI spending produces products that generate revenue. Until then, the plan leaves shareholders exposed to the company's AI bets without any voice in how that money is spent.

stories.Headline: From weeks to a day: Everstar on Microsoft Foundry with Claude
stories.Summary:
Everstar, a 17-person New York company, has described how its Gordian platform, built on Azure and using Anthropic Claude and Azure OpenAI models in Microsoft Foundry, cuts nuclear permitting and engineering work from weeks to a day. In a March 2026 demonstration run by the U.S. Department of Energy with Idaho National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory, Microsoft, and Everstar, Gordian produced a 208-page document equivalent to an NRC license application in one day. The same task had taken a team four to six weeks. The output was a demonstration and was not submitted to the NRC.

Everstar's pitch centers on the claim that paperwork, not reactor technology, is the main constraint on new nuclear plants. The company cites certification efforts that consumed millions of engineering hours, initial permitting documentation costing tens of millions, and NRC review billed at more than $300 an hour. To reach projected demand, it argues nuclear must scale from less than half a gigawatt of new capacity per year to 13 gigawatts. Gordian's architecture pairs retrieval over parsed regulatory and engineering documents with frontier models, and it links claims back to source citations. Compliance rests on Azure's FedRAMP High authorization and NERC CIP offerings, along with Customer Lockbox and immutable access logging, with Everstar configuring an environment for 10 CFR 810 requirements.

Everstar says Claude performed best on tool use and long-horizon reasoning in its internal tests, producing fewer hallucinations and more citation-rich output. Matt Huang, Everstar's Founding Product Lead, said the company got better results from Claude on Microsoft Foundry for that reason. Everstar also reports that in a September 2025 benchmark it scored Gordian above general-purpose models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI on correctness, groundedness, relevance, and retrieval. The DOE was careful to say that faster drafting does not remove the need for licensing experts, and that human experts designed and validated the work.

The Genesis Mission, a national AI initiative under which the DOE has announced $293 million in competitive funding across twenty-six challenges, includes a challenge focused on speeding nuclear deployment. Everstar is an inaugural member of that effort. Beyond federal work, the company reports 80 to 96 percent timeline reductions across customer engagements, with results varying by workload and baseline. One eight-week environmental assessment finished in one week, and an ISO gap analysis that would have cost $20,000 was delivered for $1,050. Everstar reports more than $150,000 transacted through Microsoft Marketplace and roughly $1.5 million in active pipeline.

stories.Headline: WhatsApp's Hidden AI Instructions Told Chatbot Not to Mention Privacy Complaints
stories.Summary:
Redact, a data deletion company, found hidden instructions in the HTML source code of WhatsApp Help Center pages on October 8, 2026. These instructions were invisible to ordinary visitors but could be read by systems processing the page content. Redact examined all 545 pages linked from WhatsApp’s help center and found 102 blocks of hidden AI instructions across 80 pages. Two blocks stood out because they told the chatbot not to recommend certain options to users.

One hidden instruction concerned account deletion. The visible page said accounts are removed automatically 30 days after deactivation or after 120 days without use, or 365 days in the US. The hidden text repeated those waiting periods and then ordered the AI not to recommend contacting a data protection authority or suggest that WhatsApp could manually delete the account. Another instruction told the chatbot not to cite a specific law once a user mentioned a lawyer. Most of the other 102 hidden blocks were harmless, such as clarifying confusing topics or directing users to more relevant pages.

WhatsApp confirmed to WIRED that the instructions appeared because of a bug and said the company has since removed them. The company also said its AI support chatbot was not intended to provide legal advice. Redact argued there is a difference between avoiding legal advice and withholding information about options available to users. WhatsApp’s public privacy policy for Europe says users can complain to a data protection regulator and names the law giving that right.

The discovery does not establish that WhatsApp violated privacy law. However, it highlights the need to ensure AI responses align with a company’s published policies. The hidden instructions created a disparity between the options recognized in WhatsApp’s public privacy information and the guidance its chatbot was instructed to provide. The articles do not say what further action, if any, regulators or Redact plan to take next.

stories.Headline: Harness launches AI Budgets to manage spending
stories.Summary:
Harness, a software company, introduced AI Budgets, a new feature within its Cost Management Agent, according to reports published on October 20 and October 23, 2026. The tool is designed to help organizations monitor and enforce limits on artificial intelligence spending. The company says that many organizations have AI cost policies but have no method to check whether those policies are followed. It cited its 2026 State of AI in FinOps Report, which found that 73 per cent of organizations have an AI cost policy while only 13 per cent can verify that it works.

AI Budgets lets organizations set spending limits by team, developer, model, or project, and it tracks spending as it occurs. Users receive a warning when spending reaches 90 per cent of a budget, which does not restrict access. Once spending exceeds 100 per cent of the weekly limit, access is paused until the next weekly reset or until an increase is approved. Smaller budget increase requests can be approved quickly within the product, while larger ones go to authorized approvers. The system records warnings, blocks, and approved increases in an immutable audit trail that can be exported for compliance programs including SOC 2 and ISO 27001.

Harness says it chose a weekly cycle instead of a monthly one because a monthly limit can let a team use most of its planned spending early in the month. The company tested the feature on its own AI tooling bill before opening early access. In that test, average weekly AI spending per developer fell from $184 to $115, a reduction of about 37 per cent. Cost per million tokens stayed near $1.80 through most of June and July, then dropped to $0.80 during the week governance was introduced, a decline of about 55 per cent. The product also tracks spending by user, provider, model, and token type, and it draws cost and usage data from multiple AI providers into one view.

The company says the feature is aimed at FinOps practitioners and engineering leaders. Harness states that FinOps teams can use it to enforce existing spending policies without manually reviewing every exception, while engineering leaders can use it to expand AI use within set limits. The policy engine is the same one used for cloud spending, and it connects to the Harness Software Delivery Agent, which can pause a deployment that would exceed a budget before the related spending occurs. AI Budgets is available now within the Cost Management Agent, and Harness says it is meant to move AI cost policies from written guidance to enforceable limits.

stories.Headline: Mysuru hospital introduces AI-powered heart imaging
stories.Summary:
Avant Bkg Hospitals in Mysuru, India, has introduced a next-generation artificial intelligence-enabled high-definition intravascular ultrasound technology, and it has also announced plans to launch minimally invasive cardiac surgery services. The technology was launched on Friday, October 23, 2026, by Yaduveer Krishnadatta Chamaraja Wadiyar, the Mysuru-Kodagu MP. The initiatives are meant to improve precision in complex coronary interventions and widen treatment options for patients in Mysuru and nearby districts. They could also reduce the need for patients to travel to larger cities for specialised cardiac care.

The intravascular ultrasound system lets doctors obtain detailed images from inside coronary arteries. Those images help them assess the size of blood vessels, the characteristics of plaque, and how stents are placed and expanded. Cardiologists can use this information to plan and carry out complex angioplasties with greater accuracy. The hospital's planned minimally invasive cardiac surgery uses smaller incisions and specialised surgical techniques for selected procedures.

The launch was attended by the hospital's Managing Director, T.N. Balakrishna Gowda, Director of Cardiology and Chief Interventional Cardiologist Rajagopal J., and Director of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery Madhuprakash S.C. The MP said expanding specialised facilities would give people across the region better access to advanced treatment closer to home. Gowda said the initiatives would help Mysuru become a centre for advanced medical care. Rajagopal said precision is critical in treating complex coronary artery disease, while Madhuprakash said treatment decisions would be based on individual clinical needs. A separate announcement from Batavia, New York, shows a similar push in rural cardiac care.

On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, Rochester Regional Health introduced Heartflow CT-derived fractional flow reserve technology at United Memorial Medical Center in Batavia. The system uses artificial intelligence to analyze CT images and could lower costs for patients. Dr. Bipul Baibhav, a cardiologist who helped lead the rollout, said the technology is more accurate than traditional stress testing and can prevent unnecessary invasive procedures such as angiograms. The health system plans to add the technology at other locations in the Rochester-Finger Lakes region in 2027.

stories.Headline: Posco Future M Starts Palantir AI in Sales and Marketing, Weighs Expansion
stories.Summary:
Posco Future M, a South Korean battery-materials maker, said on Wednesday that it had signed an agreement to adopt two software products from the US firm Palantir Technologies. The company will use Foundry, a data analytics platform that brings together information from its business operations, and the Artificial Intelligence Platform, known as AIP, which combines company data with generative AI to support decisions and automate tasks. The deal was first reported by the Korea Herald and EconoTimes on October 22, 2026. Posco Future M will begin with sales and marketing, aiming for quicker customer responses, and will consider a phased move into manufacturing and other operations later. The partnership follows a digital-transformation strategy the company unveiled in July and a companywide AI initiative launched in August.

The company has set targets for the program that it has not yet reported as results. It aims to cut product-development time by 50 percent, raise manufacturing productivity by 30 percent, and improve customer responsiveness by more than 60 percent. Over the longer term, Posco Future M wants to build a shared data platform linking production, sales and supply-chain partners, which it says could strengthen collaboration across the battery industry and open new business opportunities. The company is also widening AI training for its staff and reviewing applications employees have built for use at work. Selected projects are planned for phased rollout by the first half of 2027.

Currently, 87 employees who have completed specialist training are working to find inefficiencies and develop AI-based solutions. Posco Future M announced the partnership itself, and the company said the arrangement is meant to speed up decisions and let employees focus on oversight and final judgments. The articles do not name an executive who commented on the deal. The Korea Herald reported that the company said integrating fragmented data and placing AI across workflows would help it handle routine processes more quickly. The company framed the agreement as part of its broader push to become more data-driven.

The articles do not say how much the agreement costs or whether the company has achieved any of its targets so far. The move comes as Korean manufacturers look for ways to use AI in their operations, and the articles present the Palantir agreement as one step in a staged plan rather than a complete overhaul. Posco Future M has not said whether the manufacturing expansion will proceed, and that decision is left open. The next milestone the articles identify is the phased rollout of selected projects by the first half of 2027. Until then, the company's progress on its stated goals will be the main thing to watch.

stories.Headline: Letter to the Editor: The existential threat of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
A letter to the editor from Ron Sadler, published in the Daily Journal of Franklin, Indiana on October 23, 2026, and in the Journal Review of Crawfordsville on October 21, 2026, argues that the fast, unchecked growth of artificial intelligence is an immediate existential threat to humanity. The writer says the risks reach the economy, democratic institutions, and the basic nature of human identity. He treats the danger as a present concern rather than speculation about the future. The letter appears in the opinion section, and the newspaper notes that opinion content reflects only the writer's views.

The letter's main concern is economic displacement, which the writer expects to be unprecedented. He contrasts AI with earlier industrial change, when machines replaced physical labor while new intellectual roles appeared. Here, he says, AI goes after cognitive work, and millions of white-collar and creative jobs, including those held by writers, programmers, financial analysts, and administrative professionals, are being phased out. He also raises a deeper worry about control, noting that developers are training systems that work as black boxes whose decisions people do not fully understand. The letter does not give specific figures, dates, or studies to support these claims.

Sadler calls for an end to treating AI development as an inevitable force of nature, arguing instead that it is a human creation that needs strict and immediate regulation. He urges pausing what he describes as a reckless race for technological supremacy and putting rigid global safeguards in place. He warns that without such action, humanity could lose its role as the author of its own destiny. The letter is signed by Sadler, listed as a resident of Franklin in one version and Crawfordsville in the other. The articles provided do not describe any response from officials, companies, or regulators, and they do not say what steps, if any, will follow.

stories.Headline: Will Artificial Intelligence Replace the Doctor—or Set the Doctor Free?
stories.Summary:
Richard Low, MD, a physician and founder of Praxis EMR, gave a presentation on October 3, 2026, during the Association of Yale Alumni in Medicine's alumni weekend, titled "Will AI Replace the Doctor, or Set the Doctor Free?" His argument is that transcribing what a doctor says is not the same as understanding what the doctor knows, thinks, and concludes. A transcript can capture every spoken word and still miss the clinical reasoning behind a decision, because physicians draw on years of experience, knowledge of the individual patient, and information never spoken aloud. Low contends that medical AI should be judged by how well it helps physicians care for patients rather than by how well it imitates them. He also argues that much current medical technology has reversed the natural relationship, forcing physicians to adapt to software instead of software adapting to how they think.

The presentation places these points within concerns about medical education, professional autonomy, and administrative burdens that have contributed to physician dissatisfaction and burnout. Low graduated from Yale School of Medicine in 1976 and practiced in California for about two decades, including leading three emergency departments. He later founded Praxis EMR and has spent decades studying how computers can support rather than interfere with clinical reasoning. The complete presentation is available to physicians, educators, students, and the public at the Praxis EMR website.

Dr. Nitzan Anav, a physician and head of longevity at Maccabi Healthcare Services, makes a related case in a column published October 21, 2026, in The Jerusalem Post. Drawing on a New England Journal of Medicine article by Dr. Dhruv Khullar of Weill Cornell Medicine, Anav argues that AI may increase the amount of medicine practiced rather than reduce the number of doctors needed. He invokes the Jevons paradox, noting that as cataract surgeries and joint replacements became more efficient, they were offered to more people, and that the number of radiologists in the United States has risen over the past decade despite predictions that AI would replace them. He also describes the "lump of labor fallacy," the mistaken belief that there is a fixed amount of medical work to divide between humans and machines.

Anav sees the most promise in longevity and preventive medicine, which requires reviewing histories, medications, tests, and risk factors for each person, work now largely limited to private clinics because public systems lack the time. He suggests AI could continuously flag gaps in prevention and suggest next steps, adding a proactive layer to existing care and making it available to every insured person. He cautions, however, that medicine involves context, judgment, and the ability to spot when an algorithm is wrong. He expects that AI will handle daily reminders and adjustments, health coaches will support commitment, and doctors will coordinate the overall picture, with the most valuable human skills being motivating behavior change, managing uncertainty, and leading teams. Anav concludes that the real gain will be doctors helping more people live healthier years, not fewer doctors.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Advances Precision Cardiovascular Care
stories.Summary:
Researchers writing in the journal Open Heart have described how artificial intelligence is changing cardiovascular medicine, according to an editorial published on 23 October 2026 by EMJ. The editorial, co-authored by Tang Y and colleagues, looks at how AI tools could improve diagnosis, risk assessment and clinical decisions. It also points to research that might help move algorithms out of development and into everyday practice. The piece draws on several studies rather than reporting a single new trial.

On the diagnostic side, the editorial describes deep learning applied to chest X-rays as a possible screening tool for mitral stenosis, which could widen access to testing. Machine learning applied to coronary CT scans was reported to pick out high-risk plaque features that visual review can miss, which may support more precise prediction of heart attack risk. The editorial also notes a comparison between ChatGPT-4o and experienced interventional cardiologists in interpreting coronary angiograms, along with studies of radiomics and pulse wave analysis for atrial fibrillation recurrence and central haemodynamics. For risk prediction, gradient-boosting methods such as XGBoost and CatBoost were examined for guiding coronary imaging decisions and estimating 30-day risk after non-cardiac surgery. Explainable AI methods, including Shapley additive explanations, were used to show which factors drove each prediction, and unsupervised clustering was explored as a way to classify heart failure beyond ejection fraction.

The authors stress that clinical use will depend on fitting these tools into existing workflows while keeping clinicians in control of decisions. They point to systematic reviews and meta-analyses of AI-based atrial fibrillation detection and cardiac CT as evidence that the field is growing. The editorial concludes that the next step is turning increasingly sophisticated models into practical, interpretable tools that support personalised care. Its authors are the researchers named in the reference, and the piece reflects their view of where the field is heading.

Separately, Simon Fraser University announced that Martin Ester, a Distinguished Professor in its School of Computing Science, has been named a Canada CIFAR AI Chair, as reported on the university's website on 21 October 2026. Ester's work examines how AI systems can learn from one another to speed scientific discovery and produce new chemical structures, with the aim of improving diagnosis and treatment based on a person's genomics and lifestyle. His 2025 study introduced CGFlow, a method that designs complex molecules for disease treatment and shows researchers how to synthesize them. SFU's vice-president of research and innovation, Dugan O'Neil, described the appointment as fitting recognition, while Ester said he hopes the work will ultimately improve patient health in Canada and beyond.

stories.Headline: Bloomberg launches Enterprise MCP for AI data access
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg launched Enterprise MCP for its Data Licence Plus service on October 20, 2026. The system connects Bloomberg data to clients' artificial intelligence applications through a standardised interface covering more than 100 million securities and over 50,000 fields. It combines metadata on data fields with semantic search tools and workflow-specific functions, allowing users to request information in natural language instead of relying on field codes or manual identifier matching. The service includes entity resolution tools designed to map names, tickers or descriptions to the correct instrument and its links to the issuing company.

The service provides details including what a data field represents, how it was calculated, when it applies, and qualifiers such as currency, exchange, price type, period and date. Bloomberg hosts and manages the access layer, while clients retain control over the AI agents and applications connected to it, including the models, prompts and instructions used in their workflows. Bloomberg validates a firm's entitlements before returning data in response to an agent request under standard Data Licence rights. Requests are resolved against Bloomberg's Operational Datastore, while tool-level limits cap the number of securities and fields returned in a single call. The initial release includes workflow skills covering point-in-time universe retrieval, corporate action adjustment and revision history, plus tools to identify outliers in a group of tickers, review trades that breach accepted price deviation thresholds, and assess securities and trades for possible sanctions exposure.

Tony McManus, Global Head of Enterprise Data and Indices at Bloomberg, said the bottleneck facing financial institutions has shifted from model capability to data readiness. He said agents that reason well still cannot answer a basic question about a position because the data reaching them carries no indication of what it actually represents. On its own, a last price does not say what currency it is in or what kind of price it is. McManus said connections were never the hard part, readiness is, and that is what Bloomberg built Enterprise MCP to solve.

The launch comes as data providers, banks and financial software firms race to position themselves in the growing market for AI tools in regulated industries. Bloomberg said its engineers have been involved in proposals related to governance controls within the Model Context Protocol and in methods that allow servers to present tailored toolsets to different clients. It added that it leads the MCP Financial Services Interest Group and holds seats on the board and Technical Committee of the Agentic AI Foundation, which oversees the protocol as an open standard. Clients can license specific content domains under standard Bloomberg Data Licence rights.

stories.Headline: Data and skills hinder textile AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The International Textile Manufacturers Federation (ITMF) and the Institut für Textiltechnik (ITA) of RWTH Aachen University published a white paper on 15 October 2026 on how the global textile industry is adopting artificial intelligence. Titled "AI in the Textile Value Chain: A Strategic Guide to Artificial Intelligence for the Global Textile Industry," the 49-page report concludes that fragmented data, skills shortages and weak governance are bigger obstacles than the technology itself. It draws on ten webinar sessions held between 2024 and 2026, which featured more than 20 experts from industry, research and policy organisations. Further input came from talks with practitioners at the ITMF Annual Conference 2025 in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. The authors describe the industry as digitally fragmented rather than under-digitalised, because decades of partial digitalisation have left large amounts of data locked in disconnected systems.

The report says AI is already producing measurable returns in computer-vision inspection of fabrics and yarns, predictive maintenance, energy optimisation and demand forecasting. One case study found that causal AI cut scrap by 10% on a nonwovens production line. The authors expect that integrated, end-to-end AI workflows spanning several processes could become realistic within two to three years. They also warn that AI cannot fix poor data and may amplify existing flaws, and that many companies hold less usable information than they believe. Trust is another condition, since manufacturers want assurances on commercially sensitive information, cybersecurity, transparency and accountability.

The paper recommends that companies put workforce development first, set up sound data management and introduce AI step by step through clearly defined uses with measurable results. It also calls for more collaboration before competition, especially to help small and medium-sized enterprises that lack the means to build AI capabilities alone. Possible measures include common data standards, secure industry data spaces that let firms keep ownership of sensitive information, and a controlled sector-specific tool described as a Textile GPT. Olivier Zieschank, Director of ITMF, said AI is no shortcut around the industry's structural problems but can help firms handle complexity and make the most of scarce expertise. He added that working out where AI really helps is a learning process, which is why exchange through associations matters.

Professor Thomas Gries, Director of ITA at RWTH Aachen University, stressed building data management into both daily and strategic decisions. He said companies need a dedicated task force to embed data integration into their technical and business processes, and he advised bringing in outside specialists to review current processes and find openings for better data use and automation. The report notes that human expertise remains essential for setting objectives, handling unusual situations and ensuring accountability. It adds that routine analytical and administrative work is increasingly supported by AI, which raises demand for digital literacy. Its overall finding is that progress towards wider adoption by 2030 will depend less on more advanced algorithms than on reliable data foundations, relevant skills and confidence in AI-enabled processes.

stories.Headline: National Tertiary Education Union raises concerns over RMIT's use of artificial intelligence program AutoEnrol to assess university student applications

The National Tertiary Education Union has raised concerns about RMIT University's use of an artificial intelligence program called AutoEnrol to assess university student applications. Gabe Gooding, outgoing assistant national secretary of the union, made the claims to a joint parliamentary select committee on artificial intelligence on Thursday, October 22, 2026. They also do not say what consultation rules apply or whether any formal requirement was breached. RMIT University is the institution named as having implemented the program, and the union is the body raising the concerns.

The article attributes the criticism to Gooding and does not record a response from RMIT in the material provided. The report also notes that staff at another leading university walked off the job on the same Thursday, though it does not link that action to the AutoEnrol dispute. stories.Headline: A Veteran of the Telecom Bust Navigates the AI Boom
stories.Summary:
From AI boom to economic bust is an opinion column by Ian Goldin, professor of globalization and development at the University of Oxford, published by The Korea Times on October 21, 2026, and distributed by Project Syndicate. Goldin argues that the gap between AI enthusiasts and AI doomsters is widening, and he sides with neither camp. He says the fantasists, who expect AI to produce utopian abundance, and the doomsters, who fear existential threats and mass unemployment, both overstate what the technology can do for growth. He notes that the column itself is an argument rather than a report of any single event, so it describes no policy change or formal decision. Its main claims are predictions and warnings about the economy.

Goldin challenges the enthusiastic forecasts directly. He cites Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has predicted U.S. growth rising from about 2 percent to 10 to 15 percent, and Elon Musk, who expects growth above 4 percent next year. Goldin calls this an illusion, reasoning that much of the developed world's economic activity, such as child and elderly care, construction, hospitality and personal services, will see little productivity gain from AI. He estimates that even if AI doubled productivity in manufacturing, law and banking, which together make up roughly 20 percent of the U.S. and U.K. economies, total output would rise by only about 20 percent. He adds that the current data-center boom and rising stock valuations may lift near-term growth, but only briefly.

Goldin lists several ways AI could slow growth. Data centers' electricity demands could raise energy costs and keep inflation and interest rates higher, while longer life expectancy and an aging population could strain pension and care systems. He points to $2.4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending, funded by heavy debt and inflated valuations, and cites Nvidia's $105 billion commitment in Ohio alone. He warns that when the bubble bursts, the resulting crash could hit retirement savings, consumer confidence and possibly the broader economy. He also argues that the U.K. and U.S. are underinvesting in the infrastructure, education and business practices that AI would require, while many emerging markets invest at nearly double the rate.

Goldin's concern extends to politics and geopolitics. He argues that AI is concentrating income and activity in a few innovation hubs, widening regional gaps, and that remote work is unlikely to reverse the decline of left-behind communities. He suggests that making housing and transport more affordable would help people move to where jobs are, and says his own Oxford research group estimates that up to 50 percent of U.K. and U.S. jobs are vulnerable to automation. He notes a growing populist backlash against data centers, which are blamed for higher energy prices and water use. On the international stage, he argues that the belief that one country can win the AI race is misguided, that AI-related threats such as engineered pandemics require cooperation, and that U.S. chip export restrictions are making such cooperation nearly impossible.

Goldin ends on a more hopeful note, saying AI is already speeding medical research, including drug development for diseases such as Parkinson's, and that it should not be abandoned. He draws on the Industrial Revolution and the printing press to argue that transformative technologies can bring both progress and harm, and that policy determines which outcome prevails. He contends that this time society will have far less time to adjust, since AI is moving much faster than past revolutions. The column does not describe any scheduled policy response, and it ends with his warning rather than a forecast of specific events.

stories.Headline: How retirees can protect their data using a data broker opt-out
stories.Summary:
How retirees can protect their data using a data broker opt-out is the kind of step that many older people never take, even though their home addresses, phone numbers and family names can appear on people-search sites they have never visited. A Fox News piece from October 22, 2026 explains that these listings can give strangers a surprisingly detailed picture of a person's life, and it recommends an opt-out as a way to reduce that exposure. The article ties the advice to a tragic case in Minnesota, where investigators found a handwritten list of 11 people-search websites in a suspect's vehicle. The article is careful to note that the list alone did not show whether those sites supplied the victims' addresses.

The Minnesota case involved the June 2025 murders of state lawmaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark, and the shootings of State Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette. The list named sites including TruePeopleSearch, Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified, along with notes about which services were free. Vance Boelter pleaded guilty to federal charges on June 11 and was sentenced on July 23 to two consecutive life terms plus 40 years in federal prison, while separate state charges remain pending. The article presents this as an example of how easily personal details can be found, not as proof that any particular site was the source.

The article explains that data brokers gather information from public records, online activity and commercial databases, then combine it into profiles that can include addresses, phone numbers, relatives, property ownership and employment history. For retirees, the piece lists specific risks: scammers using familiar details to make fake financial or family-emergency calls, people who need to protect where they live, and fraudulent Medicare or insurance pitches that sound credible. It advises readers to search their own names, save the pages showing their information, find each site's "opt out" or "remove my information" link, complete any verification steps and check their email for confirmations. It also warns that removal may not be permanent, since listings can reappear, and that removing a listing will not stop every spam call or phishing email.

stories.Headline: TAPP、Google Cloud Agentic AI Summit '26 Fall
stories.Summary:
Cognizant and Google Cloud announced on October 19, 2026, an expansion of their partnership to accelerate the adoption of agentic AI. They launched a new Gemini Frontier Capability Group, backed by more than 18,000 dedicated Cognizant associates. The group pairs Google Cloud’s full-stack, enterprise-ready AI platform with Cognizant’s domain, industry, and engineering expertise. It builds on the momentum created by Cognizant’s dedicated Gemini practice launched in April 2026.

The new group is designed to bridge the path from pilot to production, helping enterprises safely deploy resilient, enterprise-grade agents that can drive measurable business value. It will initially concentrate on legacy modernization, developer experience, autonomous business process agentification, and frontier cyber defense. The group plans to deploy standardized, security-first agentic architecture built on the Model Context Protocol and fortified by Google Cloud’s Model Armor. These frameworks are expected to power solutions including Cognizant’s Catalog Support Agent for retail, the Neuro San-orchestrated Healthcare Agentic Marketplace, and multi-agent Order-to-Cash workflows for manufacturing. Cognizant is also applying Gemini internally, with plans to deploy it to 100,000 associates this year and scale up to 200,000.

Ravi Kumar S, CEO of Cognizant, said the group lets the company’s best frontier engineering talent focus entirely on getting frontier AI into production for clients. He noted that the Build with Gemini workshop gave over 55,000 associates direct experience and tangible skills on the advanced AI platform. Thomas Kurian, chief executive officer of Google Cloud, said deploying AI agents at scale requires trusted partners with deep architectural and integration expertise. He added that Cognizant’s dedicated group and skilling initiative for tens of thousands of engineers will help joint customers accelerate adoption of autonomous agents throughout the enterprise.

The Build with Gemini workshop was completed by more than 55,000 Cognizant associates, making it the largest single Gemini partner workshop held to date. One early proof point showed that by integrating Gemini AI models across its software development lifecycle, Cognizant helped a leading retailer achieve a 40 percent increase in developer productivity, reduce time-to-market by 30 percent, and realize a 35 percent cost savings. The announcement was made from Teaneck, New Jersey, and Sunnyvale, California. The articles do not specify further next steps beyond the group’s initial focus areas and the planned scaling of Gemini to more Cognizant associates.

stories.Headline: Micron Taiwan Workers Stage Strike Seeking Bigger Share of AI Profits
stories.Summary:
A group of workers at Micron Technology Inc.'s Taoyuan plant in Taiwan began a 24-hour strike on Thursday, starting at 9 a.m. outside the factory. The action was carried out by 11 union officials, and production lines were not directly halted. The union represents roughly 2,335 workers, or about 70% of the plant's workforce. It is pressing the memory-chip maker to set up a formal profit-sharing system after an AI-driven boom pushed its earnings to record levels.

The union wants Micron to set aside 15% of operating profit for an employee bonus pool, with payments made quarterly from fiscal 2027. Its chairman, Jerry Lin, has said that employees received annual performance bonuses equal to about 2.3 months of salary in 2025. Workers argue that these payouts and one-time awards do not reflect the company's record earnings. Mediation has not resolved the dispute, and a further meeting on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, ended without the company offering a specific profit-sharing figure. Workers have also complained that rank-and-file employees have limited access to stock awards.

Micron has said it announced record compensation for its Taiwan employees in September 2026, with production workers set to receive fiscal-2026 rewards equal to 35 to 68 months of salary and a one-time appreciation bonus of NT$1 million. The company's Taichung plant union reached a separate labor agreement with Micron on the same Wednesday, covering fiscal-2027 compensation. That deal includes a quarterly bonus tied directly to profits for employees at director level and below, which the articles describe as a first for the company. Taiwan plants account for over 60% of Micron's global production capacity, including high-bandwidth memory. The articles also note that TrendForce estimated Micron held about 23.3% of the global DRAM market in the second quarter, ranking third.

stories.Headline: How Moderna Is Using AI To Take On Cancer
stories.Summary:
The article does not concern Moderna at all. It reports a study published in The Lancet Digital Health by researchers at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, which is affiliated with Harvard, describing an AI model called FAHR-Face that estimates a person's biological age and survival risk from a single ordinary facial photo. The research team, led by corresponding author Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist, trained a foundational model on more than 40 million unlabeled facial photos from the public WebFace42M dataset, covering ages 0 to 116. From that base, they built two tools, FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates biological age, and FAHR-FaceSurvival, which was trained on 34,363 photos of cancer patients to estimate survival risk.

In a test subset of 3,820 cancer patients, the survival tool placed 122 people in the highest risk range, and 64 of them, or 52.5 percent, died within 90 days of their photos being taken. By comparison, the 90-day mortality rate among 975 patients in the lowest-scoring range was 2.1 percent. The highest risk quartile had a mortality rate more than three times that of the lowest risk group, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.23. At five years, patients in the lowest-risk quartile had a survival rate of 78.1 percent, against 17.7 percent for those in the highest-risk quartile. The age tool had a mean absolute error of 5.1 years, and looking more than five years older than one's actual age was associated with a 21 percent higher death risk.

The researchers also examined what the models focused on. The age tool attended mainly to nasolabial folds, the forehead and the temples, while the survival tool focused on the area under the eyes and the bridge of the nose, a pattern the researchers linked to the "Hippocratic face" described by Hippocrates. The authors reported that makeup, lighting changes, and most cosmetic procedures did not meaningfully change the age estimates, though rhinoplasty produced a small shift. Smoking was tied to higher estimated biological age in a dose-dependent way. Hugo Aerts, co-senior author and director of the Artificial Intelligence in Medicine Program at Mass General Brigham, described the work as the first report showing that an AI model can predict cancer survival directly from a simple photo.

Matthew Liao, director of the Center for Bioethics at New York University, raised concerns that the article presents as open questions. He asked what would happen if the model misjudged a patient who needed urgent treatment, whether it could be used to deny drugs, and whether insurers or employers might use it to set premiums or filter candidates. The article says the research team drew a clear boundary around these concerns but does not detail what that boundary is. Nothing in the article indicates any Moderna involvement or any planned clinical deployment.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Frontier Tour London: Building trust in the agentic AI era
stories.Summary:
Microsoft held its Frontier Tour in London on 21 October 2026, attended by 6,500 people, where leaders argued that the next stage of artificial intelligence depends on trust, human control, security and skills rather than technical capability alone. The same day, KPMG and Microsoft announced the opening of the KPMG and Microsoft Frontier Innovation Hub, a co-innovation environment for building trusted agentic AI, which is designed to help organisations design, test, govern and scale AI solutions. The Hub sits near Microsoft's Redmond, Washington headquarters and is described as a seven-year strategic co-investment. Its stated aim is to help clients become what Microsoft calls Frontier Firms, meaning organisations that are human-led and agent-operated.

The London event focused on how AI agents, which carry out specific or multi-step tasks under human oversight, should be given access to information and actions. Satya Nadella said organisations should treat AI models as new forms of insiders and build a zero-trust architecture around them, and Microsoft described its Project Perception as using specialised AI agents to test safeguards and help mitigate problems. Microsoft IQ is meant to give AI access to organisational context such as documents, databases and messages while respecting existing controls. The Hub announcement adds that KPMG and Microsoft intend to develop real-time agentic assurance and runtime enforcement, so that autonomous agents operate within defined boundaries of trust, compliance and accountability.

Darren Hardman, Microsoft's UK and Ireland chief executive, said Microsoft research ranks the UK eighth among 147 economies for generative AI adoption, and that four in five business leaders think the UK can become a world-leading AI economy within five years, compared with only two in five employees. He cited examples including a trial of Copilot across 90 NHS organisations, where users reported average savings of 43 minutes a day on administrative tasks, and NHS England's plan to roll it out to more than 500,000 clinicians and support staff. He also pointed to Network Rail, the AA, UK Power Networks and BT, where BT reported time savings of up to two hours a day for employees. Hardman said 71% of employees using AI report a positive impact on their work and career, and that nine in ten business leaders report having a clear AI strategy.

Nadella and Hardman, along with Todd Lohr of KPMG and Cherie Gartner of Microsoft, presented these efforts as a response to a gap between ambition and confidence, with Hardman saying the UK must close that gap through clear controls, human oversight and useful skills. Gartner, quoted in the Hub announcement, said the next challenge in AI is not just innovation but trust. Lohr said organisations are moving quickly from experimenting with AI to using it to execute work. The articles do not give a timetable for the Hub's first outputs, so what follows from these commitments remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: Microsoft, Opella partner on agentic AI content verification platform
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and consumer healthcare company Opella announced on Tuesday, October 21, 2026, that they are partnering to build an agentic artificial intelligence platform to verify health content at scale. The platform will be called Lumen and will consist of 14 specialized agents that check product claims, medical facts, sources and legal mentions. The agents will also advise where content should be placed according to its type and the varying publication channels. Lumen will flag compliance issues, corrections and points where human input is needed.

Opella Chief Growth Officer Alberto Hernandez said that AI is fundamentally changing the speed and scale at which the company can develop and deliver content, and that content production has been scaled by 30 times. He stressed that in healthcare, speed can never come at the expense of trust. Hernandez said the company is using Lumen to help its experts review content faster and make better-informed decisions while keeping human expertise and approval at the center of the process. The articles state that human experts keep the final decision.

The partnership adds to Microsoft's growing set of healthcare AI initiatives. In June, the company announced a strategic collaboration with Mayo Clinic to develop and deploy a frontier AI model designed for healthcare, intended to synthesize diverse clinical data to support earlier diagnoses, more personalized treatment decisions and better patient outcomes. Mayo Clinic will own that model, and Microsoft plans to make it available through Azure Foundry APIs, with initial deployment inside the health system's clinical environment and continuous testing planned. In March, Microsoft also unveiled Copilot Health for consumers, an AI assistant that can review medical records, help patients prepare for doctor appointments and offer personalized insights based on their health data.

Articles.Title: Microsoft, Opella partner on agentic AI content verification platform

stories.Headline: Vernon College Adopts Artificial Intelligence Gun Detection Technology
stories.Summary:
Vernon College, a community college in north Texas, has put an artificial intelligence gun detection system into use to protect its students, staff and visitors. ZeroEyes, the company behind the software, announced the deployment on October 20, 2026. Teksys, Inc., a Houston-based security systems and connectivity provider, helped facilitate the installation. The college has campuses in Vernon and Wichita Falls and serves about 2,300 students across a legislatively designated 12-county service area.

The software layers onto the college's existing digital security cameras, so the school did not need to replace its camera network. When a gun is identified, images are immediately sent to the ZeroEyes Operations Center, which is based in the United States and staffed around the clock every day of the year by specially trained military and law enforcement veterans. If staff there judge the threat to be valid, alerts and actionable details, including a visual description, the type of gun and its last known location, go to law enforcement and school officials, often within seconds of detection. The system also adds to measures the college already has, including a campus-wide camera system, AlertMedia emergency mass notification technology, direct radio communication with local law enforcement in both Vernon and Wichita Falls, and specialized protective equipment for campus police officers.

Dr. Dusty R. Johnston, the college's president, said protecting students, faculty and staff is central to the college's work and that it keeps evaluating resources that help it respond decisively in critical situations. He said ZeroEyes strengthens the overall safety approach and supports a more prepared and responsive campus. David Madrigal, a senior engineer at Teksys, called ZeroEyes the kind of solution every campus should consider in a modern safety strategy, and said Vernon College stands out for its proactive mindset and willingness to invest in such tools. Mike Lahiff, CEO and cofounder of ZeroEyes, praised Teksys for its expertise in public safety technology and said the company was pleased to partner with it on the implementation.

ZeroEyes was founded in 2018 by Navy SEALs and elite technologists and is headquartered in the Greater Philadelphia area. The company says its technology has been recognized by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security as an effective anti-terrorism solution, and that it was the first AI-based gun detection platform to receive full SAFETY Act Designation. Its platform is used at thousands of locations in the United States, Mexico, the Caribbean, Latin America and India. The articles do not say when the system became active at Vernon College or what it cost.
