stories.Headline: Texas Athletics and McCombs School of Business Launch New Bevo Lab, Bringing Together Sports, AI and Analytics
stories.Summary:
Texas Athletics and the Business of Sports Institute at the McCombs School of Business announced the launch of Bevo Lab, a collaboration that will serve as a sports intelligence platform and living laboratory for the university. The announcement was made on October 23, 2026, in cooperation with Longhorn Sports Properties, and Vice President and Folger Family Athletics Director Chris Del Conte is set to formally unveil the lab at Texas' Business of College Sports Summit that day. The lab is meant to combine sports, technology, data analytics and artificial intelligence to improve human performance while giving students hands-on learning. It will draw on the university's 21 intercollegiate teams and more than 500 student-athletes.

The lab will house four main components: the Bevo Lakehouse, a unified data warehouse that will first consolidate football data such as game film and wearable technology before expanding to all 21 varsity sports. Predictive AI and analytics models will provide coaches with insights for game strategy, scouting and player development, including a "transfer AI" tool for roster evaluation. Tailored applications will give athletes, coaches and athletic executives interfaces built for their daily workflows. A skills-training program will let UT students build AI skills and deploy live applications alongside athletic teams, including through a Google Public Sector ambassador program. The lab will be housed in Innovation Tower near campus, and as many as 40 student researchers each year will work on its modeling and data projects.

Three companies have joined as sponsors. Dell Technologies is the founding sponsor and Official Technology Infrastructure Sponsor, supplying the secure AI-ready infrastructure, while Google Cloud is the Official Cloud Provider and Enterprise AI Provider, using its platform and Gemini models. SHI International serves as the strategic technology and solutions integrator, tying the partners' technologies into one platform. Del Conte called the effort a way to make Texas Athletics the most data-driven athletic program in the country, and Kirk Goldsberry, executive director of the institute, said the partners' tools would speed up data analysis. Google Cloud's Matt Renner, a UT alumnus, said the lab would set a new benchmark for sports innovation.

The announcement comes with early results and a stated plan for growth. The articles say early work with Google Public Sector has already introduced AI workflows that save UT coaches more than 15 hours per week in game preparation. Longhorn Sports Properties, the Austin-based division of Learfield, helped develop the lab and secured its corporate sponsors. More information is to be posted on a dedicated microsite at texaslonghorns.com/bevolab.

Articles.Title: Texas Athletics and McCombs School of Business Launch New Bevo Lab, Bringing Together Sports, AI and Analytics

stories.Headline: Big Tech Can't Stop AI Spending, but the Cash Is Running Out
stories.Summary:
Big Tech's push into artificial intelligence is running into a financing squeeze, according to a Seoul Economic Daily report published on October 23, 2026. The reporters, Kim Chang-young and Cho Yang-joon, say the largest technology companies have used up internal cash, corporate bond sales and circular financing arrangements as their spending has ballooned. Even so, the companies maintain that demand for AI is overwhelming and that they cannot stop raising money. A Reuters report cited in the article projects that combined capital spending at Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle will reach $945.55 billion in January next year, roughly six times the January 2023 level. Over the same period, their free cash flow is expected to swing to a deficit of $2.87 billion from $223.11 billion.

Meta is at the center of the concern after disclosing commitments of nearly $825 billion to AI infrastructure. That figure includes $355.7 billion in operating and finance leases that do not appear on its balance sheet, along with $454.5 billion in separate non-cancelable contracts, including third-party cloud services. The total is $125 billion more than the $700 billion Meta disclosed at the end of July. Following the announcement, the premium on credit default swaps, which measures the risk of default, rose 8.9 basis points to 119.3 basis points. To raise funds quickly, Meta plans to issue non-voting Class C shares in January, first distributing one new share for each share held and later selling additional shares into the market.

Anthropic and OpenAI are also moving ahead with plans to go public despite heavy spending. Reuters reported that Anthropic may file its registration statement as early as the end of this month and hold its IPO in the middle of next month, after spending $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of this year alone. Its contractual obligations for computing power over the next decade total $450 billion, and that figure could reach $750 billion with ongoing negotiations. OpenAI, preparing an IPO next year, has reportedly lowered its valuation target to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion after some investors called the earlier figure too high. Meta has argued that large AI fundraising by Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI makes the market harder, so it needs to secure capital before rivals.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has said at a Berlin event that the constraint on AI expansion is financing rather than weak demand. He defended neocloud companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, which sit at the center of investor worries. Industry observers read Big Tech's moves as an attempt to draw more private capital through investment banks while counting on U.S. government support. The Trump administration issued an executive order in July last year offering loan guarantees, lending, subsidies, tax benefits and long-term purchase contracts for data centers, and the industry wants that support expanded. Analysts say aggressive use of these programs could ease the companies' funding strains.

Articles.Title: Big Tech Can't Stop AI Spending, but the Cash Is Running Out - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) Remains a Key AI Growth Driver Despite Benchmark Headwinds
stories.Summary:
Polen Capital's Polen Focus Growth Strategy released its third-quarter 2026 investor letter, which highlighted NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA) as a key AI growth driver despite recent benchmark pressure. The fund outperformed the Russell 1000 Growth Index in the quarter, returning 4.46% net of fees against the index's 0.92% gain. Its year-to-date net return, however, remained negative at 8.11%, compared with a 6.30% gain for the benchmark. Semiconductor and other direct AI-capital-expenditure holdings faced valuation pressure as investors reconsidered spending levels, financing, and future returns on infrastructure investment. NVIDIA was described as the portfolio's largest relative detractor during the quarter, not because its stock fell, but because the fund's roughly 7.5% position stayed materially underweight the stock's roughly 15% weight in the index.

NVIDIA's shares rose nearly 15% during the quarter. The stock closed at approximately $221.97 on October 21, 2026, with a market capitalization of about $5.21 trillion, and its one-month return was -4.00%. Over the last 52 weeks, shares traded between $164.27 and $243.37. Polen's managers wrote that NVIDIA once again delivered exceptional growth, with revenue more than doubling year over year and data center products making up about 92% of revenue. They said management indicated the growth outlook remains supply constrained rather than demand constrained.

The managers also pointed to the upcoming Vera Rubin product cycle as a possible further expansion of the company's revenue opportunity. They noted risks including possible gross margin pressure from rising memory and component costs and extended customer payment terms, while still considering NVIDIA one of the most competitively advantaged companies in the AI infrastructure ecosystem. The letter also described a broader shift in which investors began separating businesses vulnerable to AI disruption from those positioned to benefit from AI adoption. Polen said it continued rebalancing toward companies with attractive long-term growth, stronger momentum, and more visible demand, while remaining cautious about persistent inflation, higher interest rates, energy costs, and valuations. The article notes that NVIDIA was 4th on a list of 40 popular hedge fund stocks heading into 2026, with 285 hedge fund portfolios holding the stock at the end of the second quarter, up from 275 in the prior quarter.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) Remains a Key AI Growth Driver Despite Benchmark Headwinds

stories.Headline: Kakao Mobility Unveils AI Parking Tech That Cuts Exit Times 20%
stories.Summary:
Kakao Mobility, a South Korean company, presented its artificial intelligence and data-driven parking technology at the 2026 ITS World Congress in Gangneung, where it served as an official sponsor. The company spoke on the 23rd of October, 2026, about its showing at the event, which was the world's largest gathering devoted to transportation technology and was held in South Korea for the first time in 16 years. Its exclusively sponsored session, held on the 22nd under the theme "Redefining Urban Parking," focused on connecting parking facilities into smart city infrastructure. The session was chaired by Park Dong-ju, president of the Korean Society of Intelligent Transport Systems.

Park Eun-ho, head of the Platform & Commerce business division, described how the company has linked parking facilities nationwide into one platform since launching its service in 2017. He highlighted barrier-free exits, which let drivers leave without stopping because payment is automatic, and the country's first cloud-based parking control system. Seo Jung-hoon, a director on the DeepAI team, presented AI that uses cameras to read license plates and parking spaces, along with 3D indoor and outdoor mapping and digital twin technology. The company also recently signed a proof-of-concept contract for Saudi Arabia's Diriyah smart city project, which marks a push into overseas markets.

Kim Gun-woo, head of the Future Platform Economy Research Institute, closed the session with an analysis of about 1.62 million parking-related data records. According to that analysis, platform-based tools such as the Kakao T parking pass and automatic payment eased bottlenecks when vehicles leave, cutting the interval between departing cars by up to about 20 percent. Hwang Yoon-young, head of compliance management at Kakao Mobility, said the congress gave the company a chance to share its AI, data and research with transportation officials from around the world. She also said the company will keep developing its parking technology as infrastructure for urban transport and for autonomous driving, and will expand further into global markets.

Articles.Title: Kakao Mobility Unveils AI Parking Tech That Cuts Exit Times 20% - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Meta's AI rewrites the ads. From October 30, advertisers carry the risk
stories.Summary:
Meta's AI ad tools have drawn sharp criticism from advertisers this week after unwanted edits appeared in live campaigns. Bookshop.org said an ad had been altered by a generative AI feature it had not knowingly enabled, and it has since turned off all of Meta's AI ad features. Reports from Adweek on October 22 describe other advertisers pulling ads that had been changed without their approval. Meta's revised Commercial Terms, which take effect on October 30, add an "AI Features" section that makes advertisers solely responsible for changes its AI makes to their ads, including features Meta switches on itself. That section also acknowledges the tools may make mistakes and may not always produce accurate or suitable results.

The change matters because it moves the risk of those errors onto advertisers in writing. According to Adweek's reading, the new section drops an earlier condition that limited advertiser responsibility to cases where they chose to use Meta's AI creative tools. PPC Land said it could not check the quoted passages against Meta's preview, and that the earlier wording Adweek cited does not appear in the terms dated March 6, 2024. Meta's liability was already capped at the greater of $100 or the fees an advertiser paid in the previous twelve months, and advertisers already indemnify Meta against third-party claims. Separately, the October 30 terms let Meta crawl business websites and use the content to train its AI, and Meta has said the purpose is to gather accurate product information.

Meta's spokesperson told Adweek the update folds existing generative AI ad terms into the main terms and that advertisers can switch off individual Advantage+ features in Ads Manager. The spokesperson did not say whether an advertiser is liable for a feature it never turned on. Advertisers and agencies quoted in the coverage described features appearing without their request and said many of the opt-out controls sit in hidden or collapsed menus. Kayla Loecker of AdCellerant warned that shifting legal liability onto advertisers creates serious operational risk, while Asa Hiken of Emarketer said consumers may assume a brand chose the AI edits. David Dweck of Go Fish Digital said his agency will not tell clients to cut fourth-quarter spending, describing Meta's approach as a tax of advertising on the platform.

The week also brought a separate default change. Meta plans to turn on product browsing in existing Facebook and Instagram ads on October 28 unless advertisers opt out, and the switch falls 30 days before Black Friday on November 27. Meta cites a 3% average rise in conversions from an August experiment across about 117,700 advertisers, though it did not define conversion. Meta also told investors that advertising revenue grew 26% in its latest quarter, and a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion in a separate case. Advertisers have so far largely kept buying, and the central question now is whether they will accept the new terms as the cost of reaching their customers.

Articles.Title: Meta's AI rewrites the ads. From October 30, advertisers carry the risk

stories.Headline: Inside Track - Scaling AI responsibly at Microsoft: Lessons from our Customer Zero journey
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's Office of Responsible AI and its cloud supply chain organization have been working on how to govern thousands of AI agents, workflows, and copilots across the company, as reported by microsoft.com on October 22, 2026. The company's Customer Zero program, which tests its technology internally before feeding lessons back to product groups, has found that responsible AI works best as a scaling function rather than an add-on. Teams that build privacy, security, and responsible AI principles in from the start, rather than attaching them at the end, tend to face far lower resource costs over a system's life. The article describes this as the central lesson so far.

The Office of Responsible AI creates standardized policies and processes that speed up reviews and keep practices consistent across products. The team led by Alberto Carrozzo, a senior technical program manager and responsible AI leader for Microsoft Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, has completed more than 2,000 internal tool reviews. It is now using patterns from earlier work to flag cases that need closer attention and to work through a pipeline of thousands more. Carrozzo has said that the more the team learns, the more it must apply that knowledge to find and address risk quickly.

Different internal tools carry different risks, which shapes how they are governed. Supply chain agents handle confidential business information and supplier data, legal systems analyze sensitive records and must support defensible decisions, and customer support tools put AI directly in conversation with outside customers. The cloud supply chain organization, which handles sourcing, delivery, maintenance, and decommissioning of hardware for Microsoft's services, has grown its business volume fivefold in recent years while staffing stayed flat. It now runs more than 100 enterprise-grade AI agents in production, and work that once took several people days can be prepared automatically and updated continuously.

A practical lesson from this work is that scaling AI sometimes means deliberately limiting what a system can do. Jeevan Pathuri, vice president of software engineering for Cloud Supply Chain, has said that a planning agent should not answer questions about the weather and should stay grounded in the job it was built for. The article notes that testing revealed a common problem with AI tools, in which an application can allow more of a model's general capability through than its purpose requires. The article's description of the broader pattern is that these practices are still being refined as adoption grows across the company.

Articles.Title: Inside Track - Scaling AI responsibly at Microsoft: Lessons from our Customer Zero journey

stories.Headline: Korea to Fast-Track AI Data Center Permits, Allow Driverless Car Sales
stories.Summary:
South Korea's government announced plans on October 23, 2026, to speed up permits for artificial intelligence data centers and loosen rules on self-driving vehicles. The changes were unveiled by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport at the second plenary meeting of the Regulatory Rationalization Committee, which the president chairs. The plans were reported by the Seoul Economic Daily. The science ministry will create a one-stop fast-track window for AI data center permits, which it describes as the biggest obstacle to building such facilities. Facilities outside the capital area that meet certain criteria would be exempted from power grid impact assessments.

Because areas where people are present make up less than 30% of an AI data center, unmanned spaces such as server rooms and cooling and power equipment would be excluded from building size calculations. The government also plans to spend 200 billion won next year on upstream and downstream industries and to designate AI data center special zones. Deputy Prime Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, who also heads the science ministry, told a parliamentary audit the same day that leased AI data centers currently receive no tax benefits and that the government would move quickly to discuss this with fiscal authorities. The transport ministry will create a legal framework for robotaxi operators and plans to finish revising the law by next year. Pilot robotaxi operations are expected to begin around 2028 in Gwangju, a test city for self-driving technology.

Sales channels for driverless cars are set to open starting at the end of this year, under new safety standards. Corporate testing rules will also be relaxed, allowing self-driving cars without a driver's seat to travel outside designated pilot zones when heading to a depot or recharging. Raw data collected by business vehicles operated by third parties will be made available for use. The article does not say how these measures will be enforced beyond the timelines listed. More details on the tax changes and the special zones are expected as the ministries finalize their plans.

Articles.Title: Korea to Fast-Track AI Data Center Permits, Allow Driverless Car Sales - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: New Meta AI tool exposed thousands of private conversations online
stories.Summary:
Meta's new AI platform, Muse, left thousands of users' private conversations open to the public, according to a Sunday report from the internet security firm Claroc. Researchers at the firm found that a feature for generating links to share conversations was built so those links could be found through internet search. The links open a webpage that requires no login. Claroc said it identified more than 6,800 links online, and while most of the conversations were harmless, some contained personal records, internal business documents and a user's confidential preparation for an executive-search call.

The problem stems from a conversation-naming feature combined with a shared domain for the pages, which made the links searchable even though Meta had tried to keep web crawlers and search engines from indexing them. Claroc noted that similar leaks had occurred at OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI. The firm warned that such a list could serve as a ready-made resource for fraud, impersonation or social engineering. Meta suspended the sharing feature after Ars Technica asked for comment, and Claroc said previously accessible links stopped opening as of Tuesday.

Claroc said it reported the flaw to Meta on Oct. 8 through the company's bug bounty program, which pays rewards of up to $300,000 depending on the severity of a security issue. According to Claroc's chief technology officer, Asaf Aprozper, Meta did not respond through that program, and the firm's attempts to contact Meta employees directly through LinkedIn also went unanswered. A Meta spokesperson, Tracy Clayton, confirmed to SFGATE that the sharing feature is paused while the company reviews the report. Claroc did not say whether it had received or expected a payout.

Meta launched Muse on Sept. 8, and the app has become widely popular, reaching more than 10 million downloads within 40 days, which puts it among a handful of apps to do so alongside Fortnite and Pokemon Go. Meta markets Muse as a personal AI assistant that can book flights, make restaurant reservations and handle purchases, but those functions require deep personal access, which worries privacy experts given Meta's record on protecting user data. The same week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for misleading users about its data collection practices. Claroc's researchers urged users to assume that anything they share with AI assistants is public until they have verified otherwise.

Articles.Title: New Meta AI tool exposed thousands of private conversations online

stories.Headline: Why smaller CPA firms may have the AI advantage
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, but an opinion column published on Accounting Today on October 23, 2026, by Adam Hale, a partner at Anders CPAs + Advisors and co-founder of Summit CPA Group. Hale argues that small CPA firms worried about falling behind larger firms in artificial intelligence are likely overestimating the gap, since AI accounting tools are advancing quickly in tax and audit software. He cites a Wolters Kluwer finding that 70% of all accounting firms already use AI at least weekly, a figure that rises only to 76% among high-growth firms. The column also notes that a three-year, $1 billion AI spending plan announced by PwC in 2023 does not automatically produce visible results.

Hale draws on a new Gartner CFO survey to show that uncertainty about AI returns is widespread across industries. In that survey, 55% of respondents reported positive overall returns on last year's AI investments, while 57% were unclear about which AI use cases produced those results. Hale says large, private equity-backed firms face their own obstacles, because their size spreads their deployments across many areas and makes return on investment harder to track. He argues that these conditions give smaller practices room to test processes and adjust quickly. The column does not present any new figures on the size of the advantage or any regulatory change.

Hale's central point is that small firms also face pressure from clients who now build their own AI-generated analyses and expect their accountants to review them. He says that CPAs find it hard to validate client-built tools that have not been properly designed, so smaller firms can gain an edge by creating their own reliable tools with proper expertise and safeguards. His advice is for firms to identify advisory gaps affecting their largest clients and to begin testing tools and workflows that supplement existing analysis. The column is written by an industry practitioner and offers his own view, and it does not report any planned events or next steps beyond that advice.

Articles.Title: Why smaller CPA firms may have the AI advantage - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: Indian entrepreneur unveils AI model for engineering design, claims cost advantage
stories.Summary:
Skyfall AI, a company co-founded by Indian entrepreneur Sam Pasupalak, has introduced SKY-001, an AI model built for complex engineering work using computer-aided design (CAD) and building information modelling (BIM). The article, published on October 22, 2026 by TechGig, reports that the model was unveiled by Pasupalak, who is the company's CEO. The model is the product of 18 months of work by the Skyfall AI team. Pasupalak says SKY-001 is faster, cheaper, and more accurate than the leading AI systems his team tested. SKY-001 is designed to produce complete product designs by working in stages, according to Skyfall AI.

For a complex product, the model first divides it into assemblies and individual components, then maps out how each part should be built using visual representations, sketches, and construction steps. For building design, it takes a building outline and breaks it into units and rooms. The company says this approach lets the model manage projects involving hundreds or thousands of steps while keeping each component consistent with the overall design. Pasupalak claims the model runs between 51 and 125 times faster than the frontier models tested. He also says it is more than 150 to 210 times cheaper, depending on the comparison.

Pasupalak's own cost comparison puts SKY-001 at $0.005 per sample for a CAD task, compared with $0.75 for GPT-6 Astra, a figure that makes GPT-6 Astra's cost 150 times higher. On accuracy, the company reports a score of 79.7 per cent on the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric, which measures how closely an AI-generated design overlaps a reference design, against 79.1 per cent for GPT-6 Astra. The article stresses that these figures come from Skyfall AI's own tests and have not been independently verified. It also notes that the results apply only to the engineering tasks tested and do not show that SKY-001 outperforms general-purpose AI models in other uses.

Pasupalak is originally from Bhubaneswar, Odisha, and is now based in San Francisco. Pasupalak started Skyfall AI in 2025, after co-founding the AI research startup Maluuba in 2011 and serving as its CEO. Microsoft acquired Maluuba in 2017, and at the company Pasupalak led researchers and engineers working on artificial intelligence and language understanding. The article does not say whether SKY-001 will be released publicly, what pricing it will carry, or when independent testing might be carried out.

Articles.Title: Indian entrepreneur unveils AI model for engineering design, claims cost advantage - TechGig

stories.Headline: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has published research, produced with its collaborator Theorem, showing that large language models can now generate formal correctness proofs for real-world software at a scale that was previously impractical. The company used Claude to prove security properties at the assembly code level, in RISC-V, across 123 open-source libraries. The work covers 239 entry points, and the proofs check that these programs will not crash, with memory-safety errors or failed assertions, for any input under 64 MB. The post is dated October 22, 2026, and is credited to Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano and Harshikaa Agrawal.

The approach converts each library's existing fuzz tests into a formal specification, which Claude then proves. Over a span of a few weeks, the proofs came to about 180 million lines of Rocq code, with a typical proof running to roughly 600,000 lines. The proofs assume a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget running on a RISC-V CPU under Linux. Anthropic says developers would then need to trust only the formal models of RISC-V and Linux processes, the exact theorem statements, and the Rocq proof checker. The company is publishing a subset of the proofs and the trusted components so others can check them, and Theorem is offering to run the same pipeline on other open-source projects and has published a Claude skill to help developers begin.

The post frames the effort as a response to AI's growing ability to find and exploit bugs, noting that the Linux kernel recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. Anthropic says that while writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had gone undetected for years despite trillions of test runs, and that Claude patched the bugs it found so that proofs could proceed. The company states that the work does not eliminate all bugs, since remaining defects could lie in the trusted components or outside the scope of the proofs. Historically, formal verification has been costly; the post cites seL4 as taking two person-years to implement and 20 person-years to verify. Anthropic expects the cost to fall as models improve and as proofs become more reusable, and it encourages developers, especially those who tried earlier models, to revisit the technique.

Articles.Title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has published a study in Science reporting that its AI diagnostic system, called MAI-DxO, correctly diagnosed complex medical cases more than twice as often as generalist physicians in a simulation. The system coordinates several AI agents that work like a panel of doctors, questioning a patient, ordering tests, and debating a diagnosis. Using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time, compared with 36% for primary care doctors and general internists working alone with reference materials. The article notes that such complex cases are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who were not part of the comparison.

The article says the study's own data suggests much of the gain comes from stronger underlying AI models, with Microsoft's orchestration adding improvements on top. Microsoft tested the system with models from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, with its best results using OpenAI's GPT-5 and GPT-5.5. On its own, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case, while the orchestration system cut that cost by roughly $3,000 and raised accuracy by about four points. With GPT-5.5, accuracy on complex cases rose from 72% to nearly 87%, but the gains did not appear on emergency department cases. Microsoft's researchers said accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum.

Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, called the result a step toward "medical superintelligence," which the company defines as the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care. Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, said the biggest challenge in healthcare is the growing gap between demand and supply of medical expertise. Suleyman told TechCrunch that Microsoft is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a healthcare foundation model, with release planned for next year. He also predicted major progress in medical records prediction by 2027 and said he expects healthcare models to improve substantially within 24 to 36 months.

The article also describes context and next steps. Suleyman previously co-founded DeepMind, which Google acquired in 2014, and he joined Microsoft in 2024, with King following a few months later. Microsoft has partnered with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston to evaluate DxO in real-world settings, where patients receiving standard care will also consent to engage with DxO, and its recommendations will be compared against those of human doctors. Google published a related study in The Lancet this month evaluating its AMIE system in urgent care visits. Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians, and Suleyman said the company aims to have leading clinical decision support products in the coming years.

Articles.Title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’

stories.Headline: Who Is Accountable When AI Makes the Decision?
stories.Summary:
This article is not a news report of an event. It is a promotional page for a free 60-minute online masterclass on AI accountability, published by TechGig on 23 October 2026. The session is scheduled for 23 November, from 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM, and is led by Dr. Smrite Goudhaman, described as a Global Professor of Practice at Golden Gate University and a Pre-Sales Solutions leader at Datamatics. It is aimed at people building or deploying AI, people signing off on AI releases, and people using AI in recruitment and screening. Participants who complete the session receive a Certificate of Participation.

The masterclass says it will help attendees explain who is accountable when an AI system makes or influences a consequential decision, such as rejecting a job candidate or affecting patient care. It promises to distinguish principles, voluntary guidance, national strategies and binding law across countries, including India, the European Union, the United States and the African Union. Attendees will work through a five-question Accountability Test on a hypothetical AI-assisted hiring decision, and the session covers where people can review, override, stop or appeal a decision. The organisers say no technical or legal background is needed, and that participants will leave with five questions to ask before deploying any AI system.

The articles do not report any incident, regulatory action or harm that prompted the session. The only named responsibility is Dr. Goudhaman's role as presenter, and the page states that it does not imply endorsement by the organisations it discusses. The page also cites her prior work, including a moderated side event at the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva and mentoring of learners towards UNESCO Ethics of AI coursework, but these are described as background rather than as findings. The articles do not say what happens after the session beyond the Q&A and the certificate.

Articles.Title: Who Is Accountable When AI Makes the Decision? - TechGig

stories.Headline: A.M. ATL: Nay, AI - The Atlanta Journal-Constitution
stories.Summary:
A new Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll found that nearly seven in 10 voters want the U.S. government to do more to regulate AI rather than leaving companies to regulate themselves. The results included 61% of Republicans and 82% of Democrats. Three in five respondents also opposed building more data centers in Georgia to meet AI needs. Opposition was more divided by party, with 47% of Republicans and 79% of Democrats somewhat or strongly against additional construction.

Those surveyed who opposed data centers most often cited environmental impact, water and electricity consumption, and quality of life for people living near them. The issue has entered the midterm race in Georgia, where Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has called for a statewide pause on building new data centers. Republican Rick Jackson wants guardrails on the projects and says communities should make their own decisions. Both candidates have expressed varying degrees of reservation about the facilities.

Separately, the newsletter reported on Jerry Ross, a motorist in his 70s who faces felony charges after a clash with cyclists on Sugar Pike Road in Cherokee County earlier this year. Ross was indicted on counts including aggravated battery, two counts of aggravated assault and leaving the scene of an accident, and he faces court-ordered driving restrictions. Video of the encounter, in which one cyclist collided with his vehicle and fell, drew millions of views online. The article also reviewed Georgia rules, which bar cyclists from riding more than two abreast and require motorists to leave at least 3 feet of space when passing.

Articles.Title: A.M. ATL: Nay, AI - The Atlanta Journal-Constitution

stories.Headline: Cyient's Technology Order Intake Rises 39.7% as It Expands AI Capabilities
stories.Summary:
Cyient, the Indian engineering and technology services company, reported its Q2 FY27 results, with the Analytics India Magazine article published on October 23, 2026. The company said its technology order intake rose 39.7% year-on-year to $10.3 million, while its Digital, Engineering and Technology (DET) segment posted its highest EBIT in 10 quarters. The segment's EBIT margin expanded 206 basis points to 14.2%, and its order intake rose 20.8% to $158.4 million, excluding TAO Digital. Group revenue grew 15.3% year-on-year in constant currency to $233.9 million, while DET revenue rose 6.3% to $174.2 million, although organic DET revenue grew only 0.4%.

The company is building CYiNGINE, an agentic AI-enabled lifecycle engineering intelligence platform, under its Intelligent Lifecycle Engineering strategy. It has also set up an intelligent engineering unit aimed at AI-led growth in engineering, service, quality and regulatory workflows. The integration of TAO Digital added platform software and data engineering capabilities, which management says will help pursue enterprise AI and data engineering work with existing customers. Cyient did not disclose a separate revenue figure for its AI offerings. Its semiconductor business recorded 8% sequential revenue growth for a sixth straight quarter, its custom ASIC pipeline passed $100 million, and the group reported free cash flow of ₹214 crore, equal to 140% of profit after tax.

Krishna Bodanapu, Executive Vice Chairman and Managing Director, attributed the order growth to demand for the company's data, AI, digital engineering and Intelligent Engineering Solutions capabilities. He said the industry is in a strong AI-driven demand cycle but that supply is tight, with foundries running at full utilisation, which is pushing up wafer prices and lengthening planning cycles. Cyient expects these conditions to weigh on semiconductor margins in the near term and possibly slow growth in coming quarters. It also expects its high-voltage power products for AI data centres to begin generating substantial revenue in FY28.

The results come as the semiconductor business has expanded its power management portfolio through the $85 million acquisition of Kinetic Technologies. Cyient DLM, the design-led manufacturing arm, grew revenue 26.5% in rupee terms and reported a record order book with a book-to-bill ratio above 1.6 times. The board declared an interim dividend of ₹12 per share. The article does not describe any further steps beyond the expected FY28 ramp of its power products and the near-term margin pressure from supply constraints.

Articles.Title: Cyient's Technology Order Intake Rises 39.7% as It Expands AI Capabilities - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Former OpenAI Exec Raises $215 Mn to Build AI-Powered Drug Research Labs
stories.Summary:
Warp Sciences, a startup founded by former leaders from OpenAI, Meta, Terremoto Biosciences and Devoted Health, has raised $215 million to build AI-powered chemistry research facilities in the United States. The company uses artificial intelligence and robotics to help pharmaceutical and biotechnology firms develop medicines. The funding round was reported on 23 October 2026. The startup says its aim is to speed up drug discovery by combining chemists, AI models and robotic automation in its labs.

Warp will operate as a chemistry contract research organisation, making and testing molecules for its customers' drug discovery programmes. Its initial offering focuses on lead optimisation through analogue synthesis, which means producing molecular variations so researchers can compare properties and identify possible drug candidates. The company also plans to train AI models on data produced by physical experiments, creating a loop between molecular design, lab testing and later research. Warp says it will not build its own drug pipeline and that customers will decide which molecules to pursue and keep control of their programmes. Its chemists will guide experiments as automation takes over more laboratory work.

The round was led by Lightspeed, with participation from Premji Invest, Mayfield, IVP, Lux, Conviction, Menlo Ventures, 01 Advisors and other investors. Angel backers include Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, Databricks co-founder Ion Stoica and Figma CEO Dylan Field. The company was co-founded by Kevin Weil, former Chief Product Officer and Vice-President of Science at OpenAI, along with Solomon Reisberg, Manohar Paluri and DJ Patil. Weil said AI has sped up software engineering and mathematics but has not yet had the same effect on the physical sciences. Patil said the company is building infrastructure for those who develop drugs rather than developing drugs itself.

The launch comes amid concerns about the biotechnology industry's reliance on overseas research services. Warp plans to offer US-based chemistry services with a focus on speed, intellectual property protection and pricing, which it says will give drug developers more control over where sensitive research takes place. Reisberg said he had worked with overseas chemistry partners that delivered speed and value but worried about protecting intellectual property. Paluri said each experiment should make the next one smarter by linking design, execution and analysis. The articles do not give a launch date for the facilities or details on their location.

Articles.Title: Former OpenAI Exec Raises $215 Mn to Build AI-Powered Drug Research Labs - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Infosys AI Revenue Rises 29% in Q2, FY27 Growth Guidance Cut
stories.Summary:
Infosys reported its September-quarter results, and its AI revenue grew 29% sequentially, now making up 10.5% of total revenue. In the same report, the company cut its full-year FY27 revenue growth guidance to 1%-2% in constant currency, down from 1.5%-3%. Second-quarter revenue came to $5.145 billion, up 1.5% year on year and 1.2% sequentially in constant-currency terms, with operating margin holding at 21%. The figures were published by Analytics India Magazine on October 23, 2026.

The company recorded $5.2 billion in large-deal total contract value, with 62% classified as net new business. Those bookings included a mega deal worth more than $2 billion. Infosys also kept its operating margin guidance at 20%-22% for the year. Free cash flow for the quarter was $928 million, down 15.7% year on year. The article notes that the deal value points to future business, but its effect on revenue will depend on how quickly those contracts ramp up.

CEO and Managing Director Salil Parekh said the company had strong large deals, including the mega deal, and pointed to AI revenue growth in the quarter. Chief Financial Officer Jayesh Sanghrajka said the company had maintained margins despite a volatile operating environment. Sanghrajka attributed the stable margin to cost and operational efficiency measures along with continued investment. The article quotes both executives on the results and frames the reported outlook against cautious client spending, slower decision-making, and pressure on traditional IT services pricing.

The article places these results within a wider industry question about whether AI will cut the hours needed to deliver existing contracts faster than it creates new consulting, implementation, and engineering demand. It also mentions Infosys's partnership with Cognition to deploy the Devin AI software engineer across internal engineering operations and client engagements. The piece says the sector still needs to show whether vendors can win enough new business to offset those efficiencies. Beyond the guidance cut, the article does not describe further steps or timelines for the company.

Articles.Title: Infosys AI Revenue Rises 29% in Q2, FY27 Growth Guidance Cut - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: How Can AI Improve Accessible Education for All?
stories.Summary:
A visually impaired student in Pune, Seema Kharad, found it hard to get accessible study material while preparing for a PhD in political science, since many of the books and academic documents she needed were not available as audiobooks. Yogen Ghodke, an AI solutions engineer based in New York, responded by building ListenToMe, an app that converts study material into audio, and Kharad tested early versions and pointed out problems. Ghodke built an initial version using AI and spent around two months refining it with her feedback. The app has since attracted users beyond India, and the article reports that it was publicly available for only three or four weeks at the time of the interview. ListenToMe uses optical character recognition to extract text from documents and text-to-speech technology to turn that text into audio.

Users can upload PDFs, photos of documents, handwritten notes, and other supported formats from their phones. According to Ghodke, the app supports around 30 languages, including English, Marathi, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Assamese and Nepali. It is currently free with a daily processing limit of 250 pages, and Ghodke is considering a plan priced at around ₹149 that would allow up to 500 pages a day. At the time of the interview about 1,600 people had signed up and about 1,000 had submitted documents, with new sign-ups reaching around 200 a day. Ghodke said uploaded PDFs are deleted once processing finishes, while generated audio files are kept for a few days before automatic deletion.

Ghodke is the person behind the app and says he funds its operating costs himself, running the service on a Mac Mini. He estimates current processing costs at around one US cent per page and wants to reduce that to ₹1 for every 100 pages. He also said that the daily limits are partly meant to stop a small number of heavy users from using up resources needed by others, and he relies on user feedback to catch errors, such as figure numbers being read digit by digit. He described the next phase as the business side of the project, including formalising the company, raising funds, hiring people to improve the models, and reaching universities, student organisations and NGOs. He is also exploring venture capital and disability-focused funding, and he is working out how to start a company in the US while still a student.

The article ties the project to Ghodke's experience of accessibility provisions in the US, such as wheelchair ramps and accessible doors, which shaped his thinking about applying similar attention to AI-powered education. It describes ListenToMe as an example of how technology can close gaps for students with disabilities, and it notes particular interest in reaching schools in India, where affordability could determine adoption. One model under consideration would have NGOs help fund access for people who cannot pay, while subscriptions in markets such as the US cover costs. The article does not say whether any such funding has been secured.

Articles.Title: How Can AI Improve Accessible Education for All? - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Red Hat opens Singapore AI centre to scale deployment
stories.Summary:
Red Hat has opened an Asia Pacific AI Centre of Excellence in Singapore, with support from the Singapore Economic Development Board. The hub is meant to help organisations across the region move AI projects from trials into production, using open source tools and engineering support. It will also build technical skills in Singapore and serve customers across Asia Pacific. The article was published on 23 October 2026.

The centre includes engineers, forward-deployed engineers, architects and project managers who focus on supporting AI and machine learning deployments in customer environments. Its engineering teams will create software architectures for recurring industry problems and contribute code to upstream open source projects covering deployment, runtime optimisation and platform management. Red Hat says the centre will also offer training in software engineering, automation, cloud-native development and DevSecOps for customers and partners in Singapore and the wider region. Red Hat set up the centre in response to rising regional demand for AI systems that businesses can deploy.

Red Hat is also working with the Singapore Defence Science and Technology Agency, which plans to use the centre to explore and co-develop AI and cloud-native systems for defence applications. The joint work is expected to cover AI, cloud computing, application modernisation and edge computing across multi-cloud environments. It will include architectures and operating practices for DevSecOps and day-two operations for AI and cloud systems at scale, in both on-premise and off-premise settings. Red Hat says locating the centre in Singapore should shorten the feedback loop between customers, partners and its core product teams.

Daniel Aw, Vice President and General Manager of Red Hat Asia Pacific, said companies in the region are shifting their approach to AI, moving from experimentation toward execution. Yueh Chinn Seah, Vice President of Digital Industry Singapore, said the centre strengthens Singapore's position as an AI hub and creates opportunities for local talent. DSTA said its work with Red Hat is part of its effort to test and apply newer technologies to defence systems and operations. Red Hat says the facility aligns with Singapore's National AI Strategy and is intended to contribute talent, technology and operational use cases to the local ecosystem.

Articles.Title: Red Hat opens Singapore AI centre to scale deployment - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: State CIOs raise the bar for AI results
stories.Summary:
State technology leaders face a shift from proving that AI is ready to proving that it delivers results, a theme that ran through NASCIO's 2026 annual conference. Beth Howen, Executive Managing Director for State, Local, and Education at NTT DATA North America, made the point in a video interview produced by Scoop News Group for StateScoop and underwritten by NTT DATA. She said the central question is how quickly these tools can produce measurable public value. The article frames this as the real challenge beyond simply moving AI into production.

The 2026 NASCIO State CIO Survey reports that 82% of states had generative AI projects in production. It also found that 64% of CIOs named agentic AI as the emerging technology most likely to have the greatest impact over the next two to three years. Howen described agentic systems as a move from AI that answers questions to AI that can take action, which raises questions about where automation belongs and how its risks should be controlled. She cautioned against automating a task just because the technology makes it possible.

According to Howen, some processes must be redesigned before automation will work well, while others need modernized systems or stronger data governance first. The aim, she said, is not to run the most pilots but to move AI into production where it can create value safely. She argued that governance should guide these choices, with safeguards built into how AI is designed, bought, and operated. The same results-focused approach applies to cybersecurity, where she said understaffed states cannot simply hire their way out of growing threats. Automation, AI-assisted security operations, zero-trust principles, and managed services can extend the capacity of internal teams.

Howen also urged states to reassess blanket "cloud first" strategies and decide case by case where workloads belong, saying not everything belongs in the cloud. She called for modernization that is mission-driven rather than personality-driven, backed by measurable outcomes and institutional governance. She said technology strategies are more likely to survive leadership changes when they are tied to broader goals than to technology alone. The article notes that technology leaders expect successful AI adoption to depend less on flashy pilots and more on reusable infrastructure, disciplined governance, and trustworthy data.

Articles.Title: State CIOs raise the bar for AI results - StateScoop

stories.Headline: AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost
stories.Summary:
A Chinese-speaking attacker used three AI harnesses along with open-weight and public AI models to target 105 e-commerce sites over five days in September. The autonomous hacking system compromised at least 27 companies, often within a day and at most within hours. Gambit Security, which discovered the campaign, said malicious agents stole at least 600,000 payment card records from two of the companies and installed credit-card skimmers on five websites. The company also said some degree of illicit access was gained at the rest, including at least one Fortune 500 firm, and the attacker's total cost averaged $25.46 per completed target.

Gambit Security's co-founder and chief research officer, Sa'ar Elias, said the scale of the campaign was remarkable for a single week, and that work once requiring a coordinated team of skilled attackers could now be done by one person with little prior knowledge. The article places this within a wider trend of agentic AI speeding up vulnerability research, with a sharp rise in CVE assignments and attackers increasingly automating attacks. In a separate lab test, researchers at Silverfort used an orchestrating agent and publicly available Claude Opus models, and their simulated attacker gained complete domain control in eight minutes. Silverfort's Colin Ferris argued that the barrier to entry is falling and that a basic foothold rather than exotic skill is what the attacks require.

Prices in underground markets have dropped as well, according to threat intelligence firm Flashpoint, which said the average price of initial access fell from just over $1,400 to $429. Flashpoint also reported that 28 percent of victims paid ransoms in the first half of 2026, while ransomware activity still grew by 45 percent. Ian Gray, Flashpoint's vice president of intelligence, said the cost drop was measured at the initial-access stage and that AI was making other stages of attacks faster and easier to scale. Elias said attackers can now launch increasingly sophisticated attacks at very low marginal cost, and that defending against every attempt can quickly become economically unsustainable.

Experts quoted in the article say companies cannot assume obscurity or a small attack surface will protect them, since any internet-connected part of a business or partner will be targeted. XBOW's chief information security officer, Albert Ziegler, said these attacks succeed because sites have not been hardened enough, and that protecting a few crown-jewel sites is not sufficient. Ferris suggested focusing on common paths agents exploit, such as overprivileged accounts, reused credentials, and unmanaged service accounts, and automating access decisions so humans do not slow responses. Elias advised companies to identify their most important business processes, protect them, and measure security spending by how well it protects operations rather than by the number of threats or tools managed.

Articles.Title: AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: As Rogue AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage
stories.Summary:
Insurers are divided over whether to cover losses tied to artificial intelligence, after a series of data breaches this year. Some carriers now sell proactive AI policies that protect enterprises against unprovoked attacks or against attacks launched by AI agents that go rogue. Other carriers are deliberately avoiding the risk, which leaves businesses to work out how to handle it themselves. Dark Reading reported the story on October 23, 2026, and the piece was written by Stephen Lawton. Coverage for attacks by AI agents is uncommon, and many companies wrongly assume their cyber or liability policies already include it.

Often they do not. Insurers have also warned that enterprises are adopting AI and AI agents faster than they are building governance for them. Incidents such as the recent attacks attributed to OpenAI against Hugging Face and other servers have increased those concerns. In 2025, AI-related coverage was still in its early stages, and generic errors and omissions, directors and officers, and liability policies offered little protection against AI's actual risks. Specialty firms now offer AI coverage through endorsements, technology errors and omissions language, or standalone policies.

Armilla, Coalition, Corgi Insurance, Cowbell, Munich Re, and Beazley are named as providers of purpose-built policies or specialized coverage. Meanwhile, Chubb, Travelers, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, and W.R. Berkley are adopting the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsement, which removes coverage for bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising from generative AI, according to Insurance Business. The article advises executives, especially chief financial officers, general counsels, and chief information security officers, to review their policies before year-end renewals, check for exclusions, and meet with insurers offering AI-specific products. It also recommends auditing network guardrails, requiring supply chain partners to carry similar protections, limiting AI systems to the minimum rights they need, and monitoring AI agents as closely as service accounts. Underwriters judge eligibility by looking at a company's overall set of controls, including human review, guardrails, and rules, according to Armilla's Andrew Correll.

Beazley's Craig Linton says its application contains dozens of questions covering about 15 security controls. Linton also warns that employees may use unsupervised AI on corporate and personal devices, creating shadow AI risks. Corgi Insurance advises checking whether policies explicitly cover hallucinated, inaccurate, or biased model outputs, since older technology policies may be silent on them. Cowbell's Jack Kudale says buyers should ask whether a policy covers non-malicious system failures and unauthorized disclosures without intrusion, and he urges protecting infrastructure, data pipelines, and supply chains beyond direct vendors. Kudale says he worries most about the supply chain.

Articles.Title: As Rogue AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: In Depth: China’s Smartphones Get Pricier as AI Strains Chip Supply
stories.Summary:
Leading smartphone makers, including Apple, Huawei, and Xiaomi, unveiled new flagship models ahead of China's National Day holiday in October 2026, but instead of offering more power at stable prices, they raised prices across much of their lineups. Xiaomi's 18 Pro began at 5,999 yuan, up 1,000 yuan, while Huawei's Mate 90 standard model cost nearly 28% more than the previous generation. The 2-terabyte iPhone 18 Pro Max carried a price 3,500 yuan higher than its predecessor. Local brands also leaned toward premium versions, offered fewer low-end options, and raised prices on existing phones rather than discounting older models.

The main cause is a supply squeeze driven by the artificial intelligence boom, as data center operators compete for memory chips. According to TrendForce data cited in the report, server DRAM contract prices rose about 64% cumulatively in the second half of 2025, and a further cumulative increase of about 270% is projected for 2026, with suppliers prioritizing AI data centers over consumer electronics. Qualcomm China Chairman Frank Meng said he had never seen memory prices rise four or five times in a year, and he expects high prices to persist for some time, though he does not foresee significant increases ending before the end of 2027. Omdia estimated that memory made up nearly 60% of the bill of materials for phones priced below $400 in the first quarter of 2026, which hits budget devices hardest.

The timing is difficult because China's market is contracting, leaving less room to absorb higher costs or persuade buyers to pay more. Counterpoint reported that more than 40% of smartphone models saw price increases this year, lifting the global average retail price by 15%, with some models rising nearly 100%, while China's retail increase was more moderate at about 10%. China's smartphone shipments fell 4.3% year on year to about 66 million units in the second quarter of 2026, the fifth straight quarterly decline, and a double-digit annual decline is projected. Shipments of phones priced below $100 nearly halved, and Oppo's Realme withdrew from China while Meizu suspended domestic hardware projects. IDC's Francisco Jeronimo said the era of the cheap smartphone has ended, and that vendors with scale and supply leverage will be the winners.

Competition among major brands is also shifting. Huawei led the Chinese market with a 22.6% share and grew shipments nearly 25% in the second quarter, while Apple held 18.1% and grew about 20%, and Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, and Honor all posted year-on-year declines. Hardware differentiation is getting harder, and Counterpoint's Lin Keyu argued that camera competition increasingly comes down to software. Foldables and AI features are the two main bets, with IDC projecting 22.9 million foldable shipments in 2026, still only about 2% to 3% of the market, and Apple entering the category with the iPhone Duo at $1,999. Meng said the next phase will test which companies built the most complete ecosystems, though no maker has yet gained a decisive lead in AI.

Articles.Title: In Depth: China’s Smartphones Get Pricier as AI Strains Chip Supply - Caixin Global

stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: China’s first fully AI-generated feature film to hit cinemas on Friday
stories.Summary:
China's first fully AI-generated feature film, Sanxingdui, is set to open in cinemas on Friday, October 23, serving as a test of whether audiences will accept AI-made movies on the big screen. The film, which received a theatrical release permit, draws on the mysteries of the ancient Chinese civilization and tells a story spanning the past and a future shaped by artificial intelligence. Its creators say the release is an early effort to move AI-generated filmmaking from short online videos and dramas to cinemas, where standards for storytelling and production quality are higher. The project was developed over more than two years and involved generating more than 1.2 million preliminary images and more than 100 full-film iterations. The film cost over 10 million yuan, roughly $1.5 million, to make.

The production followed a conventional film-industry process rather than simply entering a prompt and letting a machine produce a movie. Specialized teams covered screenwriting, directing, art design, cinematography, lighting, sound and editing, dividing responsibilities across 17 professional functions in a virtual production environment. Jiang Defu, the film's producer and COO of Bona Film Group, said images that looked acceptable on a phone did not always hold up on a cinema screen. Reviewers examined the film frame by frame, and the team reworked it from beginning to end at least five times. Early efforts focused on whether certain scenes could be created at all, while later work concentrated on making them convincing.

Producer Qu Jixiaojiang told the Global Times that the team hopes audiences will feel the 100 minutes of runtime are worth their money. Online reactions to the trailer included skepticism about paying for images that can seemingly be created cheaply, and Qu said she understood those reservations. She said the team will judge its work by viewers' responses, both positive and negative. Qu also compared the reception of AI film to earlier shifts in cinema, such as the arrival of motion pictures and the move from film to digital cameras, which both faced resistance. The film has been presented at the Cannes Film Festival, and Malaysia is also scheduled to release it on Friday, while discussions are under way in Russia and France.

The story takes its inspiration from the Sanxingdui ruins in Sichuan Province, known for bronze masks and sculptures associated with the ancient Shu civilization. The film uses mysterious symbols engraved on Sanxingdui bronzes as a narrative link between that ancient world and a future confronting superintelligent AI. The creators consulted Sanxingdui experts during development to separate established archaeological evidence from unresolved academic questions. Qu said technical novelty alone will not decide the film's success, and that the goal is for viewers to become absorbed in the story rather than trying to identify which images were AI-generated.

Articles.Title: China’s first fully AI-generated feature film to hit cinemas on Friday - Global Times

stories.Headline: Wuzhen Summit Puts Spotlight on Tongxiang's Expanding AI Industry
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit will open on Nov. 2, bringing technology leaders, researchers and companies to the historic water town. Ahead of the event, reporters visited seven Tongxiang-based companies working in robotics, intelligent vehicles, synthetic data, industrial automation, logistics and computing infrastructure. These firms are expanding AI applications from commercial cleaning and autonomous delivery to industrial control and data-center cooling. The summit is a chance to demonstrate how local companies are commercializing AI technologies for customers at home and abroad.

CenoBots, a Tongxiang-based company, has sold cleaning robots in more than 40 countries and regions, with customers including Changi Airport, Tesco, the University of Minnesota and Novo Nordisk. This year, the company supplied about 600 autonomous cleaning robots for Tesco Express stores across the United Kingdom. CenoBots has expanded its research, development and production facilities in Tongxiang from approximately 3,000 square meters in its early years to more than 20,000 square meters. TEEMO makes drive-by-wire skateboard chassis and core components for autonomous vehicles used in last-mile delivery, patrols and logistics, and its customers span the United States, the Middle East, India and Russia. Dayan Technology, founded in Tongxiang in May 2025, provides synthetic-data and toolchain services for autonomous-driving and humanoid-robotics companies.

Freetech develops intelligent-driving systems and 4D imaging radar for passenger and commercial vehicles, and its technology has been selected for hundreds of vehicle programs. At its intelligent-manufacturing base in Wuzhen, an in-house AI system reads customer orders and calculates components and materials needed for each production line, increasing overall efficiency by more than 20%. Shuhan Technologies, founded in 2019, provides on-premises industrial AI for chemical plants, energy facilities and wastewater-treatment systems. At a coal chemical plant with annual capacity of 1.2 million metric tons, Shuhan said its system reduced raw-material consumption by 6% and generated more than 176 million yuan, or about $26 million, in annualized economic benefits, while reducing carbon emissions by more than 500,000 metric tons. SynthCool develops two-phase liquid-cooling systems that support heat dissipation of more than 3,000 watts per chip and heat flux above 250 watts per square centimeter.

CenoBots co-founder and vice president Shen Jizhong said cleaning robots are appearing in more settings, much like electric vehicles becoming a familiar sight on the roads. TEEMO director of operations Zhang Yongjian said autonomous delivery vehicles have strong potential in overseas markets where distances are long and last-mile delivery is difficult to staff. Freetech founder and CEO Dr. Zhang Lin said transportation combined with a specialized function will be an important direction for the future, with potential applications including robots, elder-care vehicles, mining equipment and agricultural machinery. Shuhan Chief Technology Officer Zhai Zhengjun said all industrial process challenges can be framed as control and optimization problems. SynthCool general manager Zhu Zhijiang said heat dissipation is infrastructure.

Articles.Title: Tongxiang tech firms showcase AI applications ahead of Wuzhen Summit - China Daily

stories.Headline: Wyndham Deploys AI Agents to Boost Hotel Bookings and Cut Franchisee Costs
stories.Summary:
Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, the hotel franchising company, said in an investor presentation released on Wednesday, October 21, that its artificial intelligence tools improve franchisees' top lines, reduce operating costs and enhance the guest experience. The company operates about 8,500 hotels across 100 countries on six continents under 25 hotel brands. Its guest agentic AI solutions, including Agentic Voice AI and AI Messaging, cover the path from initial interest to checkout. According to the presentation, these tools answer all hotel calls autonomously and instantly, raising customer satisfaction by 450 basis points and voice conversion by 500 basis points.

Wyndham AI Concierge, the company's AI-powered voice platform, now handles calls autonomously at more than 1,700 hotels worldwide, a 17% increase from the previous quarter. Wyndham has also made its rooms bookable through Google's AI Mode, OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Meta's Muse, Instinct and OpenAI's dots. The presentation says the AI tools also benefit hotel owners financially. The Wyndham Connect guest engagement platform has produced 16% year-to-date growth in owner upsell revenue, while AI Concierge bookings have lifted average daily rate by 15% at participating hotels. Wyndham Connect is now deployed at more than 5,100 hotels.

President and CEO Geoff Ballotti described the investments during the company's third quarter earnings call on Thursday, October 22. He said the company keeps investing in technology that helps franchisees grow revenue, lower costs and improve the guest experience. Ballotti also said the platform has been handling tens of thousands of calls that would otherwise have been missed, with no hold times for guests. He added that franchisee profitability and engagement remain the company's top priority. The articles do not describe any regulatory requirements or changes to franchise agreements connected to these tools, and they do not say what further steps Wyndham plans beyond the current deployments.

Articles.Title: Wyndham Deploys AI Agents to Boost Hotel Bookings and Cut Franchisee Costs

stories.Headline: China issues guidelines to promote employment amid AI advances - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China's State Council General Office has issued guidelines aimed at making the country's job market adapt to advances in artificial intelligence, according to a Xinhua report datelined Beijing on October 23. The guidelines seek to use AI to create jobs, raise the quality of employment and encourage entrepreneurship, while also reducing the job losses that AI applications may cause. The document sets out 18 tasks spread across six areas. Those areas cover expanding AI's potential to generate jobs, making AI adoption more friendly to employment, improving workers' digital skills, strengthening employment services, and protecting labor and social security.

The guidelines call for more job opportunities in emerging fields and for support to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises so they can keep and grow their workforces. They also encourage new kinds of work and business startups in the AI sector and the creation of new AI-related occupations. In traditional industries, the authorities are told to look for ways AI can add jobs and to limit the job displacement that AI tools might cause. A further measure would set up a mechanism to assess the employment risks linked to adopting AI.

The articles do not give figures on how many jobs are expected to be created or lost. The guidelines also stress improving the rules that protect workers when they work alongside machines, so that human-machine collaboration does not weaken their rights. They call for stronger social security coverage for people in flexible employment and in new forms of employment. In addition, they direct officials to refine how income is distributed so that pay arrangements keep pace with AI-driven changes.

The articles do not name any officials beyond the issuing office or say when specific measures will take effect. The announcement comes as China pushes forward with AI development across its economy, and the articles frame it as an effort to balance the technology's benefits against its disruption to workers. The articles do not describe any reaction from business groups or labor advocates, nor do they provide details on implementation timelines or enforcement. Further steps are not described in the reporting.

Articles.Title: China issues guidelines to promote employment amid AI advances - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Nasdaq dives more than 750 points as investors worry massive AI spending won't pay off
stories.Summary:
Stocks fell sharply on Thursday as investors grew uneasy about whether the huge sums being poured into artificial intelligence will ever pay off, while oil prices also climbed. Shortly before the close, the Nasdaq Composite, where many AI-exposed technology firms are listed, dropped 751 points, or 2.8%, before recovering somewhat to finish 694 points lower at 26,009. The broader S&P 500 declined 1.2%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up by less than 0.1%. Wall Street analysts said the worry centers on the heavy borrowing AI companies are taking on to fund data center construction and on whether those companies will earn the profits investors expect. Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, wrote in a research note that AI spending is far outpacing operating cash flow, so companies depend on equity and debt investors to cover it, and those markets are growing less willing to provide that funding.

He added that slowing debt issuance as credit tightens could make it harder to finance the buildout. The Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan think tank, estimates that AI infrastructure will cost more than $10 trillion between 2025 and 2032. Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics, said that would be the largest wave of investment in U.S. history, bigger than the 19th-century railroads and the dot-com boom. Although many of the leading AI players remain highly profitable, investors are re-evaluating those enormous costs even as their share prices have soared. Earnings reports added to the pressure, with mixed results across the sector.

Meta Platforms, which is promoting its Muse AI agent, fell 7% after its revenue beat estimates but its profit came in short. Tesla dropped 3.1% despite stronger-than-expected summer profits, because its revenue was weaker than analysts had forecast. Separately, oil prices rose on concerns about escalating conflict in Iran, adding to the selloff. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, traded at $99.21 a barrel, up 2.1%, while Brent crude, the international standard, was near $113 a barrel, up 3.7%.

Articles.Title: Nasdaq dives more than 750 points as investors worry massive AI spending won't pay off

stories.Headline: St. John’s Students Teach High Schoolers How to Keep the ‘Human’ in AI
stories.Summary:
St. John's University hosted an AI College Day in Jamaica, New York, where college freshmen taught visiting high school students how to use artificial intelligence ethically. The students came from Bedford-Stuyvesant New Beginnings Charter School, and the event was built around presentations that freshmen in adjunct professor Omar Lopez's AI-focused section of First Year Seminar 1000 developed over the semester. Among the visitors was 11th grader Xavier Martinez, who said he uses ChatGPT for essays and assignments, and 10th grader Adalin Dominguez, who hoped to learn how the technology could help her learn rather than take away from her learning. The presentations covered topics ranging from identifying AI bias and fact-checking its output to protecting personal information and preparing for the job market.

One group, led by freshman Benjamin Shakov, focused on resumes, since employers increasingly use AI to screen applicants. According to Shakov, ethical use goes beyond taking what the tool produces and turning it in as one's own work. Students discussed disclosing when they used AI and editing its output instead of relying on raw, unedited content. Shakov said adding a human level to AI-generated work was a key lesson. That emphasis echoes concerns raised by Pope Leo XIV in Magnifica humanitas, his first encyclical letter, published in May 2026, which stressed that technological progress should stay centered on the human person.

Lopez, who teaches the course, said students should treat AI neither as something to fear nor as a substitute for their own abilities. He compared it to the early internet, when some people refused to learn it and later found themselves behind. The program is now in its third semester, and St. John's plans to expand it in the spring. The expanded version would invite students from multiple Catholic, public, and private high schools to campus for a larger conference.

Articles.Title: St. John’s Students Teach High Schoolers How to Keep the ‘Human’ in AI
